story: I thought it over for a long time before I finally spoke:“I agree — one hundred million truly satisfies me.”The money arrived.A spider dropped onto me.“Wò cào!” (a Chinese curse)I died.
answer: I had entered a supernatural deal: after receiving the one hundred million, every sentence I spoke for the rest of my life had to end rhyming with “yì,” the Chinese word for that sum (roughly the English “ee” sound); the moment I broke the rule, I would die.I knew the rule. After weighing my words, I sealed the deal with “agree” and “me,” both ending in that sound, and the money really did arrive.When the spider dropped onto me, the fright knocked the rule out of my head, and I blurted out “Wò cào!” That exclamation does not end with the rhyme, and the deal took my life on the spot.
hints: The money is real, but taking it attached a rule that never stops applying.
The rule governs the words spoken aloud; the spider only made me forget to follow it.
Every sentence I speak must end rhyming with “yì” (the “ee” sound); my startled cry broke the deal.

title: A Wall of Certificates
story: I came home with a new award certificate, planning to hang it on the wall. Dad, who used to beam at that wall of certificates, wore a look of gloom today. Mom, on the other hand, couldn’t stop grinning.
answer: I was an excellent student, and the walls of our home were covered with award certificates. Every time Dad looked at that wall he smiled, and I always believed Dad was proud of me. Then one day I brought home a new certificate, and when Mom pulled down the old ones to make room, she stumbled upon the private money Dad had hidden behind the certificates. Mom gave Dad a furious scolding and confiscated the savings hidden across the whole wall, grinning from ear to ear; Dad, for all his painstaking scheming, had labored for nothing, and he could not help sighing over and over — a whole wall of secret savings, and he had never let himself spend a cent of it.
hints: When Dad looked at the certificates, part of what was on his mind was what lay behind them.
The new certificate needed room, so Mom took the old ones down.
Dad’s secret savings were hidden behind the old certificates, and Mom discovered and confiscated them along with those.

title: Regret
story: She is getting married. The groom wears the face I used to have.I once dated her, and I had imagined putting that ring on her finger myself.But after the accident, whenever she saw me there was only fear.At the wedding, I still sent them my blessing.
answer: My twin brother and I fell for her at the same time. Keeping it from her, we posed as one person and took turns dating her. She believed the boyfriend who came to see her each time was one and the same man.Later I was in an accident that badly injured my face and changed my looks. The next time she saw me, before I could explain who I was, her face filled with fear and she backed away. She took me for a stranger.I read that moment as proof she could not accept what I had become. I never told her the truth; I chose to bow out and let my brother carry on with her under that boyfriend’s identity.In the end she married my brother, never knowing that the person who had dated her had really been two people. All I could do was carry the part of the past she knew nothing about, and send her and my brother my blessing.
hints: The groom and I once looked exactly alike, but she never knew there had been two of us.
The accident changed my face, and when she saw me again she did not recognize me.
The twins took turns playing one and the same boyfriend; after I was injured I withdrew, and my brother carried the identity on.

title: The ‘Move Your Car’ Call
story: My colleague said he was dropping out of the race, and insisted on buying me drinks.That night, a ‘move your car’ phone call cost me my promotion.Later, he made executive and brought his wife to meet me.When I saw her face, I finally understood who had really stood that round of drinks.
answer: My colleague and I were competing for the same management position. Before the results came out, my colleague told me he was withdrawing and invited me out for drinks, and my guard came down.Over the meal I received a call asking me to move my car. Sure I only had to nudge it a few feet in the parking lot, I drove after drinking — and hit another car. The woman at the wheel called the police, and the drunk-driving incident made the company strike me from the promotion.The whole thing had been arranged by my colleague. My colleague had his wife drive over and block my car in, then place the ‘move your car’ call to me; he himself kept me company over drinks, waiting for the point where, drunk, I would still decide to drive. My colleague’s wife was right there waiting in the parking lot.In the end my colleague won the promotion. When he brought his wife to meet me, I recognized the woman driver from that night’s collision — the one who had then called the police — and only then did I understand that the ‘I’m withdrawing’ drinks had been a trap from start to finish.
hints: When my colleague bought me those drinks, he had no real intention of withdrawing.
The ‘move your car’ call led drunk me straight into the driver’s seat.
The woman driver who called the police was my colleague’s wife, working with him in advance so that I would move my car after drinking.

title: The Final Beat
story: When the music stopped, the audience still had their faces turned upward.She took one step to the side.No applause came; the screams arrived first.She died.
answer: She was a blind high-wire performer who judged her endpoint from sound cues given by the accompanist. At the end of the wire stood a platform, and she had an agreement with the accompanist: when she reached the platform, the music would stop, and she would step sideways onto it to close the show.For this performance she wore no safety harness. While she was still midway along the wire, the power suddenly cut out and the accompaniment stopped. She took the unexpected silence for the agreed endpoint signal and took one step to the side.There was no platform beside her yet. Her foot found nothing, and she fell. The audience watched with their faces turned up, unable to stop something that happened in an instant.
hints: The audience looked up because the performance was happening high off the ground.
The music stopping was itself a signal, telling her she could leave the wire.
The blind wire walker mistook the blackout’s silence for her arrival at the end, and stepped toward a platform that was not yet there.

title: The Lure
story: He set the item on the table, and in that moment I decided to buy it.Yet I kept asking about the price, and asked him to sit down and talk things over slowly.Just as he was talking at his happiest, several men walked over and took him away.They were the ones I had been waiting for all along.
answer: My father was killed in a home invasion, and our heirloom jade pendant was stolen along with it. I had always wanted to recover the pendant and find the killer from that day.I posted a high-priced wanted-to-buy listing online. He contacted me, saying he had a similar jade pendant. When we met and he laid it on the table, I recognized the fine little scratch only family members knew about, and confirmed it was ours.I quietly contacted the police, then kept haggling and kept him seated, stalling the deal until the officers arrived. The men who took him away were the police.The pendant carried the lead into the investigation; the police then traced how it had passed through his hands and reopened the old case, confirming that he had taken part in that home invasion.
hints: My high-priced buying post was laid as bait, meant to draw out whoever held the item.
I had recognized it long before, yet I kept negotiating to drag out the time.
The pendant stolen when my father was killed had surfaced; I held the seller in place and waited for the police to arrive and investigate.

title: Such a Good Mimic
story: Late at night, my screams always drew the neighbors in.From the balcony there was another voice, crying out along with me, time after time.My husband opened the door, gave a brief explanation, and the neighbors left with a laugh.The moment the door shut, my husband came back to stand before me.
answer: My husband had been beating me at home for a long time. On the balcony we kept a parrot; after hearing my screams so often, it had learned to cry out along with me. Both sounds had drawn the neighbors’ attention.When someone knocked, my husband would stop, plant himself in the doorway, point at the parrot, and explain that it loved imitating sounds from the television — what the neighbors had just heard was only the bird. The parrot would let out the very same cry, making the story all the more convincing.Under my husband’s threats, I dared not ask for help in front of him. The neighbors never saw my condition; they believed my husband’s explanation, took the whole thing for a misunderstanding, and left with a laugh.The screams that might have brought help were smothered by the parrot’s mimicry. Once the door closed, the violence continued.
hints: The voice on the balcony could mimic me, but could not explain how the sound had been learned.
My husband used the parrot on the balcony to explain away my screams, and kept himself in the doorway blocking the neighbors’ view.
The abuse was real; once the parrot had learned my screams, my husband used it to keep up the appearance that no one at home was hurt.

title: Fireflies
story: The car broke down, and Dad got out.Where the headlights shone there were many small points of light. I wanted to go catch fireflies, but I couldn’t get the door beside me to open no matter how hard I pulled.Dad suddenly ran off into the distance, and the points of light went with him.I waited all night. He never came back.
answer: At night, the car broke down on a remote mountain road, and Dad got out to check it. I was still very young and stayed in the back seat.Dad saw wolves closing in. Their eyes reflected the headlights, and through the window glass I took the distant points of light for fireflies. I wanted to get out and catch the fireflies, so Dad locked the rear doors and kept me inside the car.Dad tried to draw the approaching wolves away from the car and ran off in another direction. The wolves chased after Dad and left, and all I saw was the points of light moving away too.After daybreak people found the car and rescued me. Dad, far away, was attacked by the wolves and never came back alive. All that night, I had no idea what Dad was facing.
hints: The points of light were not glowing by themselves — they were reflecting the headlights.
After Dad locked the doors and ran into the distance, the points of light moved after him.
The ‘fireflies’ were wolves’ eyes; the father kept his daughter in the car and drew the wolves away himself.

title: The Boat Was Right There
story: Five friends took a yacht out to sea, and after anchoring, one after another they jumped into the water.The boat stayed right beside them the whole time.A few hours later, all five were dead, and the boat was empty.
answer: The weather was scorching, and after anchoring, all five couldn’t wait to jump in and cool off with a swim — forgetting to lower the boarding ladder stowed aboard.The yacht’s gunwale was high and its hull smooth near the waterline, with nothing to grip or stand on. The five friends tried again and again and never made it up; with everyone in the water, there was no one left to lower the ladder for the others.The five friends’ communications gear and belongings were still on board, and the boat sat on open water far from anyone, so no rescue came in time. All five struggled beside the boat until their strength ran out, and they drowned one after another.The boat that killed the five friends stayed in sight the whole time; the only thing missing was a ladder that could have been let down from on board.
hints: All five had gone into the water; not a single person was left aboard.
The boat’s side was high and smooth, with no foothold they could grab.
The boarding ladder stayed stowed on the boat, and with everyone in the water there was no one to lower it.

title: The Promises
story: In that high-rise by the sea, fifteen residents died one after another within a single month.A woman took advantage of the falling prices to buy a sea-facing apartment, and handed the keys to her father.A few days later, she walked into a police station and confessed that those residents had all died at her hand.She said she had finally fulfilled her father’s two promises.
answer: Father and daughter had once lived in a small cottage with a view of the sea. The father had promised that one day the daughter would live in a big house overlooking the whole of it. Then a high-rise went up across from them and shut out their view.The father worked himself to the bone for a sea-facing apartment in that tower, but the money was never enough, and his body finally gave out. So the daughter decided to use murders to drive the building’s prices down. The daughter killed fifteen residents one after another, turning the place into something people feared. When some owners grew desperate to sell, the daughter was at last able to buy one of the apartments with her savings.The daughter handed the keys to her father. Learning that the daughter had bought the apartment right on the heels of a string of serial murders, the father pressed her until the daughter confessed everything. Already gravely ill, the father could not live with what the daughter had done, and before he died he made her promise to turn herself in.After her father’s death, the daughter carried out the final promise. The first promise was living in a big house facing the sea; the second was bearing the consequences of the crimes committed to obtain that home.
hints: The woman’s purchase was directly tied to the murders in the building.
Her father could never have afforded the apartment; the murders made some owners desperate to sell.
She killed to drive the prices down, and once her father learned of it, he left one last demand: turn yourself in.

title: The Crescent Moon
story: Mother has grown old; it is my turn to go out and find food.She always warned me to be careful of the man in the wolf skin.I was caught and tied up beside the fire. The firelight lit up the crescent on my shoulder, and the man suddenly threw down his torch and untied me.I lunged at him.He never raised his gun; all that fell from his chest was a torn family photograph.
answer: This is a fictional tale in which wolves understand humans and can raise human children. The mother who raised me was a wolf.Ten years earlier, a hunter had killed the wolf king and had the wolf king’s skin made into a cloak. The wolf’s cubs later died in the hunter’s traps as well. Bereft of her children, the mother wolf waited until the hunter was away, carried off the hunter’s two-year-old child in her jaws, and raised the child as her own. That child was me.After the mother wolf grew old, I began hunting for food, often snatching sheep from the nearby village. The villagers caught me, and finding a creature with a human face living like a wolf, they tied me up to burn me. The hunter in the wolf skin was summoned too.By the firelight, the hunter made out the crescent-shaped birthmark on my shoulder, recognized the hunter’s missing child, and at once threw down his torch and set me loose.All I remembered was Mother’s warning that the man in the wolf skin was dangerous, so the moment I broke free I lunged to attack the hunter. The hunter did not raise his gun to defend himself, and in the end I bit the hunter to death. The photograph that fell from inside the hunter’s clothes was an old family photo he had carried all along.
hints: The one I called Mother had an old grudge with the man in the wolf skin.
I lived like a wolf, yet the crescent on my shoulder could prove who I was as a human.
The mother wolf raised the hunter’s child; the hunter set him free once he recognized him, and was bitten to death by a child who did not know his own father.

title: Puppy Love
story: My parents were called in over my puppy love.The homeroom teacher scolded my dad for not raising his son right; my dad complimented her looks instead.She actually smiled.While the two of them talked, I slipped out of the office.
answer: The homeroom teacher was my own mother; Mom and my dad had been each other’s early romance back in their day, and later they married.Mom had called Dad in so the two of them could discipline me together, but the more she said, the angrier she got, and she blamed Dad for failing to raise his son properly. Dad said the blame couldn’t all fall on him. Mom dug up old scores: “Back then, weren’t you the one who confessed to me first?”Dad rode the opening and paid Mom a compliment: “Who could help it, with you that pretty?” Mom laughed in spite of herself, and the two of them drifted into reminiscing, for the moment forgetting me, still standing there waiting to be scolded.While Mom and Dad talked, I quietly slipped out of the office.
hints: Dad and the homeroom teacher had known each other for many years, and they brought up the romance of their youth.
Besides teaching me at school, the homeroom teacher was also in charge of me at home.
The homeroom teacher was my mother; my parents got to talking about their own puppy love, and I seized the moment to slip away.

title: Never Growing Up
story: My classmates grew taller one after another, while I could still wear my old clothes.Mom and Dad fed me “vitamins” every day, and always told me to smile when they took my picture.They said it would be best if I just stayed this small forever.It seemed that only if I didn’t grow up would they love me more.
answer: I was a child model for children’s clothing, and my adorable looks brought the family a fair amount of money. My parents worried that once I grew up the orders would stop coming, so my parents wanted to keep me looking as young as they could.My parents told me the medication I should never have taken for so long was “vitamins,” and gave it to me every day. The long-term improper dosing damaged my body and left me growing far more slowly than children my age.My parents kept arranging photo shoots and praising me — what a good child, how pretty I looked. I understood nothing of the money involved; I only saw that my clothes never got much smaller, and that my parents treated me best when photographs were earning money, so I came to believe that as long as I never grew up, I could keep my parents’ love forever.
hints: My parents wanted me to stay small because my looks brought in money.
What I was given daily was called vitamins, but it was drugs that damaged my body.
The child model’s parents dosed him improperly to stretch out the earning years, and the child took the praise that came with the money for love.

title: The Number in My Palm
story: After Father lost his job, he grew thinner and thinner, and came home less and less.The neighbors told me to keep away from him, and I began to hate him too.Before he left, he gave me a piece of paper with nothing on it but a string of numbers.Many years later, I finally received the thing printed with that string of numbers, and clasped it tightly in my palm.
answer: My father was an undercover officer in drug enforcement. “Losing his job” and “going bad” were cover my father had built to get close to the dealers, but I was young and knew nothing of it.During the mission my father came under coercion and was harmed by drugs, and his health went from bad to worse. The people around us saw only a man moving through the world as an addict, and even I was kept at arm’s length. I took my father’s decline for a fall into ruin, and hated my father for wrecking our life.What my father left me at parting was his own police badge number, written on a piece of paper. My father later died on a mission, and only then did I learn the truth from his colleagues.I grew up, became a police officer myself, and applied to take up my father’s preserved badge number; the request was approved. The number plate I received bore the same string of digits as the paper. Closing my hand around it, I also took up the profession and the responsibility my father had left behind.
hints: The identity Father showed the outside world concealed the work he really did.
The digits on the paper were a professional number, one kept on reserve after Father’s death.
He was an undercover officer who died on duty; I became a police officer and applied to carry his badge number.

title: Finding a Friend
story: The singing outside the building drew nearer and nearer.“Searching, searching for a friend…”Clinging to my gun, I shrank into a cabinet, not daring even to breathe loudly.Metal feet stopped in front of the cabinet door, and the door was slammed open.“Found myself a good friend.”The song ended, and so did I.
answer: This is a fictional war. I was a soldier trapped inside a building while the enemy hunted for survivors with remote-controlled robot dogs carrying explosives.The operators had woven a children’s song into the search program: while moving and searching, the machine played “Searching, searching for a friend”; once a target was confirmed, the machine played “Found myself a good friend,” and then detonated. The song was deliberately used to terrify anyone in hiding.I hid in the cabinet clutching my gun. A robot dog was steered up to the cabinet door and smashed it open, and the camera showed the operator where I was. The last line of the song sounded, marking me as found. The explosion that came right after killed me.
hints: Clutching my gun in hiding, I was facing a battlefield manhunt.
The metal feet belonged to a remotely piloted machine, and the lyrics changed from one stage to the next.
Once the explosive-carrying robot dog found me, it finished the last line of the nursery rhyme and detonated.

title: Turning Back
story: I handed her the poison; she thanked me and asked me to close the door behind me when I left.I made off with the valuables from her home.I had just left the compound when I suddenly remembered something, and turned straight back.
answer: I am a burglar who cares a great deal about cleanliness. Breaking in to steal, I thought no one was home; after stowing the loot I even used her toilet.She was in the bathtub, and was startled awake by the noise. She had been trying to end her own life — she had swallowed pills earlier, yet was still alive. Seeing me, she paid no mind to being robbed; she only asked me to hand over the bottle of poison beside the tub.I did not try to save her; I simply did as she asked. She took this as a favor granted, thanked me, and reminded me to close the door well on my way out. I took the valuables and left her to go on with the poison.It was only as I was leaving the compound that I remembered I had forgotten to flush the toilet. I turned straight back to see to it — what was on my mind was still the mess I had left behind.
hints: She was trying to end her life, and took the handing over of the poison as a favor granted.
I had broken in to steal, and used the toilet along the way.
I turned back only because I had forgotten to flush; my fixation with cleanliness never made me spare a thought for her life.

title: The General Who Came with the Bride
story: When the prince celebrated his grand wedding, the bride arrived with an attendant in her retinue. Later the prince took the throne, and that attendant rose to be a general.The neighboring kingdom was invaded, and its royal family was murdered by mountain bandits as they fled. Enraged, the king sent this very general to wipe out the bandits’ stronghold.The stronghold fell. The princess who had originally come to seal the marriage alliance died inside it as well.
answer: When the neighboring kingdom’s princess set out to be married, bandits abducted the princess at the border and kept the princess at the bandits’ stronghold. The bandit chief’s younger sister took the princess’s place, brought one of the sister’s own trusted henchmen along as the attendant, and continued the journey to the prince’s kingdom. The two royal courts had never met face to face, so the prince married the stand-in.A few years later, the prince became king, the stand-in became queen, and the attendant who had come along with the stand-in became a general. The real princess stayed a captive in the stronghold the whole time.The neighboring kingdom was invaded, and its royal family set out to take refuge in the kingdom the royal family’s daughter had married into. The bandit chief knew the fleeing royals would recognize the chief’s sister as a false princess, so the chief ambushed and slaughtered the fleeing royals beforehand to protect the sister.The king, learning that his in-laws had been killed by bandits, ordered the general to wipe the bandits out. The queen, however, secretly instructed her old henchman to silence the matter for good — to kill everyone in the stronghold who knew the secret of the substitution, without even sparing the queen’s own older brother.The general killed the bandit chief, and the general killed the real princess too. The king believed the expedition was avenging the in-laws; in truth the king had removed, on the false queen’s behalf, the last people who could ever expose the stand-in.
hints: The bride and the princess who died in the stronghold at the end are two different people.
The attendant who came with the bride later became the general; he had been her trusted old henchman from the start.

The bandits swapped the chief’s sister in for the princess and killed the royals to protect her identity; the false queen then used the extermination order to silence her brother and the true princess in one stroke.

title: The Rescue
story: My wife died in a car crash, and for ten years I ached to save her.At last, one day, I sat behind the wheel again, and I saw her walk out of that same hotel from back then.I did not save her.I lost her all over again — and I have never regretted pressing down on the accelerator.
answer: I had gotten hold of a time-traveling car that could carry a person and itself back into the past. I drove the car to the day of my wife’s fatal crash, meaning to get my wife away before the accident.At that same intersection, I saw my wife come out of the hotel with a lover, and my wife and the lover embraced and kissed. In that instant I understood what my wife had been hiding from me all along.I had meant to pull over and warn my wife, but in my fury I changed my mind. I pressed the pedal, ran both my wife and the lover down, and then drove the car back to my own time, ten years later.The hit-and-run from back then, the one no culprit was ever found for, had been caused all along by me, arriving from ten years in the future. The past had always contained this journey; I did not create some new history.I had suffered ten years over my wife’s death — and in the end, at the very moment I believed I could save my wife, I caused that death with my own hands.
hints: I drove back from ten years in the future and saw her again at the intersection where she died.
What I saw outside the hotel changed my decision to save her.
The driver who killed my wife back then was me, returned through time; the past had always included that act.

title: Only I Woke Up
story: I woke up.The corridor was silent; they were all still asleep.I ran down it, pressing the buttons on one door after another, and no one answered.At last, I saw clearly the date on the screen.I broke down.
answer: I was a passenger on an interstellar liner, scheduled to hibernate alongside everyone else until we reached our destination hundreds of years from now.My hibernation pod malfunctioned and woke me early — and the pod could not be used again. There was no spare pod aboard. The other passengers’ pods were governed by the arrival program and could not be woken by hand in mid-voyage; no matter how many times I pressed the call buttons on the pod doors, the other passengers would not wake.The screen showed that the scheduled waking day still lay hundreds of years ahead. The ship could keep flying and keep me alive automatically, but I could never hibernate again, and I would not live to see that day.For every year of life I had left, I would remain wide awake aboard a ship full of sleepers. Once I understood that, I broke down.
hints: These people are in long-term hibernation, and me alone has woken early.
Only my own pod is broken; the other pods run on the arrival program, and passengers cannot be woken by hand.
The ship still has hundreds of years to fly; I cannot hibernate again, and I cannot live long enough to see the day they wake.

title: The Treatment
story: Mother had no money to treat her kidney disease. Her son said he would go and get screened as a donor.She grabbed hold of him and refused, no matter what.The son simply assumed she could not bear it for his sake.
answer: The mother needed a kidney transplant. The son wanted to donate one of the son’s kidneys to the mother, and the son had not yet gone through the donor evaluation.The mother knew the son was already down to one kidney. When the son was little, the mother had struck an illegal deal to raise money for the mother’s business and arranged for one of the son’s kidneys to be cut out, then lied to the child that it was just an operation to treat an illness. The son never knew.Now that the son had volunteered to donate, the mother could not accept the offer — and the mother feared the screening would bring the old secret to light — so the mother stopped the son with all her might.The son later went to the hospital for tests anyway, and only then discovered that the son was missing a kidney. Pressed about the missing kidney, the mother admitted what had happened, and the son finally understood why the mother had tried to stop the son.
hints: When the son offered to donate, he had not yet been evaluated and did not know the state of his own body.
The mother knows what that operation in his childhood really took out.
The mother illegally sold one of his kidneys for money when he was little and lied to him ever since; the donation screening would have exposed it.

title: The Fatal Phone Call
story: A rich man phoned his wife.The call never got answered.And yet the wife died because of that call.
answer: The rich man loved his wife dearly. That day a burglar had slipped into the house, and the wife was hiding somewhere inside. When the rich man called, the wife’s phone was not on silent; the ringtone suddenly rang out and gave away the wife’s position, and the burglar killed the wife.
hints: The ringing phone let someone hear where the wife was.
The wife was hiding in the house, trying to stay clear of an intruder.
Her phone was not silenced; her husband’s incoming call exposed her hiding place, and the intruder found her and killed her.

title: The Fatal Words
story: His wife fell from the cliff.Years later, the man brought his daughter to that same place.The daughter said one sentence to him.This time, it was he who went over the edge.
answer: Years earlier, the man had pushed the wife off the cliff and killed the wife. The man later remarried and had a daughter.In this world, reincarnation exists that carries the memories of a past life — and the daughter was the man’s late wife reborn. The daughter had always remembered being pushed over by the man.Once the daughter grew into her teens, the man took the daughter hiking up that mountain again. At the cliff’s edge, the daughter said: “This time, don’t push me off again.”The man turned to the daughter in shock. Taking advantage of the man standing off guard at the edge, the daughter gave the man a shove and sent the man over the cliff too. That sentence revealed how the daughter could know about the old days, and the sentence showed that this was no causeless accident.
hints: What the daughter said contained things about the past she had no way of knowing.
In this story, reincarnation exists that keeps the memories of a past life.
The first wife was pushed off by her husband, was reborn as his daughter, and on that same cliff pushed him off in turn.

title: Finally Full
story: After I was cursed, I stayed hungry no matter how much I ate.That day, I sneaked into someone’s house, dug out whatever food I could find and stuffed it into my mouth.The owner came home and, in a fury, threw a question at me.I answered “Yes” again and again.That meal, I was finally full.
answer: I had been a man-eating villain, and I was cursed as follows: only human flesh could ease my hunger, and I could take nothing from a person unless that person asked me whether I wanted something the person owned. Once the person asked and I accepted, that thing became mine to take — the words took effect literally.Racked by hunger, I broke into a house and rummaged for food, yet I never felt full. When the owner caught me, the owner shouted in rage: “You want a piece of me?!”The owner meant the shout as an insult, but the curse took the question as permission to take a piece of the owner. I answered “Yes” over and over, then set upon the owner, ate the owner’s flesh and blood, and my hunger was finally eased.The owner had no thought of feeding me; one furious turn of phrase met the very condition that bound me.
hints: The owner was not inviting me to a meal; what he threw at me was a stock insult.
The curse reads any question literally, letting me take that very thing from the speaker.
He shouted “You want a piece of me?” — I said yes, and took my piece of him and ate it.

title: The Spider-Silk Town
story: Dozens of townsfolk vanished one after another, and every house they left behind held traces of spider silk.A guard post went up at the town gate, and the disappearances stopped for a time.Before long, the man who lived in the hills behind town vanished too.This time, the silk stretched from the back hills all the way to the edge of the streets.
answer: In this invented world there are giant spiders that prey on people, and a man living in the hills behind town had long been raising a brood of the spiders.The man had once been disfigured by the townspeople. The man knew the townspeople who had done the disfiguring feared spiders, so the man decided to use the spiders to create terror. Over and over the man abducted townsfolk and fed the townsfolk to the giant spiders in the hills as food, and the man left spider silk in each missing person’s house so the town would suspect the spiders were at work.After the town tightened its guard, the man could no longer abduct anyone. Deprived of food, the giant spiders turned on the man who had raised the spiders, attacked and ate the man, then crawled down out of the hills and into the town to hunt.The first wave of disappearances was the man’s doing, the silk a threat the man planted deliberately; the second wave, with silk strung as far as the edge of the streets, was the giant spiders truly coming down the mountain.
hints: Between the two waves of disappearances, the hand behind them changed.
The man in the hills raised giant man-eating spiders and at first abducted people to feed them.
The guards cut off their food supply; the spiders devoured their keeper and entered the town — the disaster once only staged became real.

title: I Found My Sister
story: At Grandpa’s funeral, my big sister and I played hide-and-seek.I searched for a long, long time before I finally saw her.I ran back, tugged at Mommy’s sleeve, pointed at that blaze of flames and said: “Found her! Sis is dancing in that pretty house!”When Mommy heard me, she dropped to the ground.
answer: I was six, and my sister was eight. At the funeral, the grown-ups were getting ready to burn a grand paper effigy house built for Grandpa — the kind of funeral offering made to be burned so the dead can have the house. When my sister’s turn to hide came around, my sister climbed inside the paper house, certain I would never find my sister there.When the rite began, none of the grown-ups noticed there was a child inside, and the grown-ups set the paper house alight. My sister’s clothes caught fire; in the panic, the hem of the dress snagged on the frame inside, and my sister could not get out in time.When I found my sister, all I could see was a figure writhing in the flames. Too little to know the writhing was a struggle of pain, I took the figure to be dancing, and I ran off, thrilled, to tell Mommy.Only from my words did Mommy understand that my sister was inside the burning paper house, and Mommy fainted from the shock. The others rushed to save my sister, but my sister was already gravely burned, and in the end my sister could not be saved.
hints: That house was something meant to be burned at the funeral, and the grown-ups did not know someone was hiding inside.
My sister had hidden inside the grand paper effigy house, and I mistook her thrashing in the fire for dancing.
She was still inside when the paper house was lit; hearing my excited report, Mommy grasped the tragedy at once.

title: I’ll Be It
story: After years away from my home village, my son started clamoring for hide-and-seek the moment we walked in.I was It. My wife’s hiding spot was not that good, and yet my son just could not find her.I remembered the most hidden spot from my own childhood, and walked toward it.The child inside turned his head: “You finally found me.”Behind me, my son was calling for Daddy too.
answer: When I was little, I was about to move far away with my mother. A childhood friend whose family had already moved off snuck back into the village to say goodbye. We played hide-and-seek with the other children; I led the friend into an abandoned cellar, then pulled the lid shut — the lid could only be opened from outside — and told the friend I would come back for the friend soon.My mother suddenly hurried me into the car, and I left with my mother, forgetting the friend still trapped in the cellar. The friend’s family did not know the friend had snuck back to the village, and no one in the village knew where the friend had hidden. No one ever came for the friend, and in the end the friend died in that cellar.In this story, the friend’s ghost stayed on at the spot where the friend had hidden, still in the shape of a child.Years later I brought my wife and son back to the village, and while searching for my son I came to that cellar again. The child who turned around and spoke was my friend’s ghost. My son had actually hidden somewhere else entirely, and had run back on his own, calling for me.“You finally found me” reminded me of the thing I had left unfinished all those years ago. Later the cellar was opened, and my friend’s remains were found inside.
hints: The child who speaks and the son behind me shouting for Daddy are two different people.
As a child, I once hid another child in that place too — and never went back for him.
My childhood friend died trapped in the abandoned cellar, and his ghost went on waiting; only when I finally returned years later did he say I had found him.

title: The Selfie
story: A woman he knew only through an online romance asked him to send a selfie.When she had looked at it, she said: “Don’t get so close to the camera — I want to see where you work.”He took another one.The next day, he was dead.
answer: He was a commander on the battlefield; the woman was an operative the enemy had sent to get close to him, using the cover of an online romance to fish out intelligence.The first photo showed mostly his face, so the woman, on the pretext of wanting a look at his work environment, had him take the camp behind him into the frame as well. In the retake, he sent the woman the nearby, conspicuous terrain and installations along with everything else.The enemy already held reconnaissance data on that region, and the photos let the enemy confirm which camp he was in. The next day, the camp was hit by a drone strike, and he was killed in the blast.What the woman wanted to see, from beginning to end, was the setting in the photos; the romance was only the cover that made him willing to hand the photos over himself.
hints: The man’s workplace is a wartime camp that must stay secret.
She had him shoot more of the surroundings because she wanted the camp’s position pinned down.
The online lover came from the enemy side; the photos, matched against existing reconnaissance, confirmed the location, and the strike followed.

title: The Broken Bicycle
story: My bicycle broke, and the repairman at the school gate made a nice little sum off me.The next day, the teacher’s bicycle and every classmate’s bicycle broke too.I went and said a few words to the teacher.Later on, the repairman died.
answer: My tire was punctured, so I took the bike to the repair stand at the school gate. The repairman went on to deliberately damage parts that had been perfectly fine, forcing me to pay more. I watched the repairman do the damage, but I was young and did not dare argue with the repairman on the spot.I bore a grudge against the repairman. The next day, I wrecked the teacher’s and the whole class’s bicycles myself, then told the teacher I had seen the repairman sneak into the school and sabotage the bikes.People watched the bikes fail one after another, and having heard the repairman had a record of padding bills on purpose before, the people believed my testimony. Furious parents went to the repair stand to confront the repairman; the quarrel escalated, the repairman was beaten by the crowd, and the repairman died of the injuries.The extra damage to the first bike really was the repairman’s doing; the second batch was entirely mine. With the repairman’s past misdeeds and my own lie, I turned the fury of a crowd upon the repairman.
hints: The first bike and the second batch were damaged by different hands.
The so-called eyewitness account I gave the teacher was a lie.
To get back at the repairman, I wrecked the whole class’s bikes, framed him for it, and set off the beating by the parents that killed him.

title: The Right Key
story: The place downstairs had been under renovation for months; yesterday, it finally fell quiet.My friend and I came home from drinking. The elevator was out of service, so we had to climb the stairs.At my door, I opened it with my own key. Every piece of furniture was where it had always been, yet something felt wrong.My friend told me to lock the door good and tight, then left.The next day, he could not find me anywhere.
answer: I had refused a wealthy suitor. The suitor would not give up, and the suitor bought the unit one floor directly below mine, laid out in the same position; the renovation noise came from the suitor’s unit.Whenever I was out, the suitor entered my home, noted down how everything was arranged, and made the downstairs unit into a nearly identical copy of my rooms. The suitor even had a lock fitted that my original key would open.That night the suitor followed me, saw that both I and the friend walking me home were drunk, and deliberately shut down the elevator and swapped the floor signs on the relevant landing. Believing the signs as we climbed, we came up one floor short and stopped at the door of the suitor’s unit.My key opened the door, and the inside looked like my own home, so I sensed nothing at first. After my friend left, the suitor, hidden inside, came out and imprisoned me.The next day my friend went to my real home and, of course, could not find me. I had used my own key correctly — and unlocked my way into a forged copy of my home.
hints: The key was real, but that door’s lock had been made on purpose to open to it.
The long-renovated place was the identically placed unit one floor below, its furniture copied after mine.
The suitor switched the floor signs so that I, drunk, walked into the copied room below, and he then held me captive.

title: The Seventeenth Floor
story: She lives on the twenty-fifth floor, and heading out she always rides the elevator straight down to the first.Coming home, though, she rides only as far as the seventeenth and climbs the rest of the way herself.On the day it rained, she could ride straight up to the twenty-fifth.When someone shared the elevator with her, she could too.
answer: She is very short. In this building the elevator buttons are stacked from the lowest floor to the highest, and the seventeenth floor is the highest button she can reach; the button for the twenty-fifth floor sits beyond her grasp.Heading down in the morning, she can press the first-floor button at the very bottom. Coming home on a normal day, she can only ride to the seventeenth and take the stairs from there, because nothing she carries day to day can be used to press the higher buttons.When it rains, she has an umbrella along, and the umbrella’s tip can reach the twenty-fifth-floor button. A fellow passenger can also press the button for her — so in those two cases, she can ride all the way to the floor she lives on.
hints: Going down and going up, the buttons she needs to press sit at different heights.
A rainy day gives her one extra object long enough to reach up with.
She cannot reach the twenty-fifth-floor button; an umbrella tip, or a fellow passenger, can press it for her.

title: My Favorite
story: Mommy always feeds me vegetables and fruit; my little brother loves to feed me ice cream.I love Daddy best of all. Now my belly is full of his flesh.Ever since then, I have not seen Mommy or my brother again.Only Daddy has stayed with me, the whole time.
answer: The “I” telling this is the family’s refrigerator: the narration calls food being put into the refrigerator “eating,” and calls the family members Mommy, little brother, and Daddy.Mommy often put the vegetables and fruit Mommy bought into the fridge, and my little brother put the ice cream in. Daddy, again and again, beat Mommy and my little brother after drinking.After one such beating, Mommy killed Daddy while Daddy slept, cut Daddy’s body apart and placed the body in the fridge, then fled the house with my little brother.So the flesh came from Daddy, and the one who put the flesh there was Mommy. I never saw Mommy or my brother again because Mommy and my brother left; Daddy stayed inside, becoming the one thing that was never taken back out.
hints: “Eating” can also mean something being stored into a container; me is not a child of this family.
The vegetables and fruit, the ice cream, and at the last the flesh all went into the same refrigerator.
Mommy killed her abusive husband, hid his body in the fridge, and left with the children; the flesh that stayed behind is Daddy.

title: Tears on the Wooden Ladder
story: Late at night, a man collapsed dead drunk in the open wilds, an old, battered wooden ladder pinned under his body. When someone shook him awake, he stared at the ladder before him and suddenly broke down.
answer: The man drank out of despair, planning to end his own life by lying down on the railway tracks. Stumbling, half-blind with drink, into the wasteland, the man took a wooden ladder lying flat on the ground for the rails, and lay down on the ladder. Waking up, the man realized that the man had failed even at killing himself; grief welled up over the man, and the man sobbed aloud.
hints: The drink made him mistake the wooden ladder for something else with a similar shape.
He had been trying to end his own life.
He mistook the ladder for railway tracks; waking to find himself still alive, the despair came over him all over again.

title: The Madhouse Rhyme
story: Madhouse, madhouse, madhouse — it takes in no old folks and no sick folks, only women and little children. By day the front gate is lined with people; by night the yard is full of people — and not a single one of them alive.
answer: The word the children sing as "mad" in this rhyme was originally its homophone "wind" — as in wind-dried. The rhyme began as a peddler's cry for drumming up trade, and after so many years in children's mouths, the word was sung into "mad." That "wind-dried-people yard" belonged to a killer who made cured meat out of his victims. The meat of the old is tough and stringy, and the sick carry their sickness — either way, as "cured meat" it would be foul-tasting and dangerous — so he preyed only on tender women and children, all of them strangers he had snatched. His goods were famous for miles around: by day, the front gate was lined with customers who had come on the news to buy meat; by night, the yard hung full of freshly finished goods. The last line of the rhyme sings of the night — of all those "people" hanging in the yard, not a single one is alive.
hints: The rhyme has been passed around for many years; the words could well have been sung out of shape along the way.
The word sung as "mad" was originally another word with the very same sound, and what hung drying in that yard was "goods."
It was a yard that made cured meat out of people: by day the queuing customers came to buy meat, and by night what hung there were freshly wind-dried corpses.

title: The Mosquito
story: The moment I finished my meal, I died — covered from head to toe in blood.
answer: "I" am a mosquito. "Finishing my meal" means drinking my fill of blood. I landed on him and drank until I was full, and before I could fly away, he slapped me down with one swat — he bore me no grudge and had never met me; he was simply killing, offhand, a mosquito that had taken his blood. The instant he crushed me, the blood I had only just drunk sprayed all over my body. So I died covered in blood: it was the blood of the man who killed me — the very "meal" that killed me.
hints: "I" am not human.
That "meal" was blood, and "I" died under a slap swung without a thought.
"I" am a mosquito that drank its fill and was swatted down before it could fly off; the blood covering me sprayed out the moment I was crushed.

title: My Brother's Commands
story: My brother says: forward means backward, left means right. Forward! Forward! Forward! I can no longer hear my brother's voice. I know I won't live much longer either.
answer: We are conjoined twins — one body with two heads. I face forward; my brother grew from the back of my neck, facing backward. I was born blind, and my brother can see — all his life he has been my eyes. Because our two heads face opposite directions, he always called out directions by his own orientation: when he shouted "forward," I walked backward; when he shouted "left," I turned right. We used that "forward means backward" system our whole lives, and I never once questioned it. But my brother had long since reached his limit: all his life he could see only the road we had already walked, and the body was never his to move. That day, he steered me around the yard for a while, still shouting the same commands — "Forward! Forward! Forward!" — and obediently, step by step, I walked backward, steadily carrying him on my neck toward the steel rebar standing against the wall. My brother borrowed my legs to kill himself. From then on, I never heard my brother's voice again. I can't see a thing, I have never once left this yard on my own, and there is no one else in the family. I know I won't live much longer either.
hints: My brother's voice has always been pressed close against the back of my head.
I can't see the way; my brother is my eyes — and when he calls out directions, he always calls them by his own orientation.
We are two heads on one body, facing opposite ways: when he shouts "forward," I walk backward step by step — he borrowed my legs to send himself, riding behind me, onto the steel rebar.

title: Christmas Eve
story: I live in a hospital ward all year round. Today is Christmas Eve, heavy snow falling outside, and Mom and Dad have taken me home for the day. Dad cooks with his own hands, and Mom tends to me at my side, her sick child. A caregiver comes to the house and says it's time I went back to the hospital; to keep me there, Mom wrestles with her and kills her by accident. Dad tells me not to dwell on it, and sets out turkey and roast meat. When I'm full, I sleep in one bed with Mom and Dad — so hot, so warm — and I quickly fall asleep. The next day, I die, happy.
answer: I suffer from severe schizophrenia. My parents died years ago; I could never accept it, my illness kept getting worse, and I lived in the hospital year-round — and I split into a "Mom" who protected me and a "Dad" who cared for me. On Christmas Eve I escaped from the hospital and ran out into a park in heavy snow, with my caregiver chasing after me. In my eyes, this place was "home": the caregiver who came chasing through the door was there to take me back to the hospital; "Mom" fought her to keep me, and killed her by accident; "Dad" told me not to dwell on it, lit a fire with a lighter taken from the caregiver's body, and "cooked" the turkey and the roast — the "turkey" was flesh cut from the caregiver's body, and the "roast meat" was my own arm, frozen so numb that even being cut open, I felt no pain. After eating, I lay down to sleep with "Mom and Dad." People freezing to death feel a burning heat at the very end; I felt so warm, and slept deep and happy. The next morning, in the snow, I stopped breathing.
hints: The "I" who lives in a hospital ward all year round — the illness has to do with the family in those memories.
No one came to take me home that day — I escaped from the hospital myself.

"Mom" and "Dad" are both personalities I split into, and it was my own body that did everything; the two dishes were human flesh, and the heat and warmth were the illusion that comes before freezing to death.

title: The Most Perfect Work
story: I am a failed painter. For the sake of my career, my wife came along with me into the countryside to sketch. The mountain road was rough, and the car suddenly broke down. A herdsman leading a horse came by and took us into a nearby village to spend the night. In the evening, my wife said she was hot and thirsty, went out to find water, and never came back. I went out to look for her and saw her standing among several wells — then, with a blank stare, she jumped into one of them. Terrified and thrilled at once, I hurriedly set up my easel and painted the scene.
answer: We never made it to the countryside — on that mountain road, my wife and I had already died in the same car crash. The herdsman with the horse was a guide whose job was to lead the newly dead into that village, and that village does not belong to the world of the living. The rule of the village: souls without attachments feel a burning thirst — they drink Mengpo's soup of forgetfulness, forget this life, and walk into one of the wells to be reborn; those wells lead to the six paths of reincarnation. My wife had nothing she couldn't let go of. She drank the soup and jumped into a well with a blank stare. What kept me lingering was an unfinished obsession: a failure all my life, I had never managed to paint a perfect work — so I didn't feel thirsty at all. Watching my wife jump, I was afraid — we really were dead — and thrilled — this was exactly the image I had hunted for half my life. I finished painting it: the most perfect work of my life. The moment I set down the brush, I began to feel thirsty too.
hints: We never finished that mountain road.
The herdsman and the village do not belong to the world of the living; thirsty souls drink Mengpo's soup, and the wells are the doors to rebirth.
Only souls without attachments feel thirst: my wife drank and jumped into a well; I lingered for the unfinished painting — and the moment I finished it, I grew thirsty too.

title: Santa Claus
story: Christmas is here, and I've come again to make children's dreams come true. The first child wanted to sing — she managed it. The second child wanted to travel, so I sent her around the world — she just happened to get eaten along the way. The third child loved hide-and-seek, so I helped him hide somewhere even the police can't find — though he'll turn up on his own next year.
answer: I am a serial killer. Every Christmas I dress up as Santa Claus, listen to children tell me their wishes, and go after the ones with no adults around. The first child was born mute and had never managed to sing in her life; I stripped off her skin and stretched it into a drumhead — when it is struck, she finally makes a sound with her own body. The second child wanted to travel, so I made her into canned meat mixed into the freight; the cans were passed along and shipped out to the far corners of the world, and in the end she was eaten at some distant dinner table — that is how she "traveled the world." The third child loved hide-and-seek, so I buried him in the snow on the hill behind the house; the search teams walked right past him without finding him — and when next spring comes and the snow melts, he will "turn up" on his own.
hints: "I" get to hear children's wishes every year, because I am wearing a Santa Claus suit.
All three wishes "came true" — at the cost of three children's bodies.
The mute girl's skin became a drum that can "sing"; the second child was canned and eaten far away; the third lies buried in the snow and will only appear when it melts.

title: Blowing Out the Candle
story: The house was haunted, so I went and found a master. He said that to save my life I had to keep three rules, and if I made it through tonight I would be fine. One: never blow out the warding candle on the table — blow it out and you die. Two: tonight you are alone in this house; no matter who calls your name, do not answer — me included. Three: even after you make it through tonight, for the rest of your life, never again turn off the lights at night. When dawn came, the candle was still burning, and I was still alive. But a few months later, I died anyway.
answer: The master's rules truly worked. What ruined me was that very night — the phone rang past midnight, a voice through the receiver called my name, and I answered by reflex. Rule two said "no matter who," and the voice on the phone counted too. Once I had answered the ghost's call, it latched onto me. It dragged me into a hallucination: I believed I had safely made it to dawn, believed that in the months after, the lights stayed on every night, and lived all the way to my birthday. The birthday feast was held in the daytime; without a thought I turned off the lights and blew out the candles — and when I opened my eyes, I was back on the night the haunting began. The light I had switched off was the real light in that room; the candle I had blown out was the warding candle the master had lit; and the master stood right in front of me, reciting those three rules. From the moment I answered, those "few months" had never existed. The ghost had made me re-enact both deadly taboos with my own hands — I had already died that very night.
hints: All three rules were real; the problem was me — I broke the taboo that same night.
The one calling your name isn't necessarily at the door — the phone rang that night.

From the moment I answered, those "safe months" were all hallucination; the light turned off and the candle blown out at the birthday feast were that room's light and the master's warding candle from the haunted night — I died that night.

title: Peeping
story: A girl just moved into the neighborhood, and I have been peeping at her all this time. But today she suddenly hid herself — she seemed to have noticed me. Right after, she screamed and ran out, and then a roar came from inside the apartment: I'll kill you!
answer: What had been "peeping" at her from the window was a corpse. Days earlier, I had ended my life with charcoal smoke in the chair by my window, and after death I sat there rigid, face turned toward the street. It was winter, doors and windows sealed shut; I lived alone, with no relatives or friends who would ever come by; the curtain was drawn only halfway. Against the light, from across the way, all anyone could make out was a man who sat quietly at his window day after day. The newly moved-in girl kept going over to that household across from mine every day — she wasn't the woman of the house; she was going there for an affair with the man who lived there. She had probably noticed long before that a man at the opposite window was always facing the direction she came from. Today, she had just stepped inside when the man's wife suddenly came home, and she scrambled to hide; turning around mid-hiding, she came face to face with the corpse at the window — the one that "had been watching her all along" — and fled screaming out the door. That scream gave her away completely to the wife, and the roar came from inside right after: I'll kill you.
hints: "I" never once changed position, and never once left that window.
That position was not peeping — "I" am dead.
The girl was going across for an affair; hiding from the wife, she turned and saw "me," the corpse at the window; her scream gave her away, and the roar came from the wife inside.

title: The Massage Therapist
story: I am a massage therapist. Today, as arranged, I came to a client's home to give him a massage. He was quite the talker, chatting with me the whole time — it was just that his hands weren't well behaved, always taking advantage of me, deliberately or not. The house smelled richly of cooking; dinner must have been close. From the bathroom came the sound of running water that kept growing fainter, and from another room came a child's voice calling "Mama, Mama" — an eerie sound. The next day, the news said that all three of them, the whole family, were dead.
answer: I am a blind massage therapist. The killer had murdered the family of three in advance, then phoned me in the husband's name to book the home visit — by the time I walked in, the whole family was already dead. The killer hid nearby, posing as the husband and chatting with me, and the "client" beneath my hands was in fact the husband's corpse. The corpse's hands kept brushing against me, deliberately or not: a body only recently dead will still show nerve-reflex twitches when the muscles are pressed; I took it for a client's wandering hands, while the killer sweated through his performance. The running water from the bathroom that kept fading was him draining the corpses' blood and rinsing away the traces — the quieter it got, the closer he was to done. The rich smell of a family dinner was the family themselves, stewing in the pot — he is a cannibal. The eerie "Mama, Mama" in the other room came from the family's parrot. Blind me never suspected a thing through the whole session, and without meaning to, I testified for the killer that "the family was still alive" at the time of the crime.
hints: A massage therapist takes in the scene only through sound, smell, and touch.
The one chatting with him and the one lying under his hands were not the same person; the water in the bathroom was washing away something that should never have been left behind.

Under his hands lay the husband's corpse (the hands that touched him were death reflexes); the one doing the talking was the killer — draining blood and prepping the meat, with the family stewing in the pot, while the "Mama" was a parrot.

title: The Village
story: For the first time, the boy went back with his girlfriend to her family's home village. All along the way, the villagers' eyes on him were indescribably strange. He stayed one night at her family's home. When he woke the next morning, he discovered in horror: her father was dead, and the boy himself had become her husband.
answer: The village keeps a secret art that has been passed down for over a thousand years: transplanting an aging consciousness into a young body. The consciousness forced out stays behind in the burnt-out old shell and dies with it — the villagers have long been used to holding funerals for their "departed elders." The girlfriend and "her father" were in fact a married couple who had lived for over a thousand years: the wife had not long ago moved into a young girl's body, while the husband's old shell had reached its limit. So the wife found the boy beyond the mountains, brought him back to the village, and had her husband play "her father" so the boy wouldn't grow suspicious. That night the art was completed: the husband's consciousness entered the boy's body. The next morning, the boy's consciousness woke inside the aging body and worked out everything: outside the window, his own body was walking arm in arm with "his girlfriend," full of life, while the villagers came to the door one after another with congratulations — in their telling, "the old man" passed away in the night, and the girlfriend's "husband" was young and presentable. Now the strange looks had their answer too: there was no malice in those gazes — only a crowd of thousand-year-olds sizing up a fresh new shell. The aging body did not make it past the third day; the boy's consciousness went dark along with it. The villagers held a funeral by the old custom and buried the "departed elder."
hints: There was no malice in the villagers' strange looks — it was more like appraising something they dearly wanted.
The "father" and the girlfriend fit their father-daughter roles just right; and this family took the boy in for something that could only be done after he'd stayed a night.

That night, the bodies of the boy and of the "father" swapped occupants — and the old body was already down to its last days. "The father died" and "the boy became the husband" are two results of the same operation.

title: The Five Brothers
story: A massacre had just taken place in the abandoned church. Old Master Gao's body lay peacefully in the casket, and on the altar lay his five sons: the eldest missing his head, the second missing his chest and both hands, the third missing his abdomen, the fourth missing his thighs, the youngest missing his lower legs — every cut clean and neat. The police officers who rushed to the scene counted twice, and both times it came to five bodies. The sole heir of the Gao family — the third brother's son — trembling, told the officers: "They were trying to bring Grandfather back to life, but they summoned a demon, and the demon killed them all."
answer: The church was the Gao family's ancestral property; the old master's coffin rested there, and the family keeping vigil slept in the side hall. From beginning to end, there were only four corpses on the altar: the dead were the second, third, fourth, and fifth sons — the eldest never died at all, and the "all five sons dead" black ritual was a scheme of his own arranging. The old master's new will had cut him out, and he was sunk in debts he could never repay: a dead man owes nothing, and no one contests an estate with a dead heir. On the night of the vigil, he drugged the night-watch wine, and the four brothers were killed one by one as they slept. The bodies were cut apart after death, which is why the cuts were so clean and nearly bloodless. Then came the splicing: each corpse received exactly one cut, each cut lower than the last — the second son severed at the neck, the third at the waist, the fourth below the hips, the fifth below the knees. In the "eldest son's" place lay the second son's headless torso; in the "second son's" place, the second son's head, then a stretch of empty space, then the third son's body from the waist down; in the "third son's" place, the third son's head, chest, and both arms, a gap where the abdomen should be, then the fourth son's body below the hips; in the "fourth son's" place, the fourth son's upper body, a gap where the thighs should be, then the fifth son's body below the knees; in the "fifth son's" place, only the fifth son himself from the knees up. Four corpses, not one piece missing; the five "missing parts" stacked from head to toe make exactly one complete person — that is the "eldest brother" who never existed and can never be put back together. Of the five "corpses," this is the only one with no head and no face, impossible to verify. The boy wasn't lying: in the dark, the robed figure carrying the bodies onto the altar was, in a child's eyes, a demon — and a terrified child babbling about a "demon killing them all" played right into his hands. Before dawn, he took the family fortune he had moved out in advance and vanished into the news of his own death. Anyone who lines up the cut ends of the five "corpses" can count out the truth.
hints: Line up the five "missing parts" from top to bottom — added together, don't they look like one complete person?
Every piece of flesh is still on that altar: four whole corpses, yet five dead men were counted. Think about which one has no face.

Each corpse was cut only once, the cuts stepping lower and lower: below the "second son's" head is the "third son's" waist — four corpses misaligned into five, and the one that can never be assembled is the eldest, who walked away alive.

title: The Strange Sound
story: The volunteer teacher before me had left, and I was sent into the mountains to take his place, lodging at the village headman's house. On the headman's front door was pasted a strange sheet of yellow paper, and every night, deep in the dark, the house rang with a muffled thumping. I noticed the thumps followed a pattern, so I wrote them down: 96924482622454. Three days later, the sound stopped. And I finally understood — the sound had been spelling out a message of five syllables.
answer: The yellow paper on the headman's door was this family's funeral marker: the headman's only son had just died, not yet buried, his coffin resting in a side room that stayed locked day and night. Old and newly bereaved, the headman put all his faith in the geomancer's word — a son who dies young and unmarried is too lonely on the road to the netherworld, and a living person must be buried with him for company. The previous volunteer teacher had never left at all. The night before I arrived, the headman drugged him, locked him into that coffin, and shut him in with the corpse. The muffled thumping was him beating on the coffin wall for help — the sound came through the boards deadened and dull, and the headman told his family only that the side room was holding a rite. Wanting to leave one message for the world beyond the mountains, the man in the coffin had nothing to use but his ten fingers and the pinyin nine-key of an old cell phone: 96 (WO, "I"), 924 (ZAI, "in"), 4826 (GUAN) plus 224 (CAI) — together, guancai, "coffin" — and 54 (LI, "inside"): "I am inside the coffin." Night after night he knocked it out, hoping someone would understand. The nights I lodged in that house, he lay sleeping in those boards, one thin wall away from me. On the third night, the sound stopped: there is no water in a coffin, and no one lives to see the fourth day. Then came the burial, the yellow paper came down, and the village told the outside world that the volunteer teacher's "contract had ended and he had gone back to the city" — and asked beyond the mountains for a new teacher. For one thing, it smoothed over the hole of a "missing teacher"; for another, the geomancer had said the living who keep the dead company must come in pairs. The night I finally pieced those digits into those five syllables, I shook all over. The way the headman looked at me — I will remember it until I die. The next night, I slept in that side room too. In the end, the ones buried for company were just the two of us.
hints: The yellow paper was a funeral marker; the timing of the previous teacher's "departure" matched this family's funeral a little too perfectly.
The thumping came from the side room that never opened; the sound stopped on the third night because there was no one left inside who could knock.
Read the digits on an old phone's pinyin nine-key: 96, 924, 4826, 224, 54 — a man still alive, knocking out an SOS from inside a coffin, night after night.

title: The Balloon
story: It's so dark in here. Thank goodness Dad brought a candle, and my brother brought food — and Mom is the greatest of all: she saved me with a balloon.
answer: Our family of four met our accident inside a limestone cave. We had gone in to explore during the summer holidays when a rainstorm collapsed the way we had come, burying it under fallen rock; the flashlight was smashed, and the cave went utterly dark — all we could hear was the water rising. Dad was crushed to critical injury by falling stones in the collapse and died the next day. There was a lighter in Dad's pocket, but nothing in the cave would burn — not until I crawled back to Dad's body and found that the "candle" had been there all along: wrapped in strips of cloth, body fat catches fire, and that flame counted me through the blackest nights, one by one. My brother gave me every drop of the water he caught, and grew colder day by day. After he stopped moving, I survived on what he had left me. Mom held out until the very last moment, and fell into the rising water. She soaked in that water for days on end, and the gases of decay slowly bloated her body, swelling it round like a balloon, until she floated up to the surface. That "balloon" saved me: the rain never stopped, the water kept rising, until it reached the roof of the cave. I held on to Mom's floating body and rode the buoyancy upward, up to the crack the collapse had shaken open — the one I could never reach no matter how I stretched — and squeezed my way out through it. Outside the cave, day was just breaking and the rain had stopped. Of our family of four, I alone walked out — Dad gave me light, my brother gave me food, and Mom, at the end, carried me back to the world of the living.
hints: Where "I" was, there was no day or night — only water that kept rising; and nothing in that sentence was ever "brought" in.
Dad, my brother, and Mom were gone one after another; the "candle" and the "food" were themselves, and a "balloon" takes days of soaking in warm water before it takes shape.

Trapped by the collapse in the cave: Dad's fat wrapped in cloth became the lamp, my brother's body became the food, and Mom, soaked in the water, bloated into the "balloon" — at the last, it was the water risen to the cave's roof that floated me, clinging to her, out through the crack.

title: Rules of Leon Town
story: Rules of Leon Town:1. The town is bustling with life. Welcome, visitors, one and all.2. The town is unusually tidy; there are no cobwebs here.3. The mayor's hands are covered in calluses — they say he was once an acrobat.4. Bureau 749 holds only one right of execution, but every resident can confirm the town is free of the paranormal.5. The town's detective is alive and well.A reminder from the late detective:1. The town has already fallen. Outsiders, please evacuate.2. Do not touch the dense cobwebs covering the town.3. Beware the puppeteer. Kill it, and everything ends.4. The paranormal is real. There may be no living soul left in this town. Bureau 749 has already intervened.5. I am alive and well.6. The town is bustling with life. Welcome, visitors, one and all.This trip has no limit on attempts, until the paranormal is gone.
answer: Leon Town long ago became the puppeteer's stage — and the mayor is the puppeteer. The dense "cobwebs" strung across town are his control threads: over the years, visitors "welcomed" into town touched a thread and were reeled in, becoming smiling residents who put on a "bustling" show in the streets by day. The town resets itself every night; puppets that break are standing back in place the next morning just the same — that is the town's "loop." The town is "unusually tidy" because puppets don't live; and the official rule insisting "there are no cobwebs" is the thread-master's cover-up. The mayor's callused hands come from decades of wire-pulling — "acrobat" is the legend left for outsiders. The detective was an investigator Bureau 749 sent into town, disposed of on the very night he arrived. But 749's field agents carry one right of execution not yet used, and with his case left open, death cannot be settled on him — he died, and still gets up "alive and well" every day. At night, what remained of his consciousness carved the truth onto walls, line by line: the "reminder from the late detective." He is this town's one and only paranormal being — a dead man who cannot die. To his last he urged whoever came after to "kill the puppeteer," the road he himself had failed to walk. The keys were written in plain sight: the third rule on each side mirrors the other, naming the mayor as the puppeteer; the fourth rules contradict each other yet say the same thing — the residents are all puppets, and there is no living soul left in town for anything paranormal to harm; and the flip side of "Bureau 749 has already intervened" is that 749's entire presence in this town is the undying detective himself. When he finally understood and spent the one-time right of execution on himself, the anchor was cut and the threads gave way: the wires fell in a single night, the puppets got no next-morning reset, and the town fell completely silent. As for why the dead man's sixth rule matches the official first rule word for word — by the night he carved it, the loop had already swallowed his own words. From there on, the six reminders will turn back, one by one, into "Welcome, visitors, one and all," just like every visitor who was ever left behind.
hints: The two rule sets come from the same town: read them five against five, side by side — each pair is two versions of the same thing.
One side says the cobwebs don't exist, the other says they're everywhere — those threads have another owner. Think about a pair of callused hands, and the word "acrobat."

Each side has its own "alive and well," and both are about the detective: dead, yet up and "alive" every day, he is the paranormal itself — and all of Bureau 749 that remains in town. The one-time right of execution, spent only on himself, is what finally closes the show.

title: My Sister's Room
story: From my sister's room came the sound of many sneakers scuffing the floor. The door stood ajar. I pushed it open and looked inside — my sister's hollow eyes were staring straight at me. Terrified, I rushed off to find the security guard. And then, I died.
answer: "My sister's room" was where she lived last — the coffin in her fresh grave on the hillside. That day was the seventh day after her death, the day the dead are said to come home. I went up the mountain in the morning, and before I even reached the grave, I heard the sounds: rustling, scraping, one wave after another, muffled and dull, like many pairs of sneakers scuffing a floor. The fresh earth on the grave had been disturbed, and the coffin lid stood pried open along one edge — the sound was leaking out through the crack. I heaved the lid open, and inside was a seething mass of rats — they had been slipping in and out through that crack for days. My sister lay face-up among them, gnawed beyond all recognition, her emptied eye sockets turned right toward me — and that was "her hollow eyes staring at me." The one who had pried the lid open was the cemetery's security guard. On the day of the burial, the gold bracelet on my sister's wrist went into the coffin with her; on the first night after, the guard dug open the grave, pried the lid, and took the bracelet. He never had time to put things back the way they were: the earth was loose, the crack was open, the rats went in.
