I scrambled and tumbled down the mountain looking for help — and the nearest living soul in that cemetery was the guard in the duty room. One look at my face and he knew what I had seen. He said he'd walk me back for a look, and then, behind my back, he picked up the shovel — the grave pit was ready and waiting. Only in death did I work it out: running with all I had to "call the guard" was handing myself straight into the murderer's hands.
hints: When I heard those sounds, I was walking an open-air mountain path — "my sister's room" cannot be found in any house.
That door, standing ajar, was thick and heavy; it took all my strength to heave it open. There was no floor beyond it — wooden boards on every side.
The "sneaker sounds" were hundreds of claws scraping at coffin wood; my sister's stare was hollow because her eyes were gone — and the man who pried that door open was the very man I ran to for help.

title: The Christmas Present
story: Today Dad told me to go to bed early, but deep in the night I heard a knock at the door. After a while, curious, I pushed my door open to see whether Dad had got the Christmas presents ready. In the living room, a red Christmas tree hung full of ornaments, an unstuffed turkey lay on the dinner table, and a green Santa Claus was hiding in the fireplace. Just then, the knocking at the front door sounded again.
answer: I am red-green colorblind. It was Christmas Eve. Dad told Mom he had to work late into the night — in truth he was staying home to set up a surprise while we slept: he told me to go to bed early precisely so I wouldn't run into the presents at midnight. But Mom believed the "late shift," assumed the house was empty, and brought a strange man home. That knock in the deep of night was him. Hidden in the dark, Dad saw everything that followed. He killed the man, stripped off his skin, crumpled it, and stuffed it into the fireplace — and that became the "green Santa Claus" in my eyes. Then he killed Mom, hollowed out her body, and laid it on the dinner table — the "unstuffed turkey"; everything he took out of her, he hung on that tree, piece by piece. A real Christmas tree is green — it was only after it was hung with "ornaments" that it turned "red" in my eyes. When it was all done, Dad walked out of the house and hanged himself from the eaves outside the door. The night wind swung his body back and forth, knocking it against the door panel, once and once again — the second knock I heard was him. The "Christmas present" I waited for at the door was a house full of blood-red Christmas night — except that the red filling my eyes was the one thing I could not see.
hints: Two of the colors I named are wrong: the Christmas tree and Santa Claus are the exact opposite of what everyone else remembers.
Dad was never "working late" that night; the man who knocked first, deep in the night, was the one Mom dared bring home only because she thought the house was empty.

I'm red-green colorblind: the tree is green, and what hangs on it came out of Mom's body; the "turkey" on the table has no feathers, and the "green Santa" in the fireplace is red all over — the second knock at the door was Dad, hanging from the eaves.

title: The Letter
story: In 2000, I was born. Grandpa was my only family. He said that someday I would meet my parents. In 2009, a masked man killed Grandpa; before he died, he gave me a letter and told me to open it on my 27th birthday. After that, I was adopted. In 2023, I got pregnant. The doctor said my body was a little unusual; soon after, my boyfriend vanished without a trace. In 2024, the moment I gave birth, my baby was stolen. In 2027, I was in a car accident and had an operation; after the surgery, I saw my boyfriend again, four years gone. On my birthday, I opened Grandpa's letter and finally learned who my parents were.
answer: From beginning to end, there is only one person in this story: me. I was born intersex — that is what the doctor meant by "a little unusual." The operation after the 2027 car accident made my body fully male, and the "boyfriend I saw again" after the surgery was my own reflection in the mirror. The answer in the letter: my mother is me, and my father is me. The truth has to be read outward from the year I turned twenty-seven, in both directions. As a man, I finished the letter and went back to 2023, where I approached my four-years-younger self as the "boyfriend," made her pregnant, and left — I am the boyfriend who vanished without a trace. Then I went back to 2009, put on a mask, and went to kill "Grandpa." Grandpa was the me of the cycle before: he had carried the infant back from 2024 to 2000, raised her to nine years old, and waited for exactly this night. That night, he first pressed the letter into my hands, then went and opened the door to let the masked me in — he knew the blade could not be dodged; dodged, the circle would break. Then I settled down in 2009 and endured all the way to 2024, stealing the newborn from outside the delivery room — that newborn was "me" — and carried her back to 2000 to be her "grandpa." I would raise her to 2009, when the door would be knocked on, and the one who walked in would be the masked me. The one who wrote the letter is me; the one who receives it is me; the one who kills me is me; and the one who gives birth to me is me. This circle has no starting point and no way out. On my twenty-seventh birthday, I drew it closed one more time.
hints: Plenty of names appear, but the number of people in this story is far smaller than the number of names.
Able to carry a child, and able to become fully male through surgery — the doctor's one sentence also explains who the "boyfriend" is.

Grandpa, the masked man, the boyfriend, the stolen infant — they are all me at different points in time: I made myself pregnant, gave birth to myself, and carried myself back to 2000 to raise; the night Grandpa was killed, the circle closed.

title: Brother and Sister
story: A brother and sister live in the apartment above mine. The brother is cheerful and outgoing; the sister is quiet and almost never speaks — and yet she is a famous livestreamer. I watch her stream every day. I like her very much. And at last, one day, she noticed me. I shouted four words. Now, besides her streams, she stays with me every day.
answer: That famous streamer who "almost never speaks" never once opened her mouth on camera — because the person in front of the lens was the brother himself. The sister had been dead for a long time: the brother had harbored desires for her that he never should have, and when his confession was refused, he killed her; her body had lain on her own bed ever since. The two siblings looked almost identical. Wearing a wig and her clothes, he kept her channel going — only he never dared make a sound, and the "quiet girl" persona conveniently plugged that loophole. And I was her most devoted fan. After two years of watching her streams, I finally crossed the line: while their home was empty, I picked the lock, slipped in, and burrowed into the dark under her bed. The smell under that bed grew heavier by the day, and I lied to myself that it was some newly lit incense. At night, "she" came home to stream, and I listened through an entire broadcast from under the bed with only the bed skirt between us; after she signed off and the lights went out, I looked up through the gap beside the mattress — the sister lay face-up on the bed, her head hanging over the edge, and those long-emptied eye sockets were aimed straight down at me. She had "noticed me"; we "locked eyes." Scared clean out of my wits, I shouted four words — "Oh Mother of God." Beside the bed, everything went still at once. When the brother lifted the bed skirt, he still hadn't taken off her makeup. Now I truly have no need to hide anymore: I stayed in that room together with her — she on the bed, I beneath it. Every day, besides streaming, she stays with us — and no one else is left in this room but us.
hints: A streamer earns her bread with her voice — a streamer who never talks getting famous for two years means the secret isn't in her throat.
The "her" on camera and the her lying on the bed are two different people; the one on the bed can never open her eyes again.
I wasn't in front of the screen — I was under her bed; the four words I shouted gave me away. The "she" keeping them company now is with two corpses: one on the bed, one beneath it.

title: The Final Exam
story: In the month since I transferred schools, my whole class has decided I'm mentally disturbed; everyone keeps away from me. Only the teacher doesn't think so. But when the final exam rankings went up, I understood — something really is wrong with me.
answer: My deskmate was a student who had been dead for several years. Years before, an accident at this school had killed the boy who used to sit in that very seat — none of the students there now had ever seen him. I transferred in and became his deskmate: he showed up on time every day, went to class with me, took notes, walked into the exam hall with me — no different from anyone alive — except that I was the only person in the world who could see him. In my classmates' eyes, the seat beside me was an empty desk: day after day I chatted and laughed at empty air, passed notes, saved a seat — the verdict "mentally disturbed" followed naturally. The teacher thought differently, because the teacher knew him. Once I happened to mention my deskmate's looks and a phrase he always said, and the teacher's face changed at once — the person I was describing was a student he had taught years ago, long since dead. I could not have known those things, and I could not have invented them so precisely, so the teacher understood: I wasn't mad — I simply "saw" him. Then the final rankings went up: every name in the class was on the list except my deskmate's. The one who walked into every exam at my side had never once had a paper collected. I stared at that list for a long time and finally understood who in this month was truly "not normal" — me, the one who could see the dead.
hints: My classmates avoided me because, in their eyes, the seat beside me was always empty.
My deskmate walked into every exam with me, but no one ever collected his paper — and his name never appears on any list.
The person in that seat died years ago; the teacher knew him, so the teacher never thought I was mad. I, who can see him, am the one who is truly "not normal."

title: The Ranch
story: Mom died and left me a ranch that had sat abandoned for years. I moved in. The next day, a chicken appeared on the ranch out of nowhere; the day after, a cow; the day after that, a sheep. Over a month, the ranch kept gathering new animals. At last I worked out the pattern — and made a mad decision. The next day, a young woman appeared on the ranch. After I saw her face clearly, I went mad.
answer: The ranch can conjure life out of nothing, but it obeys a single rule: it replicates whatever living things its owner has eaten — being eaten is the deepest bond between a creature and the owner. The chicken came on the second day, the cow on the third, the sheep on the fourth — everything I had eaten over the years; and a replica always appears in its youngest, healthiest, peak form. Once I understood the rule, I made that mad decision: the only human being I had never eaten was my dead mother. I ate her remains. The young woman who appeared the next day was a replica of Mom in her youth. What drove me mad was her face — it was exactly my own. Only then did I understand that I was not the child Mom gave birth to: years ago, living alone, she had made this same mad decision — she had cut the flesh from her own body and eaten it, so that the ranch would replicate a young version of herself, a daughter she could raise. That daughter was me. After she made me, she never dared touch the ranch again; she let it fall into ruin until it passed into my hands. What stood before me was Mom in her youth — and at the same time, another me, identical to myself. I thought I was bringing Mom back. All I had done was make her mad decision one more time.
hints: The new arrivals had one thing in common: every one of them had been on my dinner table.
The ranch knows only one rule — replicate whatever its owner eats, always in the youngest, healthiest form.
That woman's face was exactly mine; years ago, Mom made the same mad decision about her own body.

title: The Child in the Wardrobe
story: Late at night, a rustling came from inside my wardrobe. I screwed up my courage and opened the door — and there, squatting inside, was a child. He looked at me and grinned: "Mommy, you found me." I was terrified — where would I have a child? I ordered him to leave my home at once; he burst into frightened tears, calling me Mommy over and over. Looking closely, he did resemble my ex-husband somewhat. But after the miscarriage eight years ago, I was never able to conceive again, and the marriage fell apart too. Sobbing, he said he had a twin little brother, and he spoke mine and my ex-husband's names. Through his tears he asked me: "Do you really not remember me?"
answer: The child was not mistaken: he is my own son — the baby I believed I had lost eight years ago. That year, two worlds crossed paths for a brief moment, and the fetus in my belly was "shifted" into the womb of another me in a parallel world. I thought I had miscarried, and my marriage came apart with it; that other me gained a "twin" out of thin air, and their family of four lived well. Both worlds now held something that should not exist, and a correction was bound to come: the extra child had to return to his own world, and every trace of him in that world had to be erased, one by one. Three years ago, on a night when the two boys were playing hide-and-seek, the elder hid inside the wardrobe — the same house in both worlds, the same wardrobe; within its closed doors the two worlds overlap — and from that world, he disappeared. The elder brother was gone from the photographs; everyone forgot him; only his twin stubbornly remembered, and for that he was diagnosed with delusional disorder, and stayed so for three years; he kept a diary because even his own memory was thinning year by year. When the last trace of him had faded out, the wardrobe door opened on my side. For the child, only a few minutes of the game had passed: he hid in the wardrobe, and Mommy found him — the same face, wearing a stranger's frightened eyes.
hints: He wasn't lying, and he wasn't mistaken — by blood, he truly is my son.
Eight years ago I didn't lose my child: he went somewhere else, grew up well, and over there, another "me" has been raising him.
The same house in two worlds shares this one wardrobe; before the extra child is sent back, he must first be erased clean from that side.

title: The Send-Off
story: An important ceremony is being held tomorrow, so I went to bed early. At midnight, half asleep, I heard a crisp clanging of metal drawing nearer, then two sets of footsteps, one ahead and one behind. When I woke in the morning, a crowd had gathered at my door — five corpses lay side by side on the ground. Once I learned the truth, I saw to it that all five of them were sent to the place they belonged.
answer: The war had just been won, but a remnant band of enemy soldiers who refused to surrender struck out in their dying throes and put a mountain village on the border to the sword. Three soldiers already on the road home stayed behind, forever, on the eve of the new era, to shield the villagers — the most seasoned of them used to say what a pity it was he'd never seen the capital. The villagers wanted to send the three heroes' remains to the capital: in half a month, a farewell ceremony for heroes would be held there. But it was more than thirteen hundred kilometers; a body cannot keep fifteen days, and no living man could walk that road in time either. Out of the crowd stepped a father and son who worked the old trade of corpse-driving: the father would ring the bell, the son would bind the remains between two great bamboo poles. The father stamped out his pipe and said: let the two of us go — someone has to see these men to where they belong. The village headman shook his head: there is no time. But corpse-drivers have a corpse-driver's way of walking — day and night without rest, driving the dead onward on the strength of their own allotted years; they covered thirteen hundred kilometers in fifteen days. I am the one in the capital who arranged the ceremony; the delivery address for the remains was written as my family's own door. That crisp clanging of metal at midnight was the father's signal bell; the cry that rode with it — "the living, stand aside" — I heard through my door. The two footsteps, one before and one behind, were the father and the son; the three heroes' remains rode the bamboo poles between them in utter silence — the dead should make no footsteps. At dawn, the bell came to rest at my door: the three heroes' remains stood upright, and the father and son could not rise again — the last stretch of that road they walked on what was left of their lives, and the letter left beside them explained everything. The next day was the farewell ceremony. I escorted the three soldiers into the hall — and I saw the father and son in with them: men who died on the road escorting heroes have earned a place at a heroes' ceremony. The most seasoned of the three soldiers did, in the end, get to see the capital.
hints: That clanging metal was a road bell — ringing it in the dead of night and calling for folk to stand aside is an old trade that deals with the dead.
The five corpses did not die together: three were delivered, and the two others were the deliverers — only the living leave footsteps.
My house was the endpoint of that escort: thirteen hundred kilometers, fifteen days — the corpse-drivers paid the road with their own years and collapsed only once the men were at my door.

title: The Diary
story: Eight: Today was my eighth birthday. Mom and Dad gave me a toy car. I'm so happy.Nine: This year on my birthday, Dad took us all out for a big dinner. My little brother fell over in the washroom, and Dad and I stood there laughing our heads off; when we got home, Mom scolded the two of us, laughing as she did.Ten: Mom passed away, and Dad's fate is unknown. I have no heart for birthdays.Twelve: This year for my birthday, Dad gave me a border collie and said he's the smartest dog there is. I'm so happy — I'll call him Xiaoguai.Thirteen: Dad tutors me in my studies, because Dad is a writer — but he won't let me read the books he writes.Fourteen: Xiaoguai hasn't had much of an appetite lately. Dad says it's from switching dog food, and he'll be fine in a few days. I admire Dad so much — he understands everything.Fifteen: Dad's book is selling wonderfully and even won an award. This year on my birthday, Dad cooked with his own hands; it was delicious — though the sounds of cooking give me headaches.Sixteen: Dad brushed my hair. Stroking my face, he said sadly that I look more and more like Mom. I know he misses her; my heart aches for him.Seventeen: After finishing the book, my feelings are complicated. I understand now why my brother wanted me to read it. I'm sorry, brother — I love Dad. I remembered Dad saying my brother was terribly afraid of scalding, so I poured boiling water over him. Watching the despair in his eyes, I smiled with joy.
answer: Age ten is the dividing line. The "Dad" in the nine-year-old entry is my stepfather: that day, Dad took my little brother to the washroom and I stood right there laughing along — because I was still a boy back then, and our family was four people: Mom, my stepdad, me, and my little brother. The year I turned ten, my birth father — who had walked out years before and come to hate this family — came back, killed Mom and my stepdad right in front of me, and cooked them into dishes. I saw it all, and the shock took my memory away — that is why the diary has no age eleven; and that same amnesia is why I accepted the "Dad who came back" without a single doubt and moved away with him. From then on, the sound of cooking brought on stress headaches. Not long after, my little brother was made into the "dog": scalded skin sewn into a dog's hide, vocal cords cut out, able to move only on all fours. The "smartest border collie, Xiaoguai," given to me on my twelfth birthday, was my little brother. The "dog food" he ate at first was the flesh of Mom and my stepdad; at fourteen he was switched to real dog food — no wonder his appetite faded. Dad once said my brother was "terribly afraid of scalding" — that was how the dog suit had come to be. He really is a writer: that bestselling, award-winning book was published as a novel, but what it records is the entire process of his crimes — which is why I "was not allowed to read it." At sixteen he brushed my hair and said, "You look more and more like your mother" — I had been born a boy; in my teens he had put me through surgery and rebuilt me into a girl, to raise at his side as Mom's stand-in. Toward this father I developed Stockholm syndrome; my love for him was real. At seventeen, Xiaoguai carried that book over and set it in front of me. I understood everything — and I understood that he was trying to save me. But I chose Dad: "I'm sorry, brother. I love Dad." I remembered Dad saying my brother was terribly afraid of scalding — so I poured a kettle of boiling water over that dog suit, and watching the despair in my brother's eyes, I smiled with joy.
hints: The diary is missing age eleven — something happened the year I turned ten that I couldn't bear to remember.
Xiaoguai is a "he," not an "it"; and Dad's bestselling book, the one I was never allowed to read, is not a novel.
On my ninth birthday, I went into the men's room with Dad to laugh at my little brother; the "me" whose long hair Dad brushed at sixteen is the same child — with one surgery in between.

title: The Swordsman
story: How I came to this bewitched place, I know not — surely by the work of that instructor's zither. What are those four-wheeled things that dart through the streets so swiftly? Several men dared show me disrespect, claiming I had "run a light" or some such. At the flash of their cold steel, I drew my sword and cut them down, and the crowd scattered in flight. Then came burly men in blue who ringed me round — by their dress, officers of the law. I had no wish to make an enemy of the authorities, so I turned to slip away — yet my lightness skill would not rise no matter what. I was seized, and taken to this place's yamen. To this hour I know not why I am here. Several young people have come to see me, weeping and calling me Father. Absurd — I am hardly older than they. But the moment I looked into the mirror, I froze — how could I have grown so old? The officers mean to take me to see a physician, yet I know full well: I am not ill. Can you help me?
answer: He was a young swordsman of renown. In that battle thirty years ago, the enemy instructor drew no blade — he only stroked his zither. The music entered the swordsman's ears, and he slowly lowered his sword, never to wake again: his fellow disciples carried him home, and he sat there for thirty years — his body aging year by year in the real world, while his mind stayed locked inside an illusion woven from the zither's notes, wandering a "city" he could make no sense of at all. The four-wheeled things that dart and race, the passersby saying he "ran a light" — all of it conjured out of that music. In that world, his martial arts work only where the illusion allows: cutting down a few passersby is permitted, but the moment he tries to flee, his lightness skill is taken away — that is his real legs speaking: an old man who has sat for thirty years simply cannot leap anymore. For nearly thirty years the illusion ran smooth as ever, but lately things from "outside" have begun to leak through: the young people weeping and calling him Father are his own son and daughter — when the zither's last note fell, they were still in swaddling clothes; now they are past thirty. The "officers" who would take him to "see a physician" — his children have finally persuaded a famed physician, and the silver needles are drawing him back, inch by inch. The aged face in the mirror is his true body. The illusion has begun to crack for exactly one reason: the treatment is working. So he insists "I am not ill," while inside those cracks he feels fear for the first time in thirty years. "Can you help me?" — he asks it of the people in the illusion, inside the illusion, and none of them can answer. Out in the real world, the old man who has sat for thirty years lets one tear slide from the corner of his eye.
hints: He didn't travel through time: he still lives in the ancient world, and the entire "modern city" is the illusion spun by that zither.
The illusion can hold back blades, but not longing — the young people calling him Father and the ones taking him to "see a physician" are all people from outside pulling him home.

The aged face in the mirror is his true body: when the zither's last note fell he was young, thirty years have passed since, and legs that have sat for thirty years can no longer carry lightness skill.

title: The Blindfolded Guessing Game
story: I woke to find myself tied to a bed, my eyes blindfolded. A voice beside me said: "Don't struggle. We're going to play blindfolded guessing. Guess them all right, and I'll let you go." I didn't know what was happening, but to survive, I could only play along.The first time, I felt a pair of hands — and I knew my wife was already dead.The second time, I felt a strip of cloth. I knew exactly where it had come from, and I broke down.Before the third round began, I heard footsteps. This object was easy to guess — but once I had felt it out, I no longer wanted to live.
answer: The three "objects," each one closer to me than the last. The first was a pair of very, very small hands — the unborn child from my wife's womb. The child had been taken out and laid by my hand; my wife, who must have shielded her with her life, was certainly already dead. The second, the strip of cloth, was the very one bound over my eyes; before the game began, he had lifted it off and pressed it into my hand — yet before my eyes everything stayed pitch black: my eyes had already been destroyed. The blindfold was only a prop, there to make me believe I could still see. The footsteps before the third round were this round's "object" walking in on its own: he took my hand and pressed it against his face — a face exactly like mine, identical down to where each whisker of stubble lay. He was an old acquaintance of mine, a man who had envied me for half his life and spent years carving himself, cut by cut, into a copy of me. He killed my wife and child because family living under my roof would see through a false me at a glance; he destroyed my eyes so that from beginning to end I could identify "me" by touch and voice alone. This blindfolded guessing game was his dress rehearsal — verification performed by the person most familiar with me in all the world: myself. I guessed everything right; the verification passed. From this day on, he will go on living with my face, my name, my home — and there is no one left in the world who can expose him. Blind and bound, I cannot even prove that I am me. The moment I felt that face, I understood all of it — and that is why I no longer wanted to live.
hints: The three "objects" come closer and closer: the first came from my wife's body, the second from my own head.
The cloth came off, and still I saw black — beneath the blindfold there were no eyes left that could see.
The third object walked in the door on its own. When I felt that face, I understood: what he wants is not my life — it's my whole self.

title: Zhang San and Li Si
story: One day, the words "You must kill Zhang San" appeared out of nowhere on my ceiling. I hurriedly wiped them away, but the next day the sentence reappeared, exactly as before. I didn't know any Zhang San — but once I understood where those words had come from, I began searching for him. Some ten years later, in 2010, I finally found Zhang San and killed him with a single stroke of the blade. He looked at me in disbelief as he died. My name is Li Si — and perhaps because I had touched him, his corpse vanished, impossibly. In the last month before my death, I finally learned why Zhang San had to die. I set down the first newspaper of the new century in my hands, and went to do the thing that should have been done long ago.
answer: My time runs opposite to this world's: everyone's days flow from 2000 toward 2020; mine flow backward from 2020 toward 2000. The words on the ceiling were a letter addressed to one person: no one but me could see them, and until I read them, they could not be destroyed — wiped away, they would reappear the next night, exactly as before — because they came from "the hand that had already written them," part of the closed loop. The one who wrote them was me: in the last days of my backward run, I left the words on a ceiling in January 2000, waiting for the me standing at the start of the backward journey — 2020 — to read them and set out after Zhang San. I searched for ten years, from 2020 to 2010, and killed him with a single stroke. Dying, Zhang San recognized my face — ten years before, it was he who had killed me. A corpse slain by a backward-runner like me cannot stay in forward-flowing time: his body vanished into thin air, hurled back into the past; his dying final sight landed on himself as a child, and with the last of his words he told that child: "You must kill Li Si." The child grew up holding those words as fate, and on January 1, 2000, he killed Li Si. The new century's first day of news ran the story under the headline "Zhang San Kills Li Si" — and by then, I was backward-running into the final month of my own life. When I finished the paper, I understood everything: Zhang San killing me is an accomplished fact no one can change; that debt of blood could only be collected by me, come back the other way around. I set down the paper, wrote that line on the ceiling of that room, then ran on to the end of my backward road and vanished, just as he had — backward-runners leave no corpse behind when they die, and Li Si's body was never found either. We are each other's murderer and each other's dying words; two closed loops bite together into one dead knot, and the paper will never print a second story about us.
hints: The words on the ceiling are a letter to one person: others can't see them, and they can't be wiped away.
My time runs the other way from this world's: I live backward from 2020 toward 2000.
Dying, Zhang San recognized my face — it was he who killed "Li Si" on January 1, 2000; and when he himself was a child, he heard that same sentence too.

title: Rules of the Dorm
story: Rules of the Dorm.Rules in black ink:1. Do not use the bathroom at night.2. The dorm provides food, but do not be greedy with it.3. There are not two roommates — there are three.Rules in red ink:4. There are only two roommates.5. There is only one roommate.
answer: This was never a dorm — it is an ordinary house, and the "I" who wrote the first three rules is a stealth lodger living in it in secret, like the family in the film Parasite, hiding inside someone else's home and living off it. The rules in black were my survival code: never use the bathroom at night, for fear my footsteps would wake the family; never eat too much, for fear the shrinking food would give me away. Rule three was the discovery I least wanted to admit: besides the husband and wife, a third person was hiding in that house — a stealth lodger who had moved in before me; all those night sounds I couldn't explain and could only blame on myself were his doing. Two pilfering mouths drained the food faster and faster, until the couple grew suspicious and started searching the house. The first-comer decided to strike first: one night, the husband was killed and buried under the ground. From my hiding place I counted the people still alive in that house and wrote the fourth rule in red ink: the wife, and the first-comer — only two roommates left. The fifth rule is in different handwriting: his. He had found me, the other one who had uncovered the same truth, and buried me alongside the husband. Now, besides him, the house holds only the wife: one roommate left. One name remains on the list, and the rules are his turn to write.
hints: The "dorm" was never a dorm — the people who own this house don't know others are living in it with them.
The first three rules are one lodger's survival code; rule three means: the people hiding in this house are more than just me.
The red ink is a countdown of the living: the hand that wrote rule four and the hand that wrote rule five are no longer the same.

title: Dad
story: My little sisters are sunbathing on the balcony, my big brother is having a bath, and the clothes were thrown into the trash by Dad. I went to the room to look for Dad. My chin is covered in blood. Dad is convulsing all over; he hasn't long left. This is the death Dad deserves most — what karma.
answer: None of this family are people — we are a litter of cats: Dad is the father cat; big brother, my little sisters, and I are his kittens. Dad abused us for a long time: he killed big brother and stewed him in the pot — that was his "bath"; the pelt he peeled off, he threw into the trash — those were the "clothes" he threw away; my little sisters he cut apart and laid out on the balcony to dry — dried into jerky, that was their "sunbathing." My limbs he had broken long before, so I could only crawl with my chin against the floor, and the whole way to him my chin scraped itself bloody. I followed the smell from the pot into the room — big brother was stewing in it. And karma had long been on its way: to kill rats, Dad had laid deadly poison all over the yard; starving, we had caught and eaten the rats that dropped where they stood, and the poison stayed inside our bodies. Today, stewing big brother, he tasted the soup — poison he laid with his own hand, hunger he brought about with his own hand, a pot he stewed with his own hand: the deadly dose came back to his own mouth through the rats, through big brother, through that soup, without one inch of detour. Now he lies convulsing all over, nearly gone. This is a death he arranged for himself, step by step — what karma.
hints: "I," "Dad," "big brother," and the "little sisters" are not people — every one of them has a tail.
"Bath," "sunbathing," and "clothes" are all literally true: the pot, the jerky, and the pelt peeled off and thrown away.
The rat poison in Dad's yard came back to his own mouth by way of a rat, then big brother, then that pot of soup.

title: The Knee Pads
story: Three years. I'm home at last. But I can't swallow the food at home. I hold out, watching my knee pads. At last, I can't hold back any longer.
answer: For those three years, my parents and I were taken by a kidnapper with monstrous tastes and forced into a "human centipede": I was the middle segment, kneeling and crawling for hours on end. He wanted us to stay alive, so the knee pads were "equipment" he issued me, swapped for new ones whenever they wore through — and for those three years, they were the only thing that belonged to me. What went into my mouth was what no ordinary person could swallow. No one died; all three of us were brought back alive. But three years of that feeding left my body accepting only that one way of eating: home again, the dishes on the table are perfectly normal, yet I cannot force down a single bite — and I crave the "taste" of those three years more and more. I came home with pica. I look at my knee pads the way one looks at the only "companion" of three years. In the end I couldn't hold back: I put the knee pads on and knelt back down onto the floor. Next to the dinner table, it is down there that I feel at ease.
hints: No one in my family died in those three years — but I never once spent a day on my feet.
The knee pads were the kidnapper's "equipment": to keep us alive longer, the knees that crawled had to be protected.
I can't swallow normal meals because my stomach and my heart both accept only what those three years gave me — what I crave was never food.

title: Grandma's Funeral
story: February 20: Grandma passed away, and Mom, Dad, and I went back to the countryside for the funeral. Sleeping in the old house that night, I was woken by the big yellow dog barking; half asleep, I heard someone chopping wood in the yard.February 21, the vigil: Dad whispered to me, "Sleep on your own tonight — there's something wrong with Mom." In the evening I went to see Mom; she gripped my hand and said, "There's something wrong with your father. First thing tomorrow, we leave."February 22: Mom seemed back to normal. But at dinner, I found the problem anyway, and quietly told Dad. Dad said he had a way to deal with it.February 23: Wonderful — Dad dealt with the problem, just as he said. Only now, he's stopped going to the gym, and Mom has stopped wearing makeup.
answer: Across these four days of diary entries, the dead were more than just Grandma — of our family of three, not one walked out of that old house alive.The ones who did it were replacements that came out of mirrors: such things cast no reflection, and they fear mirrors above all else. The "wood-chopping" on the night of February 20 was the chopping of people — my real father was killed that very night. On February 21, the false Dad struck first, telling me "something's wrong with Mom"; that evening, my real mother, sensing something wrong with her husband, said "first thing tomorrow, we leave" — and that night she was killed too, her body fed to the big yellow dog, wedding ring and all. That is why the "Mom" of the days after never once mentioned leaving: she had no way of knowing that promise ever existed.On February 22, the dog that had swallowed the bodies became living evidence, and the false parents stewed it for lunch. In my dish I found Mom's wedding ring — and then I saw the "Mom" at the table wearing one just like it: a replica the replacements had prepared in advance, precisely so they wouldn't be seen through. I understood something had happened to Mom, and quietly told "Dad." The "problem" his "way" was meant to solve was me.On February 23, the one who wrote "wonderful" was no longer the original me. The replacements never go to the gym and never wear makeup anymore, because neither can be done without a mirror — and a mirror holds no reflection of them.
hints: Across these four days, the quiet deaths in this family added up to more than just Grandma.
The wedding ring in the dish was Mom's; she never got to leave. The "Mom" wearing the matching ring on her hand stopped being her long before.
What replaced them came out of the mirror — and the gym and the makeup table cannot be lived without.

title: Hide-and-Seek
story: I brought my wife and son back to my home village to tend the family graves, and my son kicked up a fuss to play hide-and-seek — I would be "it." I know every nook and cranny of this village, and before long I had found my wife. Seeing the confident look in her eyes, I knew our son was hidden well. But this is, after all, the place I grew up in — better than anyone, I know where a person can best hide. When I reached that place, I heard one sentence, and my scalp went numb on the spot.
answer: I never did find my son — what was waiting for me in that most hidden of places was someone else.It was a gap inside the walls of the old house, a secret hiding spot only my childhood best friend and I knew about. In that game of hide-and-seek more than twenty years ago, he squeezed himself in and jammed the entrance shut behind him, hidden without a single gap to give him away. I searched round after round and couldn't find him; afraid of a scolding, I wandered off to do something else — and I never dared tell any adult about that place. The grown-ups searched for him for days on end, and in the end they all decided he had run off to some faraway place on his own.He never got out. Today I lifted open the same entrance, and what came from inside was his voice — "You finally found me." That game of hide-and-seek, he has hidden in for more than twenty years, waiting until "it" finally touched the edge of the door.
hints: My son wasn't hiding there; that place hides my own childhood.
Twenty-some years ago, in that same hiding spot, I lost a playmate — and I never told a soul.
The voice from inside belonged to my childhood friend — dead in there for twenty-some years; this game of hide-and-seek only ends today.

title: Missing Person Notice
story: Missing person notice: Yi Tian, female, 31, divorced, a doctor by profession, missing for one month.Clue one: Yi Tian held a life insurance policy; the beneficiary is her father.Clue two: Her ex-husband recently married Yi Tian's colleague.Clue three: Yi Tian's father has spent years rescuing stray cats.Clue four: In the small hours this morning, someone fell from the clock tower and died; the time of death was between three and four a.m.
answer: Yi Tian is the only killer. During the marriage, her husband had an affair with her colleague; she sat on that knowledge and quietly arranged the divorce — she had two people to punish, and patience to spare.The revenge began with a brain transplant. Yi Tian is a surgeon; the colleague, an anesthesiologist at the same hospital. Her offer to the colleague: help me carry out the surgery, and the "ex-husband" will marry you — his identity, his fortune, all of it yours. What the colleague had always wanted was the seat of "the ex-husband's wife"; Yi Tian had seen through that, which is why she dared make the offer at all.On the operating table, Yi Tian swapped brains with her ex-husband. When she woke, Yi Tian was living in the ex-husband's body; her old body, now holding the ex-husband's brain, was kept under anesthesia and never woke again. To the world outside, only one line: Yi Tian has gone missing.Afterward, the "ex-husband" married the colleague — the other half of the bargain, honored. After the wedding, the colleague disappeared too: the second name on the list, her body fed by Yi Tian's father to the stray cats he had spent years rescuing.In the small hours of this morning, Yi Tian finished the endgame: she carried the old body — with the ex-husband inside it — up the clock tower and pushed it off. Before the fall, that body was still alive; the ex-husband within stayed unconscious the whole way down, dying at last under the identity of "Yi Tian," by "Yi Tian's" chosen manner of death. The police will conclude that Yi Tian, missing for a month, came back and jumped, and close the case; the insurance money will be paid out to her father — the father knew, and he accepted this "repayment."The "Yi Tian" who fell from the clock tower did not commit suicide. The person Yi Tian killed was "herself" — and she herself is alive and well, living under her ex-husband's identity.
hints: The "Yi Tian" who fell from the clock tower in the small hours neither killed herself nor struggled — she was already unconscious long before the fall.
During this missing month, Yi Tian's body and her life never left their place; only the occupant changed.
The brain transplant: the "ex-husband's" body holds Yi Tian, and the "Yi Tian" on the clock tower held the ex-husband; the colleague who vanished after the wedding was the second name on the list.

title: Kill the Werewolf
story: Day one, daytime. On a desert island, the judge announced: "Among the five of you hides an evil werewolf. Find him." The five were me, my husband, my son, the hunter, and the witch. I drew the villager.The hunter told everyone: "My ability is setting traps. I hope to catch the werewolf with one. If anyone else steps into a trap, that's your own bad luck."Day one, night. I didn't dare sleep deeply. Sure enough, at midnight my husband's hands closed around my throat — he was the werewolf! Just as I thought I was done for, my son leapt out and saved me; he said he was the guard. Together, my son and I killed my husband. After my husband fell, a wolf's tail appeared behind his body.Day two, daytime. The judge said: "Today he died. He was a villager turned wolf, but not the werewolf." I looked at my husband's corpse; it had already been gnawed beyond recognition. I was puzzled: he wasn't the werewolf? Then who had been eating him?Day two, night. I dreamed I was in a deep pit, and on the pit wall there was a white ladder. I climbed out along it, feeling unspeakably comfortable all over, as if I had been saved.Day three, daytime. The judge said: "Today he died." My son's body lay soft and limp, but there were no marks of being eaten. The witch pointed at me: "One vial of antidote, one vial of poison. She was going to die last night — I was the one who saved her." Was it the witch who saved me? That comfortable feeling all over last night must have been her saving me.Day three, night. With my own eyes I watched the witch pour poison down the hunter's throat. I was about to ask whether she had the wrong person when she suddenly bared her teeth and tore into the hunter — she was the werewolf! I fled in terror.Day four, daytime. The judge said: "Today he died." Before me lay the hunter's bitten-to-pieces corpse. The judge said to me and the witch: "You may go." The witch asked: "Aren't we going to find the werewolf?" The judge gave me a half-smiling look: "Already found."
answer: This round of Werewolf was "my" subconscious world under deep hypnosis. The judge was not a player but the psychiatrist treating me; every scene that played out around the table was the re-enactment of a real memory.In reality there was no island. A family of three went on an outing and fell into a deep pit trap the hunter used for poaching. While the three of us cried for help, the hunter — afraid his illegal poaching would be exposed — turned and left. That is why, at the start, he said, "Step into a trap and that's your own bad luck." There was no food in the pit. Days later, my hunger-maddened husband laid hands on me; he was that first night's "werewolf." My son threw himself between us to protect his mother, and mother and son killed him together. That was the truth behind the "guard."On day two, "a villager turned wolf, but not the werewolf" was the doctor correcting me: he had only been driven mad by hunger; he was not evil. My husband's corpse was gnawed beyond recognition because we survived on his flesh.My son's wounds festered, and he died on the second night — the soft, limp body was not eaten: I am the mother. I ate my husband's flesh and never touched my son. The deep pit and the white ladder in my second-night dream were my real escape: the pit was too deep, so I pushed my family's bones one by one into the earthen wall and climbed out on the "ladder" they formed, clawing my way back to life. When the witch said, "She was going to die last night — I saved her," the one who saved me was myself.By the time I climbed out of that pit, my mind had already cracked open, and another personality had been born to act for me: she poisoned the hunter, bit him to pieces, and ate him just as she had eaten my husband. That was the "witch" — the true werewolf of this game. So on day four, when the judge said "already found," the one he looked at with a half-smile was "us."The treatment stopped there: the werewolf had been found. The murderer was my other personality.
hints: The island, the role cards, the deal — none of it exists. This is not a real game, and one of the five is not a player.
The trap, the deep pit, and the bone-white ladder all really happened; the gnawed corpses were how we stayed alive.
The witch is the other personality I split into — she is the murderer. The judge is the psychiatrist: the werewolf was inside "my" body.

title: The Red Clothes
story: I came back from a funeral, and my roommate pulled me aside: the school had been haunted lately — lots of people jolted awake in the middle of the night, each having dreamed of a figure in red standing by the bed, smiling at them. When everyone compared notes, not a single face in those dreams was the same. That night I dreamed it too; I couldn't see the face clearly, only felt that red outfit was oddly familiar. By the following night, I finally understood.
answer: No ghost came calling at this school — the dead everyone dreamed of were real, but they hadn't come on their own; they had been eaten, into people's stomachs.The canteen's contractor bought "unclaimed" and resold bodies from a shady middleman at the funeral home and turned them into dishes. This story follows a single supernatural rule: whoever eats the flesh of the dead dreams of the dead that night; he smiles as he watches you, because he recognizes who it was that ate him.The faces in my roommates' dreams were all different, because the dead numbered far more than one — with the whole school eating, a single body would never be enough. The red clothes were burial clothes: only when the very old die — at what is called a joyful funeral, a long life celebrated rather than mourned — is a full set of red worn, and that batch of "goods" at the funeral home was mostly long-lived elders from joyful funerals.The red outfit I found familiar came from the mourning hall: the funeral I had attended was a joyful one too. My relative lay in state at the front of the hall dressed in red burial clothes, and I kept vigil for three days. In the two days since returning to school, I had eaten every single meal at the canteen. In the second night's dream, that face finally drew close — it was him. My relative's body had been carried off from the funeral home before burial and sold into the canteen. Only then did I understand why the school was "haunted," and why I dreamed of him: I had been eating him for two days straight.
hints: The prerequisite for dreaming of the figure in red is simple: having eaten at the canteen that day.
The red clothes are burial clothes; every face in the dreams is different because there is more than one dead — and they are all in the canteen.
The one I dreamed of was my relative — his body was sold into the canteen, and these past few days I have been eating him too.

title: A Sense of Security
story: After my mother died protecting me, I always lived on edge, until I met a boyfriend who could give me that same sense of security. But the moment he lost his job, my unease came back. Finally, one day, he thought of a way — and being a narcissist, he drew immense satisfaction from it. A few days later, I was filled with a sense of security again.
answer: My sense of security came from the smell of the dead.My mother died protecting me: in the car crash, she pressed me down beneath her body. During the three days of the wake, I slept pressed against her body, and ever since, only that smell could give me sound sleep — to me, it was the smell of "Mom is still here."My boyfriend was a mortuary makeup artist at the funeral home. Every day he came home carrying the scent of the cold-storage room and embalming fluid — the closest thing in the world to the smell of the dead — so I felt especially at ease around him. After he lost his job, the smell was gone, and my unease returned. He had long seen my strange fixation, and he knew exactly what his unemployment meant.The way he thought of was suicide. To a narcissist like him, personally serving as "the source of her security" was the ultimate satisfaction. Two or three days after a person dies, the smell of decay begins to seep out. A few days later, the smell of rot drifted from his room, and I finally slept soundly again.
hints: What calms me was never a living person, but a certain smell.
The first time I ever slept peacefully was during a wake.
It is the smell of the dead: my boyfriend's funeral-home job used to bring it home, and his unemployment took it away; his way was to turn himself into the source of that smell.

title: Three Days
story: Day one. At midnight I suddenly heard a baby crying; a while later, the sound of a toilet flushing came from inside the house. I live alone — there couldn't be anyone in the bathroom. I was terrified and decided to get someone over to check the house the next day.Day two. The flushing sound was gone; the baby's crying was still there. I invited a spiritual master in. He studied me with a dark face for a long moment, then said: this house is haunted; I'll look into it. At midnight, a rustling came from the living room; I opened the door to look — it was the master, hunched over, groping across the floor as if searching for something. I thought nothing of it and went back to sleep.Day three. The master sat at the dining table, chin resting in both hands, motionless. I asked him how the investigation was going; he gave no response. I returned to the bedroom — the floor was strewn with scraps of paper, and a pitch-black baby was crawling toward me.
answer: Three people have died in this home — and the first to die was me, the one writing this down.My husband had someone else and wanted to start a life without us. At midnight on day one, he killed me, cut my body apart, and flushed it down the toilet piece by piece — that flushing sound was him disposing of me; the child was still alive at the time, crying from hunger and fear.The master invited on day two truly could see. His face was dark because the moment he walked in, he understood: the "ghost" haunting this house was me, the one paying him to investigate. That night he hunched and groped around the living room searching for his own head — at midnight, my husband decided he was digging too deep and hacked him to death to silence him. The one sitting at the dining table on day three, chin resting in both hands, was the master's spirit: his head had been cut off and set back in place, long past rejoining, which is why he never answered.The scraps of paper on the bedroom floor were joss paper my husband burned for me. Along with the paper money, he sent one more thing: on day three, he killed the child and burned him to me together with the paper. The pitch-black baby crawling toward me was my child.From day one, the only one in this house who didn't know she was already dead was me.
hints: Count the sounds across these three days: crying, running water, the rustle of searching — not all of their owners are alive.
The thing the master groped for all night in the dark was resting right in his own hands on day three.
I have been dead since day one: the flushing was my husband flushing my body down, the paper scraps were joss paper burned for me, and the black baby crawling toward me is my child.

title: The Inn
story: I'm the owner of an inn. Today a person died in my inn. Here is what happened today.11:30 — the middle-aged woman from Room 122 begged me in tears: save my child. A child lay unconscious in the lobby; I couldn't grasp what was going on and could only urge her to call the police at once.11:45 — I heard a great rush of water: a pipe had burst in Room 120. After I fixed it, the girl staying in Room 120 suddenly kissed me on the cheek, and I felt terribly embarrassed.12:00 — the police arrived, and a crowd filled the lobby. The old lady from Room 121 looked guilty, muttered "this has nothing to do with us," and tried to slip away. The woman from Room 122 pointed at her and cursed: "Have you no conscience?!" The two fell to grappling. At some point the unconscious child had woken up, screaming "Don't you bully my grandma!" and threw himself at the woman, hitting her. I hurried over to break up the fight and took a few punches from a middle-aged man from Room 120; he roared at me: "You shouldn't have meddled!"12:30 — the woman failed to stop the old lady from leaving. An officer shouted: "Hey, you can't leave!" But as if she hadn't heard, she took the child and left the inn. I heard the officer's voice grow farther and farther away. Ah, well — someone died here.
answer: There is no inn, and I'm not the owner — I was saving a child from the water when I myself went under, and I've been in a coma ever since. Everything above is a dream my unconscious mind stitched together out of the sounds around me and the sensations on my body: because I run an inn myself, my subconscious dressed the scene as one.The woman at 11:30 was my mother. She cried out "save my child" and called the police; the "child" lying unconscious in the lobby was me. Later in the dream, when that child "woke up," lunged at my mother, and shouted "Don't you bully my grandma!" — that was really the brat doing it. The dream sewed two children into one: first I lay there, then he did the moving for me, because he was the old lady's grandson.The rush of water at 11:45 was the ambulance arriving. "Fixing the pipe" was the nurse giving me first aid; "the girl kissed me" was her bending down for mouth-to-mouth. Later a middle-aged man appeared in Room 120 because off the "120" — the ambulance, that is — first stepped the nurse, then the doctor; the man's punches were the doctor's chest compressions, pressing my sternum one beat at a time, and "you shouldn't have meddled" was someone standing by, sighing the words aloud.At 12:00 the police arrived. The old lady in Room 121 was the brat's grandmother, afraid of being held responsible and trying to take the child and go; my mother grabbed her and they struggled; the brat threw himself at my mother and hit her. At 12:30 the old lady left with the child — morally indefensible, but beyond the law's reach. Yet the officer's "Hey, you can't leave!" was never shouted at her: it was the people rescuing me, bent close to my ear, calling to me again and again not to go. Their voices grew farther away because I was hearing less and less.Ah, well — someone died here. The one who died was me.
hints: The room numbers start at 120 — the ambulance number here — and the ambulance arrives before the police: everything in this "inn" comes from the scene of a rescue.
Room 120 holds a girl first and a middle-aged man later; the child in the lobby holds two children in turn as well.
I'm drowning, in a coma: the kiss is mouth-to-mouth, the punches are chest compressions, "you can't leave" is them begging me not to die — the one who died is me.

title: The Curse
story: The landlord confessed his feelings to me. One look at the greasy fat man in front of me and I turned him down flat. To get away from him, a girlfriend of mine introduced me to a new place; its landlord was an old granny, and only then did I relax. My first night after moving in, I vaguely heard the granny next door humming some strange tune; that night I also discovered someone crouched on my windowsill peeping in — when spotted, he bolted, and his retreating figure looked like a thin man. On the seventh day, a dry rustling filled the room; I got up and searched but found nothing, yet the moment I lay back down, it came again. Half asleep and half awake, I felt something licking me. When I woke the next morning, the sight before me made my scalp crawl.
answer: The granny, the new landlord, was the fat man's mother; this apartment and this "introduction" were all his arrangement. After I rejected him, he sought out that girlfriend of mine, paid her half upfront — asking only that she talk me into this apartment — with the balance to follow once it was done. She took the money and delivered me through this door.When I turned him down, he had heard himself called "greasy," so he began taking the knife to his own flesh, cutting it away slice by slice, until he had slimmed down a whole size. The "thin man" crouched on my windowsill at night was him — the last time I saw him, he was still fat, which is why the retreating figure never matched. The slices of flesh he delivered to his mother, package after package: "Mom, I've lost weight again. She called me a greasy man — so the flesh is for you, Mom."The granny stuffed her son's flesh into my mattress, my quilt, and my pillow, humming that "curse" next door night after night — Mom has her ways of making the girl love you. It was no spell at all, only a mother working magic on her son's behalf. By the seventh day, the flesh hidden deep in the bedding had rotted through and bred maggots: the moment I got up to search, the larvae shrank back into the meat; the moment I lay down, they stirred again. The rustling, the licking — all of it was them. When I opened my eyes the next morning, the whole bed crawled with a dense mass of maggots, working their way up the pillow toward my face.
hints: The girlfriend who introduced me to this place took someone's money; the new landlord and the old one are one family.
I couldn't recognize the thin man doing the peeping because the last time I saw him, he wasn't thin yet.
What was sewn into the bedding was flesh cut from his own body; the rotting, maggot-ridden meat is the source of the rustling.

title: Who Is the Liar
story: Number One: I killed the deadweight. Just before I died, I thought I heard someone jump off a building.Number Two: I told you all along — no infighting. Number Three strangled Number Five to death with his bare hands, and his own face had gone a frightening green.Number Three: Number Four and her boyfriend parted ways with us by bus. What I never expected was that Number Five was actually a man.Number Four: I took a bullet. With the loot split so unevenly, everyone was scheming against everyone — looks like only one of us walks out of here alive today.Number Five: Number Four caught Number Six poisoning Number Three, and shot Number Six dead over it — but she seems to have been shot herself.Number Six: I watched Number One cook the meal. After the meal, Number Two killed Number One.Of these six statements, only one person is lying. What happened?
answer: The only liar is Number Five. This was the in-fighting after a gang split their loot, in a hideout inside a building with a bus depot downstairs.Number Four was the "deadweight" Number One spoke of: she got the smallest share and the lowest standing. Number One shot her dead and turned her into that "meal" — so Number Four's "I took a bullet" is true. Number Two was Number Four's boyfriend; partway through the meal, he recognized her ring in the pot. He killed Number One, gathered up what was left of his girlfriend, and jumped from the window, falling to his death on the roof of the bus shelter below. Number One died slowly; what he heard in his last moments was that crash. Only later did Number Three see the two of them lying side by side on the shelter roof — which is why he said, "Number Four and her boyfriend parted ways with us by bus."The meal was poisoned, and the one who poisoned it was Number Five. Number Three turned green from the poison and, before dying, fought back with everything he had, strangling Number Five to death with his bare hands. In the struggle he tore open Number Five's clothes, and only at death's door came out with "Number Five was actually a man" — he died without ever understanding that what was hidden under that loose robe was more than one man's frame.Number Five and Number Six were conjoined twins; Number Six grew on Number Five's chest. Number Five cross-dressed for years in wide, loose robes precisely to hide Number Six underneath. In that one lie of his, the poisoning is true, and Number Four taking a bullet is true; only one piece was swapped out: "Number Six was shot dead" never happened. He wanted Number Six erased from the list of the dead, so that everyone who came asking would believe Number Six was gone.Number Five stopped breathing, but the one growing on his chest was still alive. Number Four said "only one of us walks out alive," and she wasn't wrong: the one who walked out of this slaughter alive was Number Six, whom no one ever counted.
hints: Check Number Five's line against the others: the poisoning is true, Number Four taking a bullet is true — only "Number Six is dead" has no second witness.
Only at death did Number Three learn for the first time that "Number Five is a man" — think about how Number Five dressed in public, and the loose coat he never once took off.

Number Five and Number Six were conjoined; Number Six was hidden on Number Five's chest all along. Number Five's lie made everyone believe Number Six was dead — the one who walked out alive in the end is Number Six.

title: The Nanny
story: The new nanny slacked off all day, and the house was an unbelievable mess. I ran to the living room to complain to my father, but he said: since when has this family ever hired a nanny? I went back to the bedroom and confronted the nanny; she put on an innocent face: isn't your father long dead? I didn't know whom to believe. I rushed out the front door and ran straight into Auntie Zhang, our neighbor. What she said made me fall apart completely.
answer: Both of them were telling the truth — the thing that was broken was "me." My father died three years ago. Since then "I" have lived alone, my old mental illness growing heavier and heavier: on the hardest days, I would "see" the father in my memory there in the living room. Today was no different: the one I went complaining to was my own hallucination. The hallucination's line "since when has this family hired a nanny" was true, because it was a fact "I" had known in my heart all along and simply refused to admit. The "nanny," though, was a real stranger — a thief who had figured out that only one sick person was left in this house; days ago she climbed in through the back window and never left, planning to carry off everything of value bit by bit. She had long since grown used to hearing "me" calling "Dad" at the empty air, so when confronted, she could shut "me" up with one line: "isn't your father long dead?" A thief ransacking the house became, in "my" eyes, a lazy nanny. Auntie Zhang saw "me" rush out with red eyes and grabbed hold of me: "Child, there's a thief in your house! This afternoon I saw with my own eyes someone climb in through your back window — you've lived alone ever since your dad passed. Call the police, quick!" The nanny is a thief; the father is a hallucination; in this house, "I" am the only one left alive. Both statements were true — the one falling apart in between them was "me."
hints: Don't rush to pick one — both of them may be telling the truth.
Only one living person remains in this house; the trouble of "seeing" Father lives in "my" eyes and "my" brain.
The "nanny" is no nanny at all: she is a thief who came in through the back window and has been hiding for days in this house where only one patient lives.

title: Karma
story: October 1, overcast. The quiet life of our family of three has been broken — they came to our door after all, calling us demons. Xiao Wang and the others have all been killed, and whether my husband lives or dies is unknown. I'm hiding in a cabinet. Wait — it sounds like someone is coming.October 2, light rain. Damn it — the police have lately taken to suspecting my husband. I've gone hungry for days now, and the child won't stop crying. There — it's finally quiet.October 3, rainstorm. Seawater has risen to the fourth floor, food is running short, and my husband has been in very poor spirits today. The child was hungry, so I had to take the inflatable boat out to look for something to eat.October 5, clear. Today my husband and I went to pay our respects at the grave of our best friend, Xiao Li; Xiao Fang and Xiao Ming came too. Ten years ago, Xiao Li led us into the mountains and saved all our lives. We all miss him.
answer: Ten years ago, Xiao Li insisted, over everyone's objections, on organizing that trip into the mountains. A landslide struck, trapping the whole group in a cave. Rescue was slow to come; to hold out until it did, they ate the injured Xiao Ming and made it out alive. Ten years later, Xiao Ming's family, having learned the truth, began their revenge, killing the survivors of that year one by one. In the instant Xiao Li died, his consciousness returned to the cave ten years ago, standing before that multiple-choice question: who gets eaten? He changed the answer again and again: swap in Xiao Fang, and Xiao Fang's family goes to the police, who put every last one of them under suspicion; swap in Xiao Wang, and the world slides into another disaster, seawater drowning the city; in one round, the one pushed out was even his own wife. But however he swapped, the reckoning only changed its face and arrived right on time — this calamity was the cause he himself had insisted on planting, and he alone had to bear its fruit. The only thing that returned to the cave with him was this diary written by his wife: in every round, the ending fell in early October ten years on, so the diary always gained one more final page. October 1 is the original timeline — Xiao Ming was the one eaten, and it was Xiao Ming's family who came for revenge; behind the October 2 page, the one eaten in that round was Xiao Fang; in the October 3 page, the one eaten was Xiao Wang — the diary says "my husband was in poor spirits" because that round's husband was Xiao Li himself, who had just watched with his own eyes as he got the answer wrong yet again. Only October 4 has no page: in that round, the one eaten was "me," the one holding the pen; the diary had no owner, and that page can never be written. On October 5, Xiao Li finally chose himself. "It was my own stubbornness that trapped us all — eat me instead." Everyone held out until rescue arrived, and the diary stopped on a clear day. In his very last moment, he glimpsed the woman who, in that world, should have become his wife: she came to mourn him, arm in arm with another.
hints: The four diary entries come from the same hand, but they do not describe the same October.
At the end of each entry, the multiple-choice question in that cave ten years ago has swapped its answer once more; first work out who was eaten in each round.
The October 4 page wasn't torn out — it can never be written, because the one holding the pen was that round's answer.

title: Twenty
story: I married far away, to another country, and was near my due date, so my best friend flew out specially to stay with me. After two days in the house, she quietly told me: something is wrong with this house — every midnight there's crying. I laughed it off as her being unable to sleep in a strange bed. That night she fell to her death in the backyard; in the soil beside her body, gouged out with her finger, were two crooked Chinese characters: twenty. After the funeral I couldn't sleep, and moved into the guest room where she had stayed. At midnight I heard the crying too — I followed the sound and pushed open the door at the end of the hallway, the one I had never once opened.
answer: My best friend wasn't just failing to sleep in a strange bed. The guest room she stayed in sits right beside the door at the end of the hallway — the "storage room" in my husband's mouth, in truth a hidden shrine room. Every midnight my husband went in to light a stick of incense and set out an offering for what was enshrined there, and in passing started a looped recording of sutra-chanting. That thin thread of human voice drifted through the air vent into the guest room — the "crying" she heard; my husband and I sleep in the master bedroom at the far end, so we never heard a thing. The far wall of that hidden room enshrines nineteen Guman Thong. In the local black practice, little ghosts refined from one's own infants are the most "potent," and my husband believed his whole fortune today was protected by these "children" — all nineteen were babies he fathered with other women, none of whom was allowed to stay alive past birth. That midnight, my friend got up following the crying and ran straight into my husband opening the door to make his offerings — and saw a whole wall of Guman Thong. In the struggle, he pushed her out the second-floor window from behind. She fell into the backyard without dying at once; my husband hurried back to the bedroom and played the man who had been asleep all along. With her last strength she drove her fingers into the soil — she could not write a name, could not write anything my husband or the local police could read; that would surely have been scrubbed away. My husband doesn't read Chinese, and hardly anyone on the local police force does either. She wrote the one thing in the world only I could recognize at a glance: twenty. I pushed open that door and, by the night light, counted the whole wall — nineteen. With the one in my belly, exactly twenty. She was telling me: run. Your child is the twentieth.
hints: My friend heard right: that "crying" truly came from inside this house, from the room closest to hers.
Those two Chinese characters weren't written for everyone — the writer was certain only one person in the world could read them at a glance.

The room at the end of the hallway enshrines nineteen Guman Thong, all dead infants of her husband's own blood; "twenty" was her telling me, once I finished counting, to take my child and run for my life.

title: Aji's Paintings
story: April 9. I'm on holiday in a small mountain village. There's a mute in the village called Aji who loves to paint. Today he painted a wooden comb on a beach; I thought it very artistic, but the villagers all say his brain is broken.April 10. This morning I picked up a kitten on the highway. I liked it so much I carried it back to the village. On the way I ran into Aji; he stared at what was in my arms for a long time. That night he painted a spread-out blanket.April 11. Aji painted several bunches of grapes today, beautifully done. Another guest at the inn came over to praise them too. The villagers looked at the two of us as though we were a pair of freaks.April 12. I'm leaving today. Aji gave me a painting as a farewell gift: two caves. Perfect. I smiled and told him: you're going to be a great painter someday.
answer: The "I" writing this diary had already died, in the night between April 11 and 12. Aji isn't mad, and there is nothing uncanny about him. He is mute; he can only paint exactly what he has seen with his own eyes — and what he sees is always dead things. The "wooden comb" of April 9 was a rotted dead fish on the beach; the "blanket" of April 10 was the kitten "I" carried back from the highway — it had long since been run over and killed, and only a freak like "me" would hold a dead cat in his arms and say "I like it so much." The "grapes" of April 11 were strings of eyeballs. The murderer was the guest at the inn who came over to praise the painting — a killer who collects eyeballs; the outsider who went missing in the village earlier was "stored" with him. He had noticed "me" early on: a kindred spirit who would smile at a dead cat and gaze at "grapes" saying "what a wonderful painting." That night he killed "me" and took "my" eyes. On the morning of April 12, Aji, finding "my" body by the river, painted what he saw — two caves, two emptied eye sockets — and left the painting beside "me." So the final diary entry was not written by "me" at all. The killer took "my" diary and, imitating "my" voice, added the April 12 entry — "I'm leaving today" — so everyone would believe "I" left the village safe and sound. He even wrote Aji's gift of the painting into it exactly as it happened, and put "Perfect" and "great painter" into "my" mouth — for only he knew that every single thing Aji painted was real. The villagers knew no one had died in their mountains; they only saw Aji painting these sinister things day after day, and the talk grew wilder and wilder — with the whole village saying Aji was mad, he was perfectly safe.
hints: Not one of Aji's paintings comes from imagination — every single thing he paints has a "true body" in reality.
Find the true body of each of the four paintings: a rotted fish, a dead cat... then think about where "grapes" and "caves" might be found.
When the April 12 page was written, "I" could no longer see that painting — the two caves are "my" eye sockets; someone else held the pen.

title: I'll Pay You Back with Myself
story: My little sister and I had only each other. After she died, I picked up a habit.Today, while at it, I was caught red-handed by her. She said: pay me back. What she demanded as payment shocked me — but it wasn't bad, actually. I liked it.Ten years later, I used my old method to look for her, found nothing, and had to go buy needle and thread. But she didn't seem to like it: she let out a scream and called the police.
answer: "I" and my little sister were orphans, each other's only family. After my sister was bitten to death by a dog, "I" came to hate every dog alive and began killing them one by one — that was the habit. That day, "I" slipped into a house's yard to kill the dog there and was pinned down on the spot by the woman of the house. She said: the dog is dead, and you will pay for it. Her way of payment was unheard of — keeping "me" as the dog, as the payment itself. She was a solitary woman who had long wanted a "family member" absolutely obedient, one who would never leave: she fed "me" every day, played with "me," and at night let "me" sleep at the foot of the bed. Never loved by anyone growing up, "I" had a home for the first time, quickly grew to love the life, and was willingly kept for ten years. Ten years later, she died of illness. "I" used the old method to "look for her" — what "I" was really looking for wasn't her, but a "master": again and again "I" broke into other people's homes to kill their dogs, then stood where "I" was, waiting to be caught, waiting for someone to demand payment again. But all "I" got in return was beatings and expulsion; no one wanted "me." In the end "I" bought needle and thread, slipped into a house, killed the dog, sewed its skin carefully onto "my" body, crawled into the doghouse to wait for the master to come home, murmuring: "I'll pay you back with myself." The master opened the door, saw a person wearing the family dog's skin lying in the doghouse, let out a scream, and called the police.
hints: That "habit" targets the culprit that bit my sister to death — dogs.
The "payment" she demanded wasn't money: a dog is dead, so there must be a "dog" again.
What he was looking for was never one particular person, but a "master"; buying needle and thread was to make himself into that "dog" given away in payment.

title: To Be Continued
story: I dreamed of a world made entirely of glass; something far away watched me, coldly."Sweetheart, time to get up." A gentle voice woke me.The first thing I did on opening my eyes was check the date — today is my birthday again. I am long sick of this day. I picked up the knife and killed the woman beside me, laughing wildly: maybe this time, it will finally work.
answer: "I" died many years ago, in a car crash on my own birthday. My wife was a researcher at a neuroscience lab; unable to accept it, she secretly took "my" brain out behind everyone's back, submerged it in a culture tank, and wired it to machines — "I" became a brain in a vat. She fixed "my" consciousness to the morning of that birthday: on the morning of the accident, the last thing she said was "Sweetheart, time to get up," and every morning since, that sentence has started a new round, right on time.
