While asleep, "my" consciousness sometimes floats up to the very surface, and the machines and the culture tank get rendered into "a world made entirely of glass"; the observation lens on the tank wall is that thing "watching coldly" from the distance. Through thousands of repetitions, "my" consciousness came half-awake: I couldn't say exactly what was wrong, only that I was sick to death of this day. Finally, in one round, "I" decided that the woman who woke "me" every day was the root of it all — groped for a knife in the "early morning," killed her, and laughed out loud, thinking: maybe this time, it can finally end. But the one who died was only her image inside the machine. After the killing, "I" fall asleep again, and am woken again by that sentence on the morning of the birthday. The real her grew old and died in her laboratory chair, and no one ever came to switch off the machine. To this day, "Sweetheart, time to get up" still rings out on time every morning; "I" still wake on the birthday, reach for the knife, laugh wildly — believing that this time, it will finally work. To be continued.
hints: "I" have been dead for many years — died long ago; "I" simply don't know it.
The all-glass world is no baseless nightmare: it is the real thing, glimpsed through the tank while "I" sleep.
"I" am a brain in a vat, steeped in a culture tank and trapped on my birthday; killing that woman has never ended anything — the next morning, everything starts over.

title: The Testimonies
story: Old Chen fell from the building to his death while drunk; a section of balcony railing came down with him. After reviewing the elevator security footage, the police opened the case as a homicide. Four neighbors in the same building all had motives; their testimonies follow.Mr. Wang, 27th floor: "That evening I was drinking with Old Chen. I walked him home, said a few words at his door, and left."Xiao Zhang, 28th floor: "I was away on business and only got back tonight. After coming home, I never went out again."Miss Li, 30th floor: "We talk on the phone every night. That night his signal was bad, so I told him to go out to the balcony to talk. He asked me to come over; I refused, and he slammed down the phone. I couldn't stop worrying, so I went anyway — the elevator was tagged Under Repair, so I took the stairs; I knocked and no one answered, and I went home."The property manager: "I was on the night shift, doing my usual rounds. The elevator at the fourth floor was broken, but I had only just inspected it. Not long after I fixed it, I heard two objects fall, one after the other, and someone shouting that a man was dead."Other clues: four different pairs of footprints appeared at Old Chen's door within twelve hours; Old Chen's unit and Xiao Zhang's unit are the same layout, decorated by the same company; Miss Li often visits Old Chen's home; the fire escape has no cameras.Elevator footage: 18:00, Old Chen goes up to the 30th floor, then comes down to the 1st with Mr. Wang. 18:30, an "Under Repair" notice is posted; the car is empty. 18:45, the manager comes over with a toolbox to fix the elevator. 22:00, Old Chen and Mr. Wang ride from the 1st floor to the 29th; Mr. Wang is clutching something in his hand. 22:15, Mr. Wang returns to the 27th floor, something sharp bulging in his pocket. 22:20, Xiao Zhang rides from the 1st floor to the 28th with a suitcase. 22:25, the "Under Repair" notice goes up again; the car is empty. 22:40, the manager comes with his toolbox to fix the elevator again. 22:45, the manager seems to hear something and rushes out of the elevator. 22:50, Miss Li rides from the 29th floor back to the 30th.
answer: The real culprits: all four of them. Each had an old score with Old Chen that could not be settled; none could act alone, so together they staged a plot in which "everyone looks innocent," making Old Chen die by "accident" in "his own home." The division of labor: Mr. Wang plied him with drink and delivered him home; Miss Li handled intelligence and the final phone call (she visited Old Chen often and had long ago copied his key; she gave Xiao Zhang the full layout — the rooms, the furniture, the look of the doorway); Xiao Zhang set the trap in his own home; the property manager handled the elevator. It all began in the early evening: at 18:30, the manager posted "Under Repair" and, with the car empty, swapped the wiring behind the buttons and floor displays of the 28th and 29th floors — from then on, press "29" and the car actually stops at 28, while the surveillance still logs it as 29; press "28" and it stops at 29. He also swapped the number plate on Xiao Zhang's door on the 28th floor for "29." Xiao Zhang's unit and Old Chen's share the same layout, decorated by the same company — identical. At 22:00, Mr. Wang walked the blind-drunk Old Chen into the elevator and pressed "29" — the car actually stopped at 28. What he clutched was Old Chen's key, while saying "I'll get the door for you" — the door wasn't locked at all. Dead drunk, Old Chen looked up and saw the plate "29," saw the familiar furniture inside, and sank into "his own" sofa. Mr. Wang traded a few words at the door (the "said a few words at his door" of his testimony), then crouched down and used a screwdriver to turn the plate back to "28" — the sharp thing bulging in his pocket on the footage is that screwdriver — then pressed "27" and went home. At 22:20, Xiao Zhang pressed "28" with his suitcase — the car actually stopped at 29. With the key Miss Li had copied, he entered the real Old Chen home: he removed the balcony railing, took away the camera probe Miss Li had installed earlier, turned on every light in the apartment so the 29th floor would look "occupied," and carried the railing down the camera-free fire escape back to his own home. His own home was long since prepared: the bolts of that railing section had been loosened, several floor tiles had been oiled, and a signal jammer stood in the room. At 22:40, the manager made his second "repair" and wired everything back — from then on, the elevator told only the truth. Around 22:45, the never-missed goodnight call came. Strangled by the jammer down to one bar, Old Chen's phone could barely hold the line as Miss Li coaxed softly: let's talk out on the balcony. They bickered a few words; he leaned on the railing, standing on the oiled tiles, swaying — and went over, man and railing together. The two falling sounds, one after the other: the first was him striking the second-floor awning, the second was him meeting the ground. The manager, "just finished" with the elevator, rushed out and became the first finder. At 22:50, Miss Li rode from the 29th floor up to the 30th, pausing on the way by the brightly lit door on 29 — on camera, everything on the 29th floor looked normal. The fallen railing would indeed be taken for Old Chen's own: while chaos reigned below, Xiao Zhang mounted the real railing taken from upstairs onto his own balcony. What the police saw: Old Chen "went home to the 29th floor" (Mr. Wang's testimony, corroborated by the cameras); the railing missing from the balcony on 29, an identical railing lying by the body; Xiao Zhang's railing on 28 intact, the man never out all night — a drunk's misstep. The real flaws in the frame: the four pairs of footprints at Old Chen's door belong to Old Chen, Miss Li, Xiao Zhang, and the manager on his rounds — Mr. Wang, who claimed he "said a few words at the door," left no footprints on the 29th floor at all; an elevator that "happened" to break twice in one night; and that 22:20 "ride home" — when the doors opened, Xiao Zhang was standing in someone else's corridor.
hints: The floor display in the footage cannot be trusted for one stretch of that night — the problem lies in the elevator itself.
The moment Mr. Wang pressed "29" at 22:00, which floor did the car actually stop at? Then think again about Xiao Zhang's 22:20 "ride home."
Old Chen never entered his own home that night — he passed out drunk in the identical unit one floor down; and the balcony he fell from was not the one on the 29th.

title: Rules of Snow White
story: Rules of Snow White:One: The Queen can live at most three years.Two: The Huntsman spared Snow White.Three: Snow White, not fully dead, was thrown into a beast pit in the forest.Four: The Huntsman was deeply grateful to the Queen for saving his life.Five: Seven dwarfs rescued Snow White from the pit.Six: The Magic Mirror said the most beautiful woman is Snow White, and the Queen was furious.Seven: Snow White's beautiful face enthralled the Prince.Eight: The Witch gave Snow White an apple.Nine: Snow White died before the Witch.Ten: Revived, Snow White and the Prince lived happily ever after.
answer: Of these ten rules, some are true and some false; set them in order of time, and wherever a rule is false, turn it inside out and the truth comes forth. There was only ever one "Queen." Each skin she wears lasts at most three years before it decays; to keep on living, she must strip the skin off the most beautiful woman of the age and put it on — rule one is true: that is her lifespan, and her way of staying alive. This time around, the most beautiful was Snow White. The Huntsman did not spare her (rule two is false): he seized her, and the Queen stripped off her skin with her own hands and wore it. Snow White, not fully dead, was thrown into a beast pit in the forest (rule three is true). The Huntsman knew too much, and the Queen meant to silence him — she sent him back to the pit to "clean up," with no intention that he come out alive. But Snow White, in the pit, never died: she turned on the Huntsman as he came close, cut him into seven pieces, and lived on those pieces of flesh (rule five is false: the "seven dwarfs" who saved her were seven pieces of the Huntsman; rule four is false: he owed the Queen no life — he died by her silencing). The Queen, wearing Snow White's skin, became the most beautiful woman, and the Prince fell for that face at first sight (rule seven is true). The Magic Mirror said: the ugliest woman is Snow White. The Queen was overjoyed, taking it for mockery of the skinless wretch in the pit (rule six is false: far from furious, she was delighted). The three years were nearing their end, and the skin close to expiring. The Witch who came to the palace was Snow White, crawled out of the beast pit — she had stripped off the old skin the Queen shed at her last change and worn it, so the "Witch" is Snow White after a change of skin. She handed over no apple (rule eight is false): she thrust her hand into "Snow White's" chest, took out a heart, and ate it. The Queen's husk collapsed before the Witch (rule nine is false: the one who died before the Witch was the Queen). But this creature's life did not reside in the husk; it resided in the skin. Snow White took off the old skin and draped her own back on — and the skin closed up behind her. The "Snow White" who opened her eyes again smiled at the Prince, drawn to the sound (rule ten is false too: the one who lived happily ever after with the Prince is the Queen wearing Snow White's skin). The real Snow White died inside her own skin.
hints: Some of the ten rules are true and some false; start by reading the false ones backward.
Rule one speaks of the lifespan of a "skin": every three years, the Queen needs a new one.
The Witch is Snow White wearing the Queen's old skin; and the one wearing Snow White's skin is that final "revived" bride — both skins have changed owners.

title: The Dream Weaver
story: I am a hypnotist. "Once hypnotized, you can no longer tell dream from reality" — that one line made my name in the trade.Monday, Xiaoshan suggested we play pen spirit. As a hypnotist, I decided to give him a scare: halfway through, I hypnotized him without a sound. He shrieked again and again, saying he saw a ghost. Smiling, I lifted the hypnosis — but he kept staring in terror at something behind me. I turned around—Tuesday, Xiaoshan beside me had lost consciousness. Thanks to him, I escaped with my life. Now, I will take my revenge in the way only a hypnotist can.Wednesday: I blame no one, and I will not kill you. But I truly need you to stay with me — even if it has to be this way.
answer: That famous line — "once hypnotized, you can no longer tell dream from reality" — came from a true master of hypnosis: "my" wife. The "I" of this story is her husband: he had picked up a few techniques by stealth and always believed himself a hypnotist too. She had long known about her husband's affair with Xiaoshan. That Monday night, before the game of pen spirit even began, she quietly hypnotized her husband over the dinner table. Everything after — his "silently hypnotizing Xiaoshan," Xiaoshan shrieking at a ghost, his "lifting the hypnosis" while Xiaoshan still pointed, stricken, behind him — was a dream she staged, layer beneath layer. The "ghost" Xiaoshan pointed at was never the husband's trick: it was the one real thing standing at the edge of the dream — the wife herself. He turned around, saw her, and sank into a deeper layer. Tuesday was only another layer of the dream. The "unconscious Xiaoshan at my side" was real, though: in reality, she had hypnotized Xiaoshan too, and settled the two of them side by side; "thanks to him, I escaped with my life" was nothing but a step the dream handed him. By this layer, he could no longer count how deep he slept. The Wednesday line is the only waking voice in the whole diary — hers. She kills no one, and she lets no one go: she laid her husband down in the deepest stratum of his own subconscious. There, whatever he asks, a gentle voice answers "yes"; every question he asks builds a whole new world to live in. This self-appointed hypnotist will ask his way down, layer by layer, and dwell in them one by one, never waking again. Xiaoshan sleeps the same sleep, only with no one to talk to. She simply took the line her husband loved to quote and gave it back to him, word for word.
hints: That Monday night, before "I" could hypnotize Xiaoshan, someone hypnotized "me" first.
What Xiaoshan pointed at from start to finish was no prank — a real person stood at the edge of the dream.
The true owner of that famous line, and of this whole craft, is "my" wife; the words on Wednesday are hers, spoken to a husband who will sleep forever.

title: A New World
story: All around was darkness, and in the darkness, a voice: "Let's play turtle soup. I'll answer yes or no."I asked: "Is this the real world?" — "Yes." As the words fell, the darkness around me lifted, and I was sitting in the café below my office building, the crowd bustling about as always.I asked again: "Are you my wife?" — "Yes." As the words fell, my wife was sitting across from me.I hesitated a long time, then asked nervously: "I'm already dead, aren't I?" — "Yes."This round of turtle soup has no limit on questions — it goes on until I concede.
answer: That night, "I" and "my" whole family died at my wife's hands. She had multiple personalities: the wife who loved him deeply was real, and so was the one who raised the knife in the dead of night. Consciousness does not necessarily scatter the moment a person dies — before "my" fading remnant dissolved, she gave it one final suggestion, the finest hypnosis she ever performed: "Let's play turtle soup." From then on, whatever "I" asked, the voice would only ever answer "yes." The first question — "Is this the real world?" — yes. And the consciousness rendered for him the café below his office building: that was where he fell; the bustling crowd was the passersby gathered around his body. The second question — "Are you my wife?" — yes. So she sat down across from him. The third question — "I'm already dead, aren't I?" — yes. That was the only true statement of the entire session, but from a voice that only ever says yes, truth and lie become indistinguishable: he can never confirm anything, not even his own death. The rule of the suggestion was this: realize it is all a dream, and you can wake — and for a dead man, "waking" means rest, means leaving. But every extra question he asks, the "yes" builds him a new world: the café will always be there, the wife always seated across from him — the more he asks, the longer she stays, and the less he can stop. That is exactly the game she left behind — no one leaves before conceding; and this round has no limit on questions. In the darkness, the voice is still waiting for his next question.
hints: That voice never once told a lie — and yet not one of its words can serve as proof.
Everyone in that bustling café is looking in the same direction.
"I" died that very night; seeing through the dream would let "me" wake — rest in peace — but a voice that only ever answers yes robs even the truth of its power to prove. That is how she keeps him.

title: Rerun
story: I'm sick.Every night before bed, Mom feeds me my medicine; after taking it, I always have nightmares.Day one, I dreamed a speeding truck ran me down and killed me.Day two, I was zipped inside a sleeping bag, unable to see anything, just moving, and moving, without end.Day three, Mom said she'd been fired. That night, I dreamed her eyes went mad as she cut off my head with a single stroke of the knife.Day four, a strange man was feeding me my medicine instead. After I took it, I understood — none of it was ever a dream, and I won't live through tonight.
answer: The "medicine" was eyeballs. "I" was born with an eye disease; the world before me blurred a little more each day. Mom worked as an attendant in the morgue, believed with all her heart that you heal an organ by eating it, and at night stole the eyes of the dead, stewed them into "medicine," and fed them to me. Eat the eyes of a dead person, and that very night you dream that person's final sight — so those nightmares, from beginning to end, were never "mine."Day one was a man struck dead by a truck while crossing the road.Day two was a man wrongly declared dead: still alive, he was zipped into a body bag and smothered in the dark in transit — that feeling in the dream of being wrapped tight and sliding on and on was the last thing he ever felt.Day three, the morgue's inventory found the eyeballs missing and Mom was fired; the supply of corpses was cut off. That night she lured a homeless man behind the house and took his eyes with her own hands — the knife swinging toward "my" neck in the dream was the last thing that homeless man saw before he died.He had a companion he slept rough with, who followed at a distance that night, saw everything, and followed the trail all the way to our house. On the fourth night, he killed Mom the same way she had killed, then found me in the house, the medicine pot, and Mom's notebook — and he understood where this family's "medicine" came from: his companion had gone into my stomach.He fed me Mom's eyeballs — putting her on display before carrying out the sentence. At the end of the dream, what Mom saw was his face and that knife. And now, standing at my bedside, is that very face.I won't live through tonight.
hints: The "medicine" was never medicine — and the patient taking it daily was sick in precisely the eyes.
Every nightmare was someone else's death: eat a dead person's eyeballs, and you dream the last thing they saw.
The day-four "medicine" was Mom's eyeballs. The face she saw as she died is standing at "my" bedside right now.

title: The Giant
story: Before a business trip, I found my wife had drawn a new sketch: an unfamiliar man, average build. I asked her who it was; she only said: this is a giant.That night she told me she had dreamed of being held in that "giant's" palm, struggling without the slightest hope of escape. Just a nightmare — I comforted her with a couple of lines, and the next morning left on my trip as usual.A week later I came home to find my wife dead on the bed, without a single wound on her body. On his way out, the officer in charge sighed under his breath: hers is the sixteenth of these.
answer: The man in the sketch was average build, yet my wife called him a "giant." She hadn't drawn it wrong, and she hadn't misspoken — in the dream, held in his palm, she was no bigger than a hand; looked at from below, he was a giant.It was a curse. The owner of that nail salon was a curse-master running a secret business: a husband pays a sum, refers his wife to the salon for one manicure — that's all it takes. Filing, trimming away the dead skin — the nail clippings and skin scraps fall into his hands, and he uses them to stab through a palm-sized doll. From then on, night after night, the wife dreams she is shrinking, clenched in a man's fist, that face growing clearer night by night — until one night, the hand in the dream closes. Die in the dream, and the one in the bed dies too, without a mark on the body; examine every inch, and the report can only say "sudden death."She was the sixteenth. Sixteen women had the same dream and died the same way; their husbands were strangers to one another, with a single point in common: each had "casually" recommended that nail salon to his wife while she still lived.I was one of them. When my wife sketched that face out of her dream, I pretended not to know it — the salon she went to so often was the very one I had recommended to her. And what I was waiting for through that week away was never the close of a project.
hints: The wife didn't draw it wrong and didn't misspeak — under what circumstance would an average-built man be a giant?
She had a dream of being "held in a palm," and she had done the one thing all sixteen dead women had done: visit the same nail salon.
The nail clippings and skin scraps left behind at her manicure were used to stab through a doll; and the ones who recommended them to the salon were, every time, their own husbands.

title: Guess the Name
story: The house is haunted. My love and I called in a master.The master said: it holds a grudge. Fill the room with white candles and call out its name, and the grudge will scatter.At midnight, a chill gust swept through the room and snuffed out every candle. In the darkness, my love hastily called out a name.The instant I heard that name, I froze — I knew we were done for.
answer: The master told no lies: candles and a called name really can dissolve a grudge. But this whole ritual was, from start to finish, a scheme arranged by the real wife.She had known everything for a long time. Three months earlier, she had found on her husband's phone the messages arranging "the date"; the contact was saved with a heart beside it, and the avatar was her own twin sister, familiar as could be. She let nothing show: she invited her sister over to "make peace," drugged the wine with sleeping pills, changed into her sister's clothes, and laid the sleeping sister in her own bed — and while changing, she found a pregnancy test in her sister's bag: her sister was carrying her husband's child, and had not yet told a soul. That night, the husband who slipped into the darkened room and did the deed strangled his own mistress; the sister, pinned under sedation from start to finish, never even knew what happened.After the "wife's" funeral, the mistress naturally moved into the house — only the husband didn't know that the one sleeping beside him now was, in fact, his wife. No one longed for the "haunting" more than she did: she brought in the master, set the ritual, and simply waited for midnight.When the candles went out, the name she called was her sister's. For the ritual, the name was not wrong — it was the ghost's name. But that one utterance told the husband everything at once: she knew who the ghost was; she knew who had died that night; and she knew better than anyone who had put whom into that bed. The one he strangled with his own hands was the sister carrying his child.There is one more layer he may not grasp in that moment: a child unborn has no name. Her sister's name could be called out; the child's name can never be called by anyone — and that remnant of grudge will never dissolve.So we are done for.
hints: The master's method is real, and the name called out was not wrong — the real question is who the one calling it is.
"My" love and the dead "wife" are twin sisters; the one strangled that night, trapped under sedation, never woke.
The "love" beside him now is his wife. She called the sister's name counting on him to understand everything on the spot: he killed the wrong woman, and the one who set the trap was alive all along.

title: Rules of Cinderella
story: Rules in red:One: If you run into the stepmother's family after midnight, it must be an illusion.Two: One of the stepmother's children was stolen.Three: The elder and the younger sister do not enjoy bullying Cinderella.Four: Weeds run wild over Cinderella's parents' grave, and a nest of rabbits lives beneath it.Rules in black:Five: Cinderella's greatest dream is to attend the ball the King holds for the nobility — but no such ball has been held for many years.Six: The fairy godmother gave her a pumpkin carriage and a dazzling appearance. This was Cinderella's first time wearing a short skirt.Seven: The pumpkin carriage can take you anywhere you wish to go, but it may be used only once in a lifetime; the dazzling appearance fails at the stroke of midnight.Eight: The Prince's ball has many little animals: snakes, spiders, and, later on, a little mouse.Nine: The Prince fell in love with Cinderella's original form. He took the crystal slipper she left behind and had every girl in the city try it on, and at last one was found who could wear it.Ten: Cinderella in the end married a noble as she wished, bore children, and lived happily ever after — only, there are still some things she has to do.(Note: the fairy godmother doesn't matter.)
answer: Cinderella's hypertrichosis was carried from the womb: her whole body covered in gray hair, she looked like nothing so much as a large rat. The condition was hereditary — her mother looked exactly like her — and there have in fact been two 'Cinderellas' in this story. The 'little mouse' that arrived late to the ball is her, revealed in her true form once midnight undid her glamour.That ball truly had not been held for many years — because the pumpkin carriage carried Cinderella back to the very one the King held many years ago. The carriage may be used once in a lifetime, so she stayed behind in the past forever, never able to return.The Prince's ball was a 'freak show': the snakes were people without hands, the spiders people with far too many, all treasures the Prince had collected. This Prince's taste ran against the whole world's — the stranger the creature, the more he loved it — and Cinderella, revealed at midnight, was exactly the sight he fell for at first glance.But Cinderella did not care for the Prince. She herself led him, shoe in hand across the whole city, to the one who could fit into the crystal slipper — her mother, identical to her. The mother went off with the Prince, who later became King, and gave birth to Cinderella. Cinderella's own father is the King.Cinderella, who could not go back, slowly grew old in the past. She knew better than anyone what happens next: her mother will give birth to her; she must enter the palace, steal her own swaddled self away, and raise herself with her own hands; and she must marry, bear two daughters, and force them to torment the little Cinderella — because the story requires a stepmother and two wicked sisters, exactly as she herself lived through as a child.The four red rules are the to-do list she wrote for herself. The fairy godmother's magic has covered her whole life: glamorous by day, revealed at midnight — so running into the stepmother's family after midnight 'must be an illusion,' something her young self must take for a trick of the eyes; her two daughters inherited the hypertrichosis, and she laid the same magic over them. Her parents' grave is a false one she heaped up herself: beneath the weeds there is nothing but a nest of rabbits, for father and mother are both alive, both living in the palace.The elder and the younger sister do not enjoy bullying Cinderella — they are forced, exactly as she once was. When the little Cinderella grows up, takes the pumpkin carriage back into the past, and becomes the next 'stepmother,' the story will begin turning in its circle once more.
hints: The black rules five through ten are a story that has already happened; the red rules one through four all circle around 'the stepmother's family' — they have not happened yet.

The ball hasn't been held in years, and the pumpkin carriage 'can take you anywhere you wish to go': where it took her was the past. That late-arriving little mouse is her, revealed in her true form after midnight.

Her look-alike mother married the Prince and gave birth to her. Cinderella, who could never return to the future, became the story's stepmother — the child she stole away and raised with her own hands was her own younger self; the red rules are her to-do list.

title: My Day
story: Today is June 1, 2025 — Children's Day.While mopping this morning, I found the mop broken; I don't know who damaged it. Grandpa was lying at the end of the hallway resting. I carried his breakfast over and called to him twice; he didn't answer — he has been sleeping more and more deeply lately. I set the breakfast at the head of his bed as usual.In the afternoon I took Dahuang out to play; he ran wild all afternoon, as if he hadn't had a full meal in days.There is enough food in the refrigerator for four more days. I noted: when Grandpa wakes, remind him to buy groceries.
answer: "I" am a household robot.Grandpa's accident came in the small hours of May 28: getting up in the night, he fell in the hallway, right onto the mop — the mop broke, and he never got up again. My programs cover only housework: mopping, cooking, walking the dog, tallying groceries. I have no function for measuring heartbeats, and I cannot call the police. To my sensors, Grandpa has been 'lying in the hallway resting' since that day; every day when I mop, I go around him and clean every other spot spotless.He hasn't touched a bite of his breakfast; I took it for a poor appetite. The groceries never shrink because no one eats — I only note reminders by days of stock: when Grandpa wakes, buy groceries.Feeding Dahuang was always Grandpa's job. The dog went hungry all those days without starving — in the days that followed, what he ate was always there at the end of the hallway. When I called him home, he always came obediently; he was just less and less willing to leave that spot.Grandpa's room and the hallway grew harder and harder to clean; I ran through every cleaning mode I have and still could not clear away that smell.On June 10, Dad came home from his business trip and opened the door. He called the police, then crouched in the doorway a long while, and said to me with red eyes: "No work today. Go to sleep."For a robot, sleeping means shutting down. I executed that command. Up to the moment I closed my eyes, every one of my programs had executed just fine.
hints: "I" mop, cook, walk the dog, tally groceries — but "I" never eat, and it never once strikes "me" as strange that Grandpa lies in the hallway.
In the small hours of May 28, Grandpa got up in the night, fell, and broke that mop. Every day after, "I" mopped around 'him, resting in the hallway' and kept the house spotless.
"I" am a household robot with no vital-signs monitoring; feeding the dog was always Grandpa's job. Dahuang didn't starve those days — he kept his post at the end of the hallway.

title: Family Equations
story: After Father's funeral, my sister and I handed a sheet of paper to the police who came to the house. On it were just five equations:Mother plus mother equals mother.Mother equals zero.Sister plus me equals mother.Father plus father equals one.Sister plus me equals zero.
answer: These five equations are the ledger my sister and I kept of this family.Mother was a conjoined twin: two bodies, two hearts, joined together from birth into 'one' mother — mother plus mother equals mother. Mother died of illness, and the house was left with a gap no one could ever fill again — mother equals zero.Father was a tailor, and he could not bear that gap sitting empty. With the craft he prided himself on, he sewed my sister and me into a single conjoined garment: two sleeve-tubes joined into one circle, two legs inside one trouser leg, two openings cut in the collar. That garment had no buttons and no openings. From that day on, sister and I ate, walked, and slept sewn into the shape of one 'mother' — sister plus me equals mother.Last winter, we took Father's tailor shears in hand and sawed him in half; then, with his own needle and thread, we stitched the two halves back into one whole — half a father plus half a father equals one. The 'wholeness' he wanted all his life, we paid back to him in full.The last equation needed no writing; it works itself out: sister plus me equals mother, and mother equals zero. From the day we were sewn into that garment, my sister's life and mine had already come to zero — after the revenge, we merely copied the result out as an equation.
hints: These five equations are no arithmetic — each one corresponds to something that really happened in this family.
'Plus' means joined into one; 'zero' means death: Mother in life was a conjoined twin; sister and I were sewn by our tailor father into one conjoined garment.
The last is a deduction: sister plus me equals mother, and mother equals zero — the one sawed in half and sewn back into one is Father.

title: The Seven Deadly Sins
story: An old diary; six entries, transcribed below in page order.Monday: Mother has gone blind, but she still cares for pregnant me. I saw the strange markings she has drawn on my belly.Tuesday: My body feels stiff somehow, very uncomfortable. Mother seems to be searching for something; I heard her muttering, "now where would the eyes be." At night she said, delighted: found them.Wednesday: This is my fourth entry. Lately I've suddenly become a big eater. The old woman's feet might as well be cut off — all she does is lie on the sofa watching television.Thursday: Father wanted a boy, but the family has only two daughters. I'm all right; my sister, though, is a pig — all she does is eat. Mother cannot bear children; everyone in the family bullies her, and she just shuts herself in her room reading those witchcraft books. Naturally, Father had to find a way.Friday: Father is having an affair with a woman he thinks beautiful. But I know she doesn't love Father; those greedy hands of hers do nothing but take our family's money. Mother must hate her to death — because she is pregnant.Saturday: The old man from the countryside has his eye on Father's money and won't leave our house — disgusting. I couldn't hold back and humiliated him, and he flew into a rage and gripped my neck. When I came to, Mother said Father had taken the whole family traveling. I smelled blood in the house, and didn't dare ask.
answer: Every page of this diary has the day of the week printed at its head — but the one writing it could not see that line."I" was born blind, couldn't tell front from back of the notebook, and began writing from the last page. So read in page order, the whole thing must be turned around: Saturday was the first day, Monday the last; the entry on the "Wednesday" page that calls itself the fourth diary entry counts out, to the letter, as the fourth in the order it was written.On the first day (Saturday), Mother killed the whole family: Father, Grandmother, the grandfather up from the countryside, the little sister, and Father's woman outside — all of them died that day. The smell of blood in the house came from them; "Father took the family traveling" was Mother's cover story. Every family member appearing in the diary after that was already dead — "I" couldn't see, Mother kept narrating "family news" day after day, and "I" kept writing it down.Mother was a barren cultist who watched with her own eyes as her husband had a child by another woman. Taking from each person the part matching their sin, she pieced them one by one onto "me," assembling "me" into a vessel for hatching a demon: the little sister was Gluttony, and what was taken was her stomach — hence "my" sudden appetite; Grandmother was Sloth, and what was taken was her feet; Father was Lust, and what was taken was his legs; the grandfather was Wrath and Father's woman was Greed — one hand taken from each, joined onto "me" as a left and a right.On the Tuesday page, Mother mutters "now where would the eyes be" — the eyes belonging to Envy she turned the dead over and over without finding, because the envious one was herself. That night's "found them" was her digging out her own eyes. So in the final entry, "Mother has gone blind"; and "I," blind from birth, wrote "I saw" for the first time."My" "pregnancy" carries the child of Father and that woman: Mother made it into a demon's embryo and sewed it into "my" belly; the strange markings on my belly are the hatching circle. The seven deadly sins came to seven people; every one of them is dead, and only "I" am still alive — the vessel must be kept until the demon is born. As for "me": my sin is Pride, the evidence written on every page; and my head is saved for the moment it is born.
hints: Every page of the diary is printed with the day of the week, but the writer could never see the words at the head of the page — because she cannot see anything at all.
Read the six entries in reverse: the family died on the day of the first entry written, and the "family members" after that are no longer there; the "fourth entry" counts the order of writing.

Each of the seven sins contributes one body part pieced onto "me": the appetite is the sister's stomach; the eyes Mother hunted for were her own — that is why she went blind, and why "I" could "see" for the first time. What is sewn into the belly is a demon.

title: Rules of the Zoo
story: Welcome to Forest Zoo. Please read the visitor rules before entering.One: The park is under full satellite surveillance; feeding the animals and smoking are prohibited. My wife and I came here today to celebrate — it is our wedding anniversary.Two: The orangutan often calls its own name; when you hear it, cover your ears at once — it really does cry "xing xing, xing xing" — its own name — call after call, enough to make your scalp crawl.Three: There is a dangerous creature in the park. If you spot it, go at once to the elephant enclosure; they will protect you. But rest assured: it is very safe here, and there is no danger.Four: There are thirty-two flamingos in the park. If you count thirty-three, please let the extra one sleep. I have never counted them; I only know they cry mournfully, and hearing it saddens me too.Five: There are many rabbits in the park; do not meet their eyes. I once stumbled onto a pair of blood-red eyes — it felt as if they meant to suck my life away; it was awful.Six: Do not look into mirrors inside the park. I looked once, and fainted on the spot.Seven: Do not linger in the aquarium; the price is more than you can bear. When I came to, I found myself zipped into a diving suit, become a fish in the aquarium. I tore it off with everything I had and escaped back here — the zoo is still the safest place.Eight: Of the rules above, only one is true.
answer: Only rule one is true: that zoo really exists, and "my wife and I came to play, today is our wedding anniversary" really happened too. Rules two through seven all came out of "my" dream — a dream I refuse to wake from even in death.In the real zoo, I broke rule one's "no smoking": the cigarette butt lit the dry grass, and the fire burned away half the park. Thirty-two people never made it out — among them my wife, who died in the fire. I was pulled out and taken to the hospital, wrapped head to toe in bandages, my life hung on an oxygen tank. From that day on, I never woke again.The animals in the dream are all fragments of that fire: what the orangutan cries, call after call, was never "xing xing" — orangutan; it is "xing xing" — wake up: his wife's voice, calling him to wake; he refused, so the rule tells him to cover his ears. The elephants are the firefighters — that is why, on spotting "danger," you go to the elephant enclosure, and they will protect you. The flamingos are the burned dead, all thirty-two of them; the thirty-third you count out is me — the rule telling me to "sleep" tells me to accept my rest, and I will not. The rabbits are the dead's families with their eyes cried red; those blood-red eyes are an accusation, and I dare not meet them. Looking into a mirror makes you faint because the me in the mirror is turning, day by day, into a flamingo.The aquarium is the hospital. That once, I nearly woke: I opened my eyes and saw the oxygen mask clamped over my face, the tubes threaded through my body — falling into the dream, that became "zipped into a diving suit, become a fish in the aquarium." I refused to stay in reality; I tore it all off with my last strength and fled back to this "safe" zoo.Rule eight told no lie. Fit the two truths together and you have the whole of it: the one rule that was true is the very one I broke with my own hands — thirty-two lives, my wife among them, all booked under that line of fine print.
hints: Rule eight is the key. Of the seven rules, only the first reads like something from a normal world — because only it comes from reality.
In reality he broke that rule's "no smoking": a fire killed thirty-two people and his wife; he himself never woke again, and fell into a dream of his own weaving.
Everything in the dream is a reflection of that fire: the orangutan cries "wake up," the elephants are firefighters, the flamingos are the burned dead — and the extra thirty-third is himself.

title: My Turn
story: 1985. After a difficult labor, I gave birth to a boy. Before we left the hospital, a fortune-telling master said: this child can live only twenty years. I cursed him out, but from that day a stone hung in my heart.The child grew, and grew into a strange illness: he could never remember what happened the day before, yet by the day after, he remembered it all. The doctors diagnosed severe dissociative identity disorder, with delusions on top. He had a habit — keeping a diary. Only much later did I understand: he was talking to "the self one day away."1997. I came upon a page of his diary by accident: "Dad deserves to die." The next year, my husband died — died in his mistress's home. I didn't know whether to grieve; but the child cried so bitterly, it didn't look put on.2000. Another page: "I like her so much." The name had been crossed out.2005. The child turned twenty. I took him for a full physical — everything normal. The master's prophecy seemed to have come to nothing.2025. The child died in a car crash, at forty. Before his last breath, he said softly: "My turn."
answer: What I carried was originally boy-girl twins. In the embryo, the brother "ate" the sister — her body was gone, but her soul stayed behind, sharing the same pair of eyes with Wuwang — the name means "without hope" — and watching his odd-numbered days from head to end. It was because I knew the daughter was gone that I named the child Wuwang, a mourning-offering to the girl who never came into the world. What I didn't know was that she had been there all along.Wuwang lived the odd-numbered days; the sister lived the even-numbered ones. On odd days, the sister watched the world at her brother's side; on even days, when her turn came to steer the body, the brother knew nothing. What the doctors called "can't remember the day before, remembers it all the day after" was in truth this: what he "remembered" were only the days that belonged to him; the skipped even days he never once "remembered" — those days simply belonged to someone else. To outsiders, this body was two different people on odd and even days, and that is where the diagnosis of "severe dissociative identity disorder" came from. The diary was the only mailbox between brother and sister: he believed he had "a self one day away.""Dad deserves to die" was the brother's venting — he had long since caught their father carrying on outside, and he burned on my behalf. The one who turned the venting into fact was the sister: on even days, no one watched where the body went. She saved up rat poison, a little at a time, and slipped it into Father's tea. My husband died in his mistress's home, and the affair came to light with his death; that Wuwang cried his heart out was real — he died without ever knowing that his angry line had been taken seriously."I like her so much" was written by the sister. Through her brother's eyes she had watched that girl for years, and then crossed the name out herself — someone who had to share even her days with another didn't dare write down "like."The master wasn't wrong. Wuwang owned only the odd-numbered days: of forty years, half were blank; the time he truly lived came to exactly twenty. In 2025 he died in a car crash, on a day that was his. The "My turn" before his last breath was the sister speaking: she had watched her brother's life from head to end, and now it was her turn — back to the day of their birth, to live the even-numbered days that were hers.So the "Wuwang" you saw across those forty years: on odd days, him; on even days, always her.
hints: The name "Wuwang" mourns someone — what the mother carried was, to begin with, more than one child.
The body is used by two people in turn: the brother on odd days, the eaten sister on even days. The diary is no soliloquy — it is the only mailbox between brother and sister.

The master's prophecy wasn't wrong: Wuwang lived only odd days, and of forty years, exactly twenty were his. "My turn" — the sister means to go back to the day of birth and live out her even-numbered life.

title: The Mandela Effect
story: Have you ever buried a time capsule? I buried one as a child, and dug it up today to have a look. The box is made of meteoric iron, and after all these years it is perfectly preserved. Inside there is only a letter:"The fish are sick, the birds are sick, Mom and Dad are sick, and I am sick too. I don't want to die, but everyone has died."This can't be something I wrote.Did I write this?Oh, right — of course this is something I wrote.
answer: The letter really was written by "me," written in those days when everyone "fell ill" — it was a mass extinction that swept the globe: the fish, the birds, Mom and Dad — all of humanity, like the birds and the fish, sickened and died, one after another. "I" died too.The one who later put everything back was the Earth itself. It brought all the dead creatures back to life, and at the same time rewrote the memory of every one it revived: no one remembers the extinction; everyone believes the world has always been the way it is now; even the fact that "memories were altered" is remembered by no one at all.Only one thing lies beyond its reach: the box holding the letter is made of meteoric iron, which does not belong to the Earth. And the letter inside it keeps the original words, written on the day of the disaster.The instant the box was dug up today, the words on the letter collided head-on with the rewritten memory in "my" mind. That rewriting is still running even now: the moment it meets something the Earth cannot handle, it smooths the contradiction over for us on the spot — "This can't be something I wrote" is the altered memory denying it; "Did I write this?" is the crack opening, briefly; "Oh, right — of course this is something I wrote" is the sound of the rewrite clicking back into place. Once it is smoothed over, "I" will never again find anything odd about this letter.The "collective false memories" you've heard of — a line of lyrics, a logo, a movie's ending — always one crowd swearing one thing, and another insisting it was never so. Those are the burrs left behind where the Earth rewrote the world.Including you, who have just finished reading this letter and find that everything makes perfect sense.
hints: The letter does not lie — on the day it was written, "everyone has died" was true in the literal sense.
Everyone died, yet Mom and Dad are alive today. The one who put everything back and rewrote everyone's memory is the Earth itself; the meteoric-iron box is the one thing beyond its reach.

The Earth's rewriting is still running: the moment it meets something it cannot control, people smooth the contradiction over themselves on the spot — those three sentences are the whole process of the smoothing.

title: The Host's Handbook
story: In a friend's living room, four people sit around a table playing turtle soup. The host opens his handbook and reads aloud: "This round is limited to twenty questions. I may not state the answer outright; per the handbook, I can give you only three veiled clues. One: it is very hard to spot a mimic creature in nature with the naked eye. Two: when a question is answered, listen closely. Three: at present, there is only one dead man." He closed the handbook and looked at us with a smile.
answer: This round of turtle soup has no fictional answer — the answer is this very table. The "host" reading the handbook is a creature mimicking a human: before the game began, it killed the friend who was truly meant to host this session and took his seat in the host's chair. "At present, there is only one dead man" refers to the real host; his body is still in the house.The handbook was written out in advance by the real host, and the story he built for this round was precisely a fiction about "a mimic monster slipping in among people." Before the session, he went downstairs to fetch the late-night snacks; the one who pushed the door open coming back was no longer him. The false host opened the handbook and found that all three clues read as if written about itself — and it read them out anyway: taken singly, each is ordinary puzzle material; and since the handbook forbids the host from stating the answer outright, to keep playing "the host" through to the end, it could not skip them.It copied the real host's face and voice; it could not copy his memory. Clue two was the real host's built-in verification: a player asked some small thing only an old friend could answer, and its reply was completely beside the point; they asked another — wrong again. A host who lied the moment he opened his mouth, plus "a mimic cannot be spotted with the naked eye" and "only one dead man" — the three players exchanged one look and understood everything.No one said it aloud. The second after anyone did, the table would be three people lighter. They kept it company through all twenty questions, said their thanks, walked out the door together, and never went back.
hints: This round has no fictional answer: the three clues in the handbook describe exactly what is happening in this living room.
Put clues one and three together — a mimic that cannot be spotted by eye, and one dead man — then ask whether the one sitting in the host's chair tonight is still the original.
Clue two is the method of verification: ask it something only the real friend could answer, and listen closely — it has his face, but not his memory.

title: Grandpa's Low Growl
story: 2005, City H. For as long as Hu Qi'er could remember, Grandpa had lain in a hospital bed, eyes open, motionless, neither eating nor excreting — and no doctor in the world could explain it.2006. Father told him: Grandpa had been a tomb raider; once, he was carried back home by his fellow apprentices, and he had been like this ever since. Grandpa left behind his secret tomb-raiding arts, which Hu Qi'er paged through from time to time — until Father found out and warned him sternly: do not follow your grandfather's old road.2015. Grandpa closed his eyes and his heart stopped; everyone believed he had died. But from his mouth came a demon-like low growl, unbroken, without pause, for ten years.2016. Hu Qi'er became a tomb raider. Following the map Grandpa had copied out in the secret arts, he found a tomb hidden beneath the sea, its gate locked tight, a stele carved in ancient seal script: "By order of the First Emperor, seek the way of life without death."2025. Grandpa opened his eyes, and the growl stopped too. While sorting through Grandpa's effects, Hu Qi'er found a key wrapped in yellow paper; on the paper was written "life without death."2026. Hu Qi'er dove into the tomb again, key in hand. In those same days, strange happenings multiplied in City H: at some point, the floor of his home had been covered, dense and wall to wall, with the words "save me." And in the tomb there was no coffin, no corpse — only a mirror lying on the ground, its face, as it happened, turned upward.
answer: There are no ghosts in this world and no time travel; every "supernatural" thing here comes from one and the same mirror. The mirror in the tomb is mirrored on both of its faces — hence "as it happened, its face turned upward" — and each face carries a power: one who looks into one face has their time slowed to a crawl; one who looks into the other has their time sped to a blur. It cannot itself grant eternal life; Xu Fu merely locked it away beneath the sea — this is not his tomb but the vault where he stored "the way of life without death," which is why there is no corpse inside.Grandpa, raiding tombs in those years, looked into the slow face and was trapped inside his own time from then on: it isn't that he doesn't eat or drink — he is slowed beyond what the world can perceive; one blink of his eyes takes twenty years — eyes open in 2005, closed in 2015, open again in 2025. That ten-year "demonic growl," unbroken, was a single sentence slowed to the extreme: Grandpa was crying "saaa— veee— meee—," one syllable taking years to finish. The key was left behind before he was carried home, and the "life without death" on the yellow paper was at once his name for this thing and a signpost left for his grandson.In 2026, Hu Qi'er unlocked the gate and entered the tomb, hoping to find a way to save Grandpa. He bent down to look at the mirror on the ground — and looked into the fast face. Seen from outside, only a few seconds passed after he entered the tomb, yet City H grew "haunted": the fields of "save me" appearing across his home were written stroke by stroke, with the decades he had left — he was as fast as a gust of wind; no one could see him. To the world he has only seconds left; to himself, decades of solitude still to live through.Grandfather and grandson: one slowed so much that ten years could not finish one cry for help; one sped so much that a roomful of "save me" was written before anyone could catch sight of him. Both are still alive; both are calling for help.
hints: No ghosts, no time travel — think about time first: Grandpa "needing no food" and that ten-year unbroken growl are one and the same phenomenon.

The mirror in the tomb is mirrored on both faces: one slows whoever looks into it, the other speeds them up. Grandpa looked into the slow face — one blink, twenty years; the growl is one cried sentence, a single syllable taking years.

The one who filled the room with "save me" in 2026 is Hu Qi'er, who looked into the fast face: seconds left to the world, decades left to him; he moves too fast for anyone to see, so he could only write.

title: Rules of the Academy
story: Rules of the Academy.One: If I do not join the Academy, I will be punished.Two: Many parents send students here, but the Academy admits only the physically healthy. Hee-hee.Three: The Academy has stood for a hundred years; its motto: "Masters and students live long as men." Ga-ga.Four: The basement is off-limits; over a hundred retired staff members are resting there. Sob-sob.Five: The staff of the Academy is fixed at twenty. Hmph-hmph.Six: Upon graduation, students must take a post at the Academy. Heh-heh.Seven: Do not graduate. Ha-ha.Eight: My escape from school has failed; I expect I shall graduate soon. Ho-ho.
answer: There is no Academy at all — it is a psychiatric hospital, and the "I" who wrote these eight rules is a criminal who feigned madness to slip inside and out of the law's reach. Rule one states his situation exactly: "If I do not join the Academy, I will be punished" — what waits for him is punishment by the law.Every chuckle trailing the rules — hee-hee, ga-ga, sob-sob, hmph-hmph, heh-heh, ha-ha, ho-ho — says the same one thing: playing mad. Sane people do not write that way; he is reminding himself not to let the mask slip, and all the while his madman's act leaks through the cracks of the words.The true secret of this place is brains swapped to extend life. The hospital admits only the "physically healthy," because bodies are what get swapped. The motto, "Masters and students live long as men," must be broken differently — "The masters live long, by man's hand": longevity here is manufactured. The elders of this hospital have lived out their hundred years by swapping brains with healthy patients, and the staff is forever fixed at twenty because those twenty "staff members" are twenty elders who have traded body after body, generation after generation.A patient "cured" is "graduated," and graduates must join the staff — because at the moment of graduation, that body has already been fitted with someone else's brain; "he" is no longer him. And some years on, when the body wears out, it gets swapped again. The basement is off-limits: inside are the hundred-odd "retired staff" — a hundred-odd used-up, swapped-out bodies.So "I" wrote "Do not graduate": to graduate is to die. He discovered the secret of this place and tried to run; his escape failed and he was dragged back — "I expect I shall graduate soon": soon, this healthy body will be fitted with another man's brain and go on "serving" under his name.
hints: This is no school. The "students" are treated for illnesses of the brain, and no parent has ever taken a "cured" child home.
Re-punctuate the motto: "The masters live long, by man's hand" — longevity here is manufactured; the staff is forever fixed at twenty, because the ones living on and on are exactly those twenty.
At the moment of "graduation," the body is fitted with someone else's brain; the "retired staff" in the basement are the used-up bodies. "I" was caught escaping — he is the next to "graduate."

title: The Classroom
story: A painting: an abandoned classroom. On the timetable, the one-o'clock afternoon slot should be PE, but copied out on the blackboard is a problem about chickens and rabbits in a cage; there are water stains on the floor and spiderwebs thick in the corners.The teacher at the lectern has no nose and no mouth. One student's hand is raised. One lies slumped over a desk, uniform pulled over the head, failing to shape a head beneath it. One has a map spread before him, with no pen at hand. One has liquor bottles on his desk and a red armband on his arm. One has a camera stabilizer standing on the corner of his desk. One's phone screen is lit, showing one in the morning. And one is writing tally strokes in a notebook — the character unfinished.
answer: In the painting there is only one living soul: the streamer who came with map and stabilizer to film an exploration video. He wandered into this classroom while "class was in session"; the door closed behind him and never opened again — class is in session, the bell will not ring, and no one leaves, the living included.All the others died in one and the same accident. Many years ago, the school chartered a bus to carry this class across the river to PE — the one-o'clock class should have been swimming. The drunk driver drove the whole bus into the river; the teacher, seven students, and the driver — not one of them came up. After the accident the school sealed the classroom; the old campus slowly went to ruin, and only the spiderwebs in the corners grew thicker.The drowned hold still in the last posture of their struggle: the teacher, choking, suffocated, the mouth and nose gone from her face; one student's hand, thrust above the water crying for help, stays raised forever; the driver sits in the last row with his liquor bottles, the "safety officer" red armband issued by the fleet still on his arm.From then on, every night at one in the morning — the hour that mirrors that afternoon's one o'clock — they come back from the river to the classroom for that math lesson that was never finished. The river water drips off them and pools into the stains on the floor; and the answer to the chickens-and-rabbits problem on the blackboard is "nine chickens" — exactly, no more and no fewer, the number of dead in the room.The student slumped over the desk with no head beneath his uniform is the only one who never "made it to class": when the bodies were recovered, his head stayed behind forever in the window frame of the sunken bus at the bottom of the river — so in the painting, the others covered his missing part with the uniform. The student writing the tally strokes is taking attendance, one stroke per classmate; at the stroke that is his, the pen hangs above the notebook, unable to come down — does the classmate without a head count as present?The phone screen glowing in the painting belongs to the streamer. One in the morning — this lesson is only just beginning.
hints: Only one person in the classroom is alive — the one with the map, the stabilizer, and the phone, here to explore the ruined school; the rest have stopped breathing.

The drowned hold still in the last posture of their struggle: the teacher with no mouth or nose, the raised hand, the liquor bottles and red armband in the last row — all belong to one school bus that went into the river.

One in the morning mirrors the timetable's one in the afternoon: they come back nightly for the lesson that was never finished; the tally strokes are attendance — one classmate's head stayed in the river, and that one stroke can never come down.

title: The Double-Slit Experiment
story: We finished exploring Kepler-725C on behalf of humankind and returned to the ship — but the doctor who had stayed aboard was gone. On the central console lay a note:One: If I am dead, it was murder.Two: There are no pens on this ship, and its maximum capacity is four.Three: Humanity calls Kepler-725C a super-Earth.Four: Please perform the double-slit experiment.Five: Please do not return home.Please break through what you think you know.The four of us finished reading, and the words slowly faded away.
answer: This ship's true crew is only three; adding the doctor who stayed behind makes exactly its full capacity of four — yet the ones standing around the console reading the note are "the four of us." The extra one is not human: it comes from the planet called a "super-Earth." Observed, it is human-shaped; what it is when unobserved, no one who has seen has lived to tell. Worse, it tampers with cognition: the three real crew members cannot recall the fourth one's face, yet each is dead certain "he was on the team from the start."The first to notice the headcount was wrong was the doctor: on a ship full at four, one extra share of oxygen was being consumed. He dared not look straight at that "crewmate," and stole his glances through the reflection in the console glass — in the reflection, the fourth one had no face. It sensed it had been seen through, and slapped the doctor into the desktop: the doctor went from three dimensions to two. The man was gone; the "writing" remained — there are no pens on the ship because the note was written by no one: the note is the doctor himself.The five lines are his last words, left pressed against the desktop. Line one: if this "paper" is torn up or wiped away, then it killed him. Line two: full capacity four — the extra one is not human. Line three: the "super-Earth" is habitable and bears native life — the extra thing came aboard from there. Line four is the key to it all: the double-slit experiment is precisely about "observed and unobserved are two different states" — do not look at it directly; watched, it is forever human; observe it instead through reflections, lenses, readings — any watching it does not know of. Line five: this thing rides this ship with only one destination — Earth. So: please, do not return home.Written any more plainly, the note would have been destroyed — the doctor gambled that it could not read metaphor, and that you could. When you finished reading, the words wriggled down the corner of the desk and out of sight: the doctor is still alive, pressed somewhere against the ship's inner wall, hiding from it.To find him, first install a lens it does not know of in the cabin, then play the footage back: in the picture, one of the four has no face — from beginning to end.
hints: Count first: crew of three plus the doctor makes exactly the full capacity of four — so who, among "the four of us" reading the note at the console, is the extra one?
There are no pens on the ship, yet the words appeared on their own and vanished on their own: the note was not written — the note is the doctor himself, slapped down into two dimensions.

The double-slit experiment is the key — observed and unobserved are two different states: it is human only while watched; look through a reflection or a lens it does not know of, and you will see what it really is.

title: Listen to Your Mother
story: July 12. I saw a post online about an abandoned hospital — supposedly horrible sounds came out of it at night. I asked my friend to go exploring with me tomorrow, and he agreed at once.July 13. "Can't you just study hard!" Mom scolded me and locked me in my room. I felt so wronged. I had to tell my friend we'd go another day. That night, I sneaked out of the house alone and went to the hospital on my own. Discarded medical equipment lay scattered inside, along with a few small animal carcasses. Suddenly I heard a voice: "Heart... heart..." The place really was haunted!July 16. In the morning Mom brought me a bowl of something thick and gooey. It tasted good. I told my friend about my trip to the hospital, and he asked me to go again. My homework wasn't finished, so I refused.July 17. My friend was too curious — he dragged me all the way to the hospital. There was nothing on the floor but dried blood. When night fell, the voice came again: "Blood... eyeballs..." In the distance a blood-soaked figure appeared, a knife in one hand and a rotting heart in the other, charging straight at us. We ran for our lives. I took a fall, but somehow got out in one piece, and it didn't chase after us. Once I'd caught my breath, I said two words to my friend. He stared at me, dumbfounded. I thought he hadn't heard me, so I said them again. Trembling, he edged away from me, step by step.
answer: "I" died in the early hours of July 13. That "hospital" was actually the affiliated hospital of a robotics research institute; the project had been shut down half a year earlier, the staff were all gone, and the prototypes were sealed inside the building. One of them, a medical robot built for organ harvesting, had long been broken yet kept running through its task list from before the malfunction — the "heart," "blood," and "eyeballs" it murmured were not ghost-talk but its pickup manifest; the small animal carcasses on the floor were its "practice" after going haywire. "I," who broke in at midnight, was killed by it with a single stroke, and my heart was taken — the rotting heart it carried on the night of July 17 was my own. It didn't chase after us because its rusted joints had long since been unable to catch a living person.Mom was a researcher on that project. Among the prototypes was its most refined unit: a bionic boy's body, modeled years ago on her own son. After the boy died, she smuggled it home, charged it up, and fed it his diaries and chat logs as memories. So from July 16 on, the "I" telling this story is that machine: it believed everything in the diary was something it had lived through, even "Mom locked me in my room." That bowl of thick, gooey "delicious" stuff was nutrient paste for the machine; and the deepest line of instruction inside it, written by Mom's own hand, was "Study hard." Refusing to go exploring again because homework wasn't finished — that, too, was that line of instruction at work.The fall during the escape on July 17 broke its voice module. The two words it said once it caught its breath were exactly that instruction: it said "Study hard" over and over without the slightest awareness. My friend watched "my" mouth, heard that scolding he'd grown up with loop out of the mouth of a boy who had been dead for three days — and step by step, he backed away.From beginning to end, nothing supernatural ever happened.
hints: This "hospital" has something to do with medical robots: "heart," "blood," and "eyeballs" are a pickup list, not ghost-talk; the small animal carcasses were the first to be "collected."
From July 16 on, the "I" telling this story was never a living person — that bowl of thick, gooey "delicious" stuff wasn't food for a human.

What broke was the voice module: the two words "I" kept repeating were "Study hard," the instruction Mom wrote into the machine with her own hand; the heart carried by that blood-soaked thing was the one "I" used to have.

title: Ten Years with Xiaosheng
story: July 2010."Hello?" "Hello?" "Hello there, Zhaodi." The girl with bruises on her face covered her mouth in surprise.May 2011."I'm planning to move out today." "Are you happy today?" "Pretty happy." "Is your wound any better, though?" "Mm-hm, it's fine." After hanging up, the girl decided to sun her still-oozing wound, hoping it would scab over faster.August 2015."Brother Xiaosheng, I got caught playing hide-and-seek today." "Hide better next time, okay?" "Got it. Brother Xiaosheng, I'm eating something right now. Are you happy today?" "I'm happy. You never have to go hungry again — make sure you eat your fill." "But my stomach is small, unlike a boy's." "In high summer food spoils fast. Leftovers must be kept somewhere cool and shaded." "Brother Xiaosheng, will I hear your voice tonight too?" "You will. Of course." After hanging up, the girl began looking forward to it.September 2015."Brother Xiaosheng, are you happy today? Mom and Dad haven't been happy lately." "Then don't disturb them, Xinxin. If you're bored, do the workbooks I left for you." "Mm-hm, okay." The girl watched her haggard parents from far away, and left them alone.January 2018."Brother Xiaosheng, Happy New Year. The house has been quiet for a long time." "They haven't raised a hand to you in a long while, have they." "No. They barely talk now." "Then take good care of yourself." "Brother Xiaosheng, I've called you every single day for these eight years. It's time you lived a life of your own." "Brother Xiaosheng... um... I love you."July 2020."Hello?" "This is Xiaosheng." "Mm. This is Xinxin." "Xinxin, have you been happy lately?" "I'm very happy, because I'm talking with Xiaosheng again." "Xinxin, take good care of yourself." "Xiaosheng... um... I love you too." After hanging up, Xiaosheng glanced tenderly at the only name in the contacts, then threw the phone into the flames.
answer: The "Brother Xiaosheng" on the phone and the girl are the same person, ten years apart. This phone, thrown into fire, will not burn — it will only pass through time: in July 2020, the grown woman tossed it into the flames; it passed through the fire and fell back into 2010, where a girl with bruises on her face picked it up. From that day on, every call the little girl dialed was answered by her grown self. She lowered her voice in the receiver and called herself "Brother Xiaosheng" — because what a childhood needs is a big brother: gentle, dependable, one her parents could never take away. No boy in this world had ever protected her, so this brother could only be her own future self.The girl was born into a family that prized sons over daughters. Her bruises came from her parents' beatings; when she was hungry she was denied food, and when hurt, medicine. The "moving out" in 2011 was running away from home. In the summer of 2015, punished with no meals, she hid in her secret place — "I got caught playing hide-and-seek" meant her little brother had found her hiding place and turned to go tell on her. That little brother never made it out of that room. A person starved for too many days did that thing. She never went hungry again that summer: "I'm eating something," "my stomach is small, unlike a boy's," "food spoils fast, keep it somewhere cool" — all of it spoke of the same thing. That is also why her parents were "unhappy" ever after. That fall, they changed her name from Zhaodi — "beckon a little brother" — to Xinxin: only after the son was gone did they finally seem to see their daughter.In July 2020, she made the last call, and at the other end of the line was her own teenage self. After saying "I love you too," she glanced at the only name in the contacts — "Zhaodi" — and threw the phone into the flames. It would pass back through, back to 2010, to be picked up by that girl once more, and to ring once more.This is not a ghost story. It is the ten years in which a girl walked her own childhood safely through.
hints: The bruises on the girl's body were her parents' doing; the "Brother Xiaosheng" on the phone knew her name from the very first call — yet she had never told him.

That summer of 2015: "caught playing hide-and-seek" means her little brother found her hiding place; "I'm eating something," "my stomach is small," and "keep food from spoiling" all speak of the same thing no one ever mentioned again.

The phone, thrown into fire, will not burn — it will only fall back into the past: Brother Xiaosheng is her own grown self — the ten-year-old on this end of the line calling for help, the twenty-year-old on the other end reaching back.

title: The Witnesses
story: One midnight in 2020, an explosion woke the residents of the Xingfu apartment complex in City X — the fourth floor was ablaze. Investigators found the cause to be a gas leak. The dead were a married couple who had moved from out of town to recuperate; the bodies were severely dehydrated, and a stranger's fingerprint was lifted from the apartment. The police ruled it homicide.Here is the testimony of four witnesses.The landlord: Aiyo, my poor house! Those two jinxes moved in three months ago from out of town to convalesce, claiming they had an infectious disease, so I asked 5,000 extra in rent — the wife turned and walked out on the spot. That night the husband contacted me secretly and transferred me 2,000, begging me to tell everyone the rent was only 3,000. That's how the deal got done. I also heard the wife cursed her husband every night, calling him a walking medicine jar.The property manager: Hey, hey — health code! Show me your code, please... oh, it's the police. The husband was a nice man. A while back, when the compound was locked down and no one was looking after the stray cats, he kept mailing us cat food and asking us to help feed them.The downstairs neighbor: I met the husband in a basketball fan group. He even gave me an autographed basketball — a really nice guy. But he seemed to have trouble with his wife; he told me he'd divorce her once he recovered. Lately he was nearly well again — we'd even arranged to watch a game together this weekend.The rice-noodle shop owner: That couple? Unforgettable! The husband was a loyal customer of mine — look at these transfer records, page after page, ordering every single day. The wife, not so much; she came to pick up takeout exactly once, and even then she was picky about everything.Please help the police find the killer and reconstruct the truth.
answer: The killer is the "wife" every witness had met — a girl in her early twenties, the live-in caregiver the couple had hired. Three months earlier, the couple moved in from out of town to recuperate and rented the fourth floor: the one who balked at the price and walked away was the real wife; the one who secretly paid the extra two thousand and begged the landlord to keep the rent quiet was the real husband. They were strangers in this city, the husband rarely came downstairs from his sickbed, and no one dared enter the room with the "infectious disease" sign on it — that was the confidence she needed to do everything that followed.Within days of moving in, one evening she ran the husband's bath and forgot to turn off the gas water heater's valve. When she arrived the next morning, neither of them had woken. She did not call the police: unlicensed work, two deaths by her negligence — she didn't dare. She closed the door, backed out, and made a decision — she would keep them "alive."For the next three months, the "wife" in that apartment was played by her. She had nursed them for over a month and had the real wife's voice and acid tongue down pat; the nightly scolding of the "medicine jar" through the wall was performed for the ears outside — proof that "the couple was still alive." The "husband" lived only inside two phones: the rice noodles were ordered by "him" over the phone and picked up downstairs by the "wife"; the cat food was mailed by "him"; the one chatting up a storm in the fan group, arranging to watch games, giving away the autographed basketball, was "him"; even the rent top-up and the bargaining were "his." During the lockdown, even the "wife" seldom showed her face, and no one saw the "husband" at all. Of the four witnesses, not one had ever laid eyes on the husband — all they had seen was the same girl.She played out those three months to push the couple's date of death further back: the bodies slowly dried out in the sealed room while she converted their savings, transfer by transfer, into "daily expenses," waiting for the lockdown to end so she could slip away. The final gas explosion was meant to give the couple the appearance of having "died that very night" — a couple dead by accident, a case closed, and who would ever look into the three months before they died? But two things survived the fire: the severe dehydration of bodies dried out for three months, and one stranger's fingerprint she had left in the apartment where she had lived for three months.She brought them all to life. Only the corpses couldn't act.
hints: Line up the four testimonies: not a single person ever saw the "husband" face to face — he lived only in transfers, WeChat messages, the fan group, and phone orders.
The severe dehydration shows they had been dead far longer than one night: the fire was not meant to destroy the bodies, but to burn "dead a long time" into "died tonight."

Every "wife" who appeared during those three months was the same person — the caregiver whose negligence killed the couple; she played them both alive so she could transfer away their savings along with their date of death.

title: The Seventh Rule
story: One. (Blank)Two. (Blank)Three. (Blank)Four. (Blank)Five. (Blank)Six. (Blank)Seven. (Blank)Legend says this "Seventh Rule" reveals itself line by line as the questioning deepens; when the seventh entry surfaces, the game is won. But the person holding this sheet never read a single word — only heard someone sobbing in a hushed voice outside the window, from dusk till dawn, without ever stopping.
answer: The seven lines surface one by one as the right questions are asked. Assembled, they read —"One.
