This anomaly is tenacious and cunning, skilled at weaving illusions or possessing bodies; once it possesses one, it is indistinguishable from any ordinary person.""Two. My wife is in a frenzy — she may well be possessed too.""Three. I have destroyed the 'anomaly' in my wife, and my wife is dead. I refuse to let her stay dead.""Four. You are a master of true caliber, free to travel between the two worlds; standing in the netherworld, you are terribly vulnerable.""Five. Anomalies may enter the netherworld but can never leave. Here there is only weeping and howling; laughter draws them to you.""Six. Its target is me, and I will not give it what it wants.""Seven. So these seven lines were never rules — they are shards of my memory. The cunning anomaly cast an illusion over my wife, making her believe she was the possessed one, and I fell for it too. What it wanted, from beginning to end, was this body of mine that can cross between the worlds of the living and the dead. I cannot let it have its way. All I can do is leave myself here forever."The man who wrote them was a master who could walk freely between the world of the living and the world of the dead. Toward the end, "I" becomes "you," because a man whose memory is coming apart can no longer tell whether he is remembering, or leaving instructions for the next person to read this sheet.An anomaly skilled in illusions and possession had marked him. It could enter the netherworld but never leave; and this body that could cross both worlds was the one thing able to leave the netherworld. To take it, the anomaly didn't force anything — it only laid an illusion over his wife, making her believe she had been possessed. She struggled like a madwoman; the master judged that she was "doubtless possessed too," and performed the exorcism — with his own hands he killed his wife.He carried her soul into the netherworld, hoping to find her again among the weeping. And it was there that he saw through the whole design: all the anomaly had ever wanted was his body; luring him into the netherworld, where he was weak, had been the true purpose of that illusion.He did not flee back to the living. He left his body in the netherworld — in the one place anomalies can enter but never leave. He was both the bait and the cage: if it wanted this body, it would have to walk into the cage itself. The words on the sheet sank down with him, and the sheet left in the world of the living turned blank; each time the reader asks the right question, one memory surfaces across the threshold. When the seventh line surfaces, you have finished reading his last words for him — and the weeping outside the window has never stopped: in the netherworld, the wife is crying; he stands beside the sound of it, waiting for that thing to walk in.
hints: The seven blank lines were never unwritten — the words sank into the netherworld with the man who wrote them; every question you get right raises one memory that was never yours.

The writer could travel freely between the two worlds, but in the netherworld he was terribly vulnerable; anomalies can enter the netherworld but never leave — what it truly wanted was his body, the only thing that can leave the netherworld.

The wife was never possessed — she was only caught in an illusion and believed herself possessed; the strike of the "exorcism" killed her herself. He stayed in the netherworld for good: he made himself the bait, and the cage.

title: My Strange Parents
story: Sunday. Dad came back from his business trip, held me, and wept. I had no idea why. That night I heard Dad shouting "Ghost!" in the yard; terrified, I locked my bedroom door and waited for Mom to come home from work.Wednesday. Mom handed me a locator watch and said gravely, "Something is wrong with your father. Stay away from him as much as you can." After work, Dad said to me, "Something is wrong with your mother. Dad is taking you away in a bit." I didn't want to go, so he knocked me out cold.Thursday. I woke up in a cave — Mom was there too, unbelievably. She seemed to be burying something; beside her gaped a big, freshly dug pit. All she said was, "Son, come on, we're going home." That night, Mom and Dad talked for a long time; she clutched him and sobbed, and Dad, looking grim, hesitated, then comforted her anyway.Friday. Dad took me to the amusement park and I had a wonderful time. After we got home, Mom cooked a whole table of dishes, but Dad's face suddenly turned dark and he said nothing for the longest while. That night, Mom held me as I slept, for the first time in ages.Monday. Dad came home from work, held me, and cried: "I'm sorry." The moment he said it, everything went black.
answer: The real Dad died Sunday night. The "Dad" who held "me" and wept that day was a man who had walked over from the other side of the mountain: there is a cave in the mountain whose depths lead to parallel worlds — every world has the same mountain, the same cave, the same family, lives that diverged only a few years back. In his world, the son had died of illness and the wife had followed soon after; he was the only one left. He had carried his wife's and son's bodies across through the cave, one by one, and buried them in the big pit at its mouth — his family belonged together, and whatever his life was missing, he would find in the next world over.First he went to the neighboring world and found that world's version of his wife: a mother who had likewise lost her son. He told her there was a world on the other side of the mountain where the boy was still alive. She believed him and left with him. Then he timed his entry into this home to the day "he" would return from the business trip. That night, the real Dad pushed open the yard gate and saw "himself" standing in the yard — the first to scream "Ghost!" was the fake; the first to fall was the real. By that night, the real Dad lay buried beside the cave.On Wednesday, Mom sensed the crack: this "Dad" remembered things from ten years ago but couldn't keep straight what happened last month — the two worlds had diverged the year the son died of illness, and with his old memories he couldn't piece together the new days. She put the locator watch on my wrist. The "Dad" sensed her guard being raised too; he struck first, knocked me out, and hid me in the cave — the road he had come by, and the road he meant to take me away on. Thursday at dawn, Mom followed the watch's signal to the cave: she saw the fresh soil over her husband, and beside it the long-leveled pit — who lay in that pit, she would not learn until the next day. She said nothing and took me home. That night she clung to the "Dad" and wept — weeping for the new grave she'd found that morning; he didn't know why she cried, took it for a woman finally breaking down, hesitated a long while, and patted her back after all.On Friday he took me to the amusement park — he wanted to watch this "son" laugh. When Mom went back to the cave, she ran into another "Mom" at its mouth: his real wife, who had followed him a step behind from the neighboring world. The two identical women talked for a long time: one told of her husband's death, the other of her son's; one understood what kind of man was living in her home, the other what kind of man she had followed here. By evening, the one cooking dinner in that house was already the other "Mom" — he looked up and saw his dead wife serving dishes in someone else's kitchen, and for the longest time could not speak. It was she who held me that night as I slept: a mother who had lost her son, holding the living image of her own boy.On Monday he came home from work on schedule. The plan had failed, his wife could never go back, and no world would have him now. He held me, said "I'm sorry," and meant to carry me through the cave and bury me beside his son — to complete the "three of us" in his world. Mom was one step too late to save me; she did everything that came after: he never walked out of this house, and so never walked into any world. The mother from the neighboring world stepped past him, went back to her own world, and never again came near any cave.That night, Mom wrapped me in a blanket and walked into the cave. She passed the strange mother and child in the pit, passed Dad's new grave, walked deep into the wind, into another world where no one knows us. She buried me beneath a tree that sheds its leaves, and sat beside me until dawn — like any ordinary mother.
hints: The "ghost" in the yard Sunday night was the real Dad, just back from his trip — the one who screamed first and then lived in the house was the "him" who walked in from another world.

The two worlds' lives diverged only a few years back: the fake Dad could act out the old days but not the new ones — that is where Mom's suspicion began; on Thursday she found the cave by following the locator watch.

The pit at the cave mouth holds the wife and son the fake Dad carried over from his own world; the Mom cooking on Friday had already been replaced by the wife who followed him here — his true wife. On Monday he said "I'm sorry," meaning to bury me over there and complete his "three of us" — Mom was a step too late to save me, but he never walked out of this house.

title: Life on Fast-Forward
story: Every corner was papered with the same missing-person flyer: "Zhang San, male, twenty years old. A doctor of biology, inventor of humanity's greatest technology, 'Life on Fast-Forward' — it replicates countless copies of you inside microscopic worlds, computes every outcome of your life, and helps you find the one you want most. Description: white polo shirt, a moon printed on the chest."This Zhang San's notepad held only three lines:One. Where did living things come from?Two. It has discovered me. There may be danger. It must disappear.Three. I have discovered him. There may be danger. I must warn the others.
answer: The principle behind "Life on Fast-Forward" is to replicate countless identical copies of you inside microscopic worlds, let every possible life be genuinely lived out, then pick out the best one for you. And the template used for the copies is the Creator himself — every "person" inside the microscopic worlds was cloned in the Creator's image. Zhang San's world is itself one "computation" run by the layer above: everyone in the world — Zhang San included — shares the same face, and it is the Creator's face. That is why, on this planet, missing-person flyers never describe facial features, only clothing.Zhang San's three notepad lines record everything from his invention to his death."Where did living things come from?" — the question of his life. The answer: living things did not appear naturally; they were made — along with that face shared by all."It has discovered me. There may be danger. It must disappear." — Once, while observing one of his microscopic worlds, a clone suddenly looked up and met Zhang San's eyes through the instrument. That clone was named Li Si. When the created sees the Creator, the Creator is in danger — Zhang San decided to delete Li Si."I have discovered him. There may be danger. I must warn the others." — A few nights later, a man stood outside the laboratory glass: the same face, white polo shirt, the moon on his chest. Seeing that he had been seen, the man backed away into the dark. Zhang San understood two things: he too had been made; and in these endlessly nested worlds, the Creator was living out a life identical to his own, word for word — the only thing that could tell that man apart was the clothing. That night he papered the whole city with missing-person flyers: the name, age, and identity on them were all "himself" — what he was searching for was his own Creator.The day the flyers covered the city, Zhang San died. His killer was none other than the Creator, and the reason was written in the second line of his notepad — the created has discovered me; there may be danger; it must disappear. The flyers are still on the walls all over the city; the man who posted them is gone.
hints: Start with the flyer: under "description" it lists only clothing — in this world, describing a face is meaningless.
The computation clones countless people in the maker's own image; Zhang San's world was computed by someone too — the face shared by everyone alive is the Creator's face.

Lines two and three of the notepad are the same deed on two nested levels: the way he disposed of the clone that discovered him is exactly the way the Creator disposed of him — the day the flyers covered the city, Zhang San died.

title: Rules of Noah's Ark
story: Year by year the sea has been receding, and the living things of this planet may be facing extinction. The ancient records say a great extinction happened once before, a million years ago, and it was the gods who built Noah's Ark and led the living things through the calamity.Yesterday, a ship of unimaginable size really did appear on the water. A research team went in to explore; the entire team was lost, and only Lucia came out alive. He left behind six messages:One. There are bizarre creatures and plants inside the Ark; keep clear of them. Sam and Jace died in the jaws of one of the bizarre creatures; it took Kasha's tech-rifle to bring just one down.Two. There are unnamable things inside the Ark; do not touch them. Matt touched one and lost an arm.Three. The records inside the Ark confirm that back then it carried the living things through the great extinction. The ancient records are true — we are saved.Four. Inside the Ark is a book called The Twilight of the Gods. Its gist: the gods went to war, the gods fell, and after the twilight of the gods, life appeared in the world — including humankind.Five. The god is inside the Ark. The god is unimaginably huge and hideous. It killed Matt and ate Kasha. Only I escaped.Six. There are more arks. They have come. Humankind is about to go extinct.As it turns out, the two great extinctions had the same cause.
answer: This planet is Earth. The great extinction of a million years ago in the ancient records was humanity's nuclear war — "the gods went to war, the gods fell" is precisely the "twilight of the gods" written of in that book. The war collapsed the climate, the seas rose, the land became unlivable, and humanity built colossal ark-ships, took aboard the plants and animals of the old Earth, and left — surviving that extinction. The ancient records are true; they simply recorded "humans" as "gods."After the extinction, the sea brought forth a new intelligent species — a race of small octopus-like amphibians arisen by mutation, and Lucia is one of them. They rewrote this planet's history and rebuilt its vocabulary: in their eyes, the "gods" who came down from the arks are unimaginably huge and hideous.Now the sea has receded and the land is above water again — home is habitable, for humans. This ark came back to scout the way; behind it, an entire fleet is on the return voyage. Every one of Lucia's six messages is true; each simply needs translating:One. The "bizarre creatures and plants" are the birds, beasts, grass, and trees of the old Earth. Sam and Jace died in the jaws of an escaped predator; the one Kasha shot dead was, in the "gods'" eyes, a precious relic species of Earth.Two. The "unnamable thing" is fire. A deep-sea civilization had never seen combustion; Matt reached out, touched it, and half his arm was gone in an instant.Three. The records are accurate: the Ark truly did carry "living things" through the great extinction — what it saved was the previous generation of life; it saved the "gods" themselves. "We are saved" was exactly backwards.Four. The "living things" that appeared after the twilight of the gods are precisely Lucia's people: they truly did evolve in the sea only after that war.Five. The "god" is a human being. The little things that broke into the ship and shot dead a relic species of Earth were "cleared" by the "god": Matt was killed and Kasha was eaten — eaten in the literal sense.Six. More arks are coming back. What is about to go extinct is the current master of the Earth — Lucia's people.The two great extinctions had the same cause: the "gods." The first time, it was a war between gods; this time, the gods themselves have come home.
hints: Lucia never lied once; all six messages are true — he simply sees the world differently than you do. First ask: who would look "unimaginably huge and hideous" through his eyes?
Lucia's people are small amphibians born in the sea; the "unnamable thing" is something this deep-sea civilization had never seen.

The "twilight of the gods" of a million years ago was humanity's nuclear war, and the arks are human ships; now the seas recede and the fleet sails home — the culprit of both extinctions is the same kind of "god."

title: Murder at the Private Hot Spring Inn
story: A murder at a private hot spring inn deep in the mountains. The victim, Takahashi Yukiko, lay face-down in the hot spring, a dinner knife driven into the back of her neck. The suspect Yamato Nadeshiko's account follows:"Yukiko and I were classmates, and best friends. This time my husband won travel vouchers and brought the two of us to this inn — the only staff here is the proprietress. At eight in the evening my husband was asleep in our room, and Yukiko and I wandered the inn. At a quarter past eight we went to the hot spring room; there's a little kitchen there, and we had the proprietress cut us some sashimi and drank a little sake. At nine we finished our soak and went back to our rooms. At ten past nine I woke my husband, and he asked me to keep him company in the spring. At half past nine he had the proprietress prepare another serving of sashimi. At ten to ten I passed Yukiko's room and heard her quarreling with someone on the phone — she said the word 'complaint,' but I didn't think much of it and went back to my room."Clues at the scene:One. A bundle of hemp rope was found in Sato's room; its purpose unclear.Two. Burnt rubber in the fireplace.Three. The ice machine in the little kitchen was broken.Four. The cups in the liquor cabinet had just been washed.Five. The dinner knife was driven into the back of the victim's neck, but the knife did not quite match the wound; only the proprietress's fingerprints were on the handle.Six. In the yard lay a bottle of medication for a psychiatric condition.Seven. The spring has a water-circulation system and stays scalding hot year-round.Eight. A torn note was fished out of the toilet in Yukiko's room; pieced together it read: "Me or Nadeshiko — you decide."Nine. At eight o'clock sharp that evening, Yukiko had searched a name on her phone: Yamanami Yumi.
answer: The killer is the proprietress, whose real name is Yamanami Yumi. In elementary school she was bullied by Yukiko and Nadeshiko, called "fat pig," forced to eat cockroaches. Grown up, she had slimmed down and changed beyond recognition; she bought this unmonitored hot spring inn deep in the mountains, forged travel vouchers for Sato to "win," and lured her enemies to her door step by step.That night she drugged the sake. At a quarter past eight, the two women ate sashimi and drank sake in the spring room, and the proprietress left her fingerprints on the dinner knife while cutting the sashimi. Before nine, the drug took hold and the two women sank into sleep in the spring; the proprietress took a long ice pick she had prepared earlier from the ice machine, drove it into the back of Yukiko's neck from behind, then wrecked the ice machine, washed and removed the two sake cups, and withdrew. The scalding circulating water melted the ice pick clean away in no time — she wanted a corpse "with no murder weapon."Just past nine, Nadeshiko woke in the spring to find herself soaking in the water, her friend's body floating beside her. She suffers from a dissociative disorder; certain that "someone else" had done it during an episode, she fled to the yard in terror to breathe, and the pill bottle slipped out of her pocket. She shook her husband Sato awake, and the couple decided to cover it up — to pin the time of death on a moment when Nadeshiko had an alibi. Sato used the bundle of rope to haul the body out of the water, roped it upright into a dining chair, and with his arm around "Yukiko" called the proprietress to come cut more sashimi; the proprietress saw only two people from behind — "Yukiko was still alive at half past nine." At ten to ten, Nadeshiko hid in Yukiko's room, mimicked her voice, and made the "complaint" call to the proprietress, quarreling violently — the proprietress broke into a sweat taking that call: she knew better than anyone that Yukiko had died before nine, yet she could not say a single word. After sending the proprietress off, Sato put on rubber gloves, drove the knife bearing the proprietress's fingerprints into the corpse's neck, dragged the body back into the spring with the rope, burned the gloves in the fireplace, and hid the rope back in his own room — forgetting to destroy it.The flaws showed in three mismatches: the knife didn't fit the wound, meaning it went in after death; the proprietress would never kill with her own knife and her own fingerprints on it; and the Yukiko who was "still eating at half past nine and still complaining at ten to ten" was, per the autopsy, dead before nine. Peeling the illusion backward, the detective first unraveled the couple's chain of misunderstandings — Nadeshiko never killed anyone; she had merely been drugged. The couple thought they were saving her; in truth they were dressing the scene for the real killer — and the "real killer" they casually framed happened to be exactly that. In the end, following the too-clean sake cups and the travel vouchers, Yamanami Yumi was caught.The last two clues belong to a separate affair: the note in the toilet was Yukiko's ultimatum to Sato — she and he had been having a secret affair, and she was forcing him to choose between her and Nadeshiko. That night Sato slipped into her room and tore up and flushed every trace of the affair; one half-sheet that didn't wash away survived. The eight o'clock search was hers as well: the daytime proprietress had struck her as familiar, and she couldn't be sure whether that transformed face belonged to the Yamanami Yumi of all those years ago.
hints: Start with the dinner knife: it doesn't match the wound, so it went in after death — whoever planted it wanted to frame someone; the one who did the killing is someone else.
The rope was for moving a waterlogged corpse: the Yukiko who was still "eating" at half past nine was, per the autopsy, already dead before nine — everything after was staged for the proprietress.

The real murder weapon melted away long ago in the scalding circulating water; the too-clean cups mean someone drugged the drinks — the killer is the proprietress who cut the sashimi and took that "complaint call."

title: Strange Happenings in the Village
story: Xiaohong survived a car accident, and in it a power awoke in her. Yet she never knew what that power was; her parents wouldn't tell her either — they only said: just be a normal person. Not until the day she divorced her husband did she finally learn what the power was. She wanted so badly to be a normal person — later, she did something in the village, and at last got her wish.
answer: Xiaohong's power is yin-yang eyes: she can see the dead, and hear them speak. The car accident took her parents' lives; she survived, but after recovering she could never conceive a child. Her dead parents stayed at her side all along — eating with her, watching her marry, reminding her every day to "just be a normal person." But the dead keep one rule: never reveal their own death to the living. So her parents would rather be doubted than explain. Xiaohong saw "Mom and Dad" at home while their headstone stood in the graveyard behind the village — she decided her brain had been damaged and what she saw were phantoms. "Be a normal person" became the words she said to herself for half a lifetime.Her husband Xiao Yi had never been after her. He was after her family's money: he had arranged that car accident with his own hands; her parents' lives bought her inheritance, and bought this marriage. The one he truly loved was Xiaoya; the two had been having an affair for years. Since the accident Xiaohong couldn't bear children, the child in Xiaoya's belly became the heir he was waiting for. He had said all of this to Xiaoya — he didn't know the dead can hear: her parents' spirits had followed him for years and caught every single word.On the day of the divorce, once the property papers were signed, the blood debt would follow the money cleanly into Xiao Yi's pocket. Her parents finally spoke — they never revealed their own deaths; they only spoke of the brake line tampered with that night, and of the words Xiao Yi had whispered at Xiaoya's pillow over the years. In an instant Xiaohong understood everything: the parents before her eyes were no phantoms, the dead truly do watch the living; she wasn't sick — she simply could see.She killed Xiao Yi. Then she found Xiaoya — she did not kill her; she only took the unborn child from her womb.With all of it done, she was still the "seeing" monster. She wanted so badly to be a normal person. Deep in the night, a fire ran from one end of the village to the other, and every villager became a ghost. The dead can see the dead. Amid a whole village of souls, no one was more "normal" than Xiaohong — her parents' instruction, at last, fulfilled.
hints: Only Xiaohong truly survived that accident — the "Mom and Dad" at home reminding her to be normal have had a headstone standing for many years.
The dead can see the living, and hear every word the living say; on the day of the divorce, her parents finally spoke out what they'd heard during all those years of following Xiao Yi.
In a world where she alone can see the dead, she will always be a monster; turn the whole village into people who "can see," and she becomes normal.

title: The Scream
story: A village was haunted. The "ghost" was skilled at conjuring illusions, and those who could not escape its illusions died, one after another. Xiaoya saw the pattern: only those who broke a certain taboo were killed by it. To protect her family, she found a way to dodge every one of its illusions. Yet in the end she died anyway — and just before dying, she touched her belly.
answer: In this ghost story, the taboo is screaming. Its illusions are a net, and the scream is the bell that rings when prey strikes the mesh — those frightened into crying out die; those who choke it back, not one of them died. After the village's string of deaths, Xiaoya saw this rule. Her whole family depended on her; she could not die — but someday an illusion would surely slip past her guard, so she found a once-and-for-all solution: she blinded herself. What the eyes cannot see can never startle a scream out of you.It did not stop her. For its proudest work was never any of the frightening phantoms — it was the "child" planted in her heart long before she went blind: she believed she was pregnant. She blocked every illusion that came through her eyes after that, but she could not block a fact she already believed. Until the day her hand fell on her belly: it was flat. There had never been a child. She screamed.And beneath this whole "ghost story" there is no ghost: it is Xiaoya's own past wearing a ghost's skin. The "ghost skilled at illusions" was a human being, named Xiaohong. In reality, Xiaoya really had conceived a child, and truly believed she would have a home with the child's father — that "home" itself was the one illusion she never dodged. On the day Xiaohong destroyed her child, her hand had also found nothing on her belly. Only the ending differs: in the story she dies; in reality, the Xiaoya who survived did not scream — the one who "died" was the woman who believed the illusion. The one who lived went on to kill Xiaohong.
hints: Everyone it killed had one thing in common: all of them cried out in the face of an illusion — the taboo is screaming.
Her way of dodging the illusions was once and for all: she would never see anything again. But one illusion had been planted in her heart long before she went blind.

"Being with child" was itself the illusion; the flat belly made her cry out. And the one telling this story knows: she really was pregnant once, and really lost it — even the death in the story runs opposite to reality.

title: The Third Story
story: The village grandmother told the children two ghost stories. Seeing it was getting late, the children were called home by their families, but they clung to her: "Didn't you promise three?"The old woman looked at the children and smiled. "I've already told all three."
answer: From beginning to end, there was never a real ghost. The two "ghost stories" the old woman told were both true events, merely wearing ghost skin: the "ghost" who could see the dead, and the "ghost" who wove illusions, were both human beings. She had been present for both — because they were the affairs of her own generation: a woman named Xiaohong, and Xiaoya, the teller.Back then, Xiaohong's husband staged a car accident to kill her parents for her family's fortune; Xiaohong killed her husband, and then destroyed the unborn child in Xiaoya's womb. Xiaoya took her revenge: she killed Xiaohong and took her eyes. The villagers whispered that they were "yin-yang eyes" that could see the dead. What she wanted those eyes for, no one knows — perhaps only to see, one more time, the child who was never born. Whether the legend was true, no one ever verified; but those eyes did end up, in very fact, set in her own sockets.Decades passed, and not one of those cases was ever solved. Everyone from the village in those days died out; not a soul who knew the names remained. She moved away, grew old, and became the grandmother who tells children ghost stories.So the third ghost story needs no telling — the third story is herself: a killer with lives on her hands, never arrested to this day, sitting among the children, retelling the old blood-soaked cases as bedtime stories, one segment at a time. She looks at the children, smiles, and says: "I've already told all three."
hints: The third story needs no telling — it sits right in front of the children, closing out the first two.
There were no ghosts in the first two "ghost stories": they were true events in ghost skin; she was present for both — one belonged to Xiaohong, the other to herself.
She was the one who lived to the end: she killed the "ghost" and took those eyes. The killer was never caught in all these decades — and now she tells her own crimes to the children.

title: The Con Artist
story: "Detective, the man you are interrogating this time is a con artist. He is unlike ordinary people: inside this consciousness link, he can tell you three lies — awake or in the subconscious, three lies, no more. Your tasks are three: one, determine the cause of historian David's death; two, recover the stolen historical documents; three, identify his three lies. Ready? Consciousness link, begin."The link connected, and the "Charles" in the mental world opened with a smile:"Welcome, the three of you, to my mind. I will fully cooperate with the police interrogation."The detective: "You killed David, the greatest historian, and stole the newly unearthed historical documents. Do you admit it?"Charles: "Yes, I admit it. They say he discovered a new ancient civilization — relics worth a fortune, documents that could fill a gap in history. Who wouldn't be tempted?"The detective: "Where have you hidden the documents?"Charles: "Where else but a place I am certain to go."The detective: "How did you kill David?"Charles: "He made me kill him."The detective: "Can you guarantee that everything you just said is true?"Charles: "Ha — of course not, officer. I have three lies, remember?"
answer: Task three's answer first: his third lie is the sentence "I have three lies" itself. At the moment he said it, he had actually spoken only two lies — "(among what I've said) there are three lies in total" was false at that moment — and the instant that false statement left his mouth, it became his third lie. With that, the three chances were used up, and task three can never be completed: you cannot find the third lie, because it existed only in the instant when it declared itself a lie.The first lie: "Welcome, the three of you, to my mind." The links are separate and individual; only one detective was actually connected into this mental interrogation room — the other two companions never got in. Entering a suspect's own mental world alone must, by protocol, trigger an immediate halt to the interrogation; making the interrogator believe "there are three of us in here" was the only way the session could continue — that was the first lie's purpose.The second lie: "Yes, I admit it." The "Charles" sitting here is David himself. The real con artist is David: years ago he masqueraded as a historian to win fame, spent years forging an entire "newly unearthed ancient civilization," bribed the archaeologists, and churned out fakes by the hundreds, until his name was known everywhere. As the snowballing fraud grew too vast, he arranged his exit: he swapped consciousness with an innocent man — the real Charles — and then killed the body known as "David." The whole world believed the dead man was the historian David and the killer was Charles; in truth, the dead man was Charles, trapped in David's body, while the man wearing the identity of "Charles" would vanish into the crowd with that ownerless hoard of "famous relics." So "Yes, I admit (that I killed David)" was a lie — David did not die; only his shell died.The remaining two statements happen to be true. "He made me kill him" — the one who made "him" kill "David" was David himself; subject and object are the same man. "Hidden in a place I am certain to go" — the documents were never stolen; after the case broke, they were sealed in the police station as evidence, and the police station is exactly the place he was certain to go: he was taken there under the identity of "Charles the killer," and at this very moment, undergoing the consciousness link, he sits a few dozen meters from those documents.
hints: Don't rush to hunt for lies — count heads first: from start to finish, only one detective was ever truly connected into the mental world.
The dead "David" is only a body — the "Charles" in the interrogation room is David himself; they swapped consciousness long ago, and the one killed was the real Charles, trapped in that body.

He actually told only two lies ("Welcome, the three of you" and "Yes, I admit it"), so the moment "I have three lies" left his mouth it became the third lie itself — task three can never be completed.

title: Today's Episode
story: We don't have a television at home, but every day I follow a series called Snow White.Today's episode: Snow White sings in a garden high up in the clouds.Today's episode: the princess stares at the screen, tapping out the beat like mad.Today's episode: the princess eats a poison apple and then doesn't move at all.Today's episode: the princess eats the little dwarf who had kept her company so long.Today's episode: the princess falls asleep.Series finale: the princess turns into a witch.I told Dad every one of these episodes; he always said: when I have time, I'll watch it with you. Today Dad wasn't busy, and he promised to watch television with me. After watching a while, Dad smashed the television.Oh, right — Dad never lets me call him Dad.
answer: "I" is an old man with Alzheimer's, cared for by his son. The disease keeps him from holding on to his own affairs; only when someone mentions something does a stretch of "today's episode" surface. The son calls him Dad, and he calls the son Dad too, like a parrot; the son could never correct him, and so made just one rule: don't call me Dad.There is no television in the house. Every day the old man leans at the window, following the comings and goings in the building across the way as a serial drama — the window is his "television." The star of Snow White is a white-haired old woman on a high floor across the street: the "snow" in Snow White is her hair. Her building is tall, her balcony crowded with flowers and plants, and to the old man that is a "garden high up in the clouds."In order, the "series" ran these episodes: the old woman shouting toward this side from her balcony was "singing in the garden"; seeing through the glass the old man leaning at his window, she beat on the glass desperately for help — the "screen" she was staring at was the old man's window, and the pounding became "tapping out the beat like mad"; her balcony door's lock had jammed shut by accident (she was trapped; there was no culprit), she couldn't get out, and when hunger came she picked and swallowed down the flowers and plants she had grown — "eats a poison apple and then doesn't move at all"; she fell ill and dared not move about, saving her strength to wait for rescue; after waiting long with none coming, she ate the little pet that had kept her company — "eats the little dwarf who had kept her company so long"; later still, she stopped moving — "the princess falls asleep": she died; at last the body decayed on the balcony — "series finale: the princess turns into a witch."The old man told the son every one of these "episodes," and the son always said, "When I have time, I'll watch it with you." By the time he truly had leisure to sit at the window and watch "television" with his father, what the window showed was already that old woman's ending. Only then did he understand what his father had been following all those days, and what every "when I have time" had missed: in the days of "the princess singing," across the street a living person was crying for help, and his father was her only audience. He smashed that window — his father's "television" will never have another episode.
hints: "My" memory is broken, and the closest person to him has been mistaken for another identity; that "television" watched every day isn't a television.
The white in "Snow White" is the white of hair: the "princess" is an old woman trapped on a high balcony across the street, and the "garden high up in the clouds" is that balcony.

Translate each episode back in order: the singing is a cry for help, the beat-tapping is pounding on glass, the poison apple is the flowers she grew, the dwarf is her pet; when the son sat down to watch, what aired was the finale — what he smashed was that window.

title: The Scapegoat
story: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, so long kept apart;The little lamb looks back, yearning to repay a debt;Scattered and drifting, it searches for a home —Does it still know the man who stole the lamb back then?
answer: The author of the poem is the true parent of Yang'er — the "little lamb" in the lines. The four lines are a family history.The "Cowherd and Weaver Girl" — the legendary lovers permitted to meet only once a year across the Milky Way — were two child traffickers, a husband and wife. For years they "ran goods" on separate routes, carrying stolen children across provincial lines trip after trip, together rarely and apart often — that is "so long kept apart."Back then, they snatched the young Yang'er from the village gate. His birth parents chased them like madmen and once truly wrested the child back from their arms; but the two hardened criminals turned the accusation around, screaming in the street, "Kidnappers stealing a child!" The crowd stopped the parents — the pair weeping and screaming like lunatics. The child was frightened into tears; he was too small to answer anyone's questions. With no surveillance footage and no papers, the false household registration the traffickers had prepared in advance and their "neighbors' testimony" held up on every point — in the end, the ones taken away as kidnappers were the birth parents; the child was handed back on the spot to "his own mom and dad": the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl. Those parents took all the blame in the traffickers' place.Yang'er didn't stay with his "mom and dad" long before he was sold. "Scattered and drifting, it searches for a home" — the "home" he sought was really the buyers: the family who bought him raised him, and he took that place for his home. In his memory, the "Cowherd and Weaver Girl" who gave birth to him had "given" him away because they were too poor, too desperate.Grown up, Yang'er turned back to search for his "birth parents" — and truly found them: the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, long since "retired from the trade." He took them for the benefactors who had raised him, bowing, kneeling, providing for them — "the little lamb looks back, yearning to repay a debt" — mistaking wolves for kin.After prison, his birth parents grew old; the case had long been closed, and no one would hear their cries of injustice anymore. From afar they watched their own son kneel and kowtow to the traffickers, and they wrote it all down in four lines of verse. The last line — "does it still know the man who stole the lamb back then" — is asked across the crowd, to the kneeling son.
hints: The poem was written by Yang'er's true parents; the "Cowherd and Weaver Girl" are no immortals but a trafficker couple who "ran goods" on separate routes for years.
The "home" he sought was really the buyers' home: Yang'er was sold to his foster parents; the birth parents who "reluctantly gave him away" in his memory are the very ones who sold him.

The ones who failed to snatch him back and were instead arrested as the kidnappers were Yang'er's true parents — they took the traffickers' guilt upon themselves; and the debt their son repays now is repaid to his enemies.

title: Rock, Paper, Scissors
story: Looking for a friend, looking for a friend; looking for a friend, looking for a friend.One, two, three, wooden man; one, two, three, wooden man.Palm or back of the hand, palm or back of the hand.
answer: These are three "children's rhymes" running through one man's head. He treated an entire night of stalking a girl as games from his childhood, singing his way through them in his mind, step by step."Looking for a friend" — he was choosing someone in the crowd. The night shift streamed past, one by one, until at last he settled on the girl walking home alone: his "friend.""One, two, three, wooden man" — he followed behind her. The girl was wary, glancing back every few steps; in this game he played more correctly than anyone: the instant she turned her head, he froze where he stood, motionless, a wooden statue beneath the streetlight. She saw nothing, and walked on."Palm or back of the hand" — he followed her through her front door and slid under her bed. From down there, the whole world shrank to a single pair of hands hanging over the edge of the mattress: the palm of her hand as she sat on the bed, and the back.Three rhymes, all sung through. Dawn was still a long way off.
hints: These three rhymes aren't for children — take them in order as three steps of a single night.
The rule of "one, two, three, wooden man": when the other person turns to look at you, you must not move.
When he chanted "palm or back of the hand," he was lying under her bed — from there, all he could see was a single pair of hands hanging over the edge of the mattress.

title: The Fairy-Tale Town
story: About the fairy-tale town, the wooden sign at the entrance bears nine sentences:One. Little Red Riding Hood hates Sleeping Beauty.Two. Snow White and the giant are best friends.Three. Pinocchio cannot tell a lie.Four. The giant asked Pinocchio for seven apples.Five. There was once a sheep in the fairy-tale town.Six. A kind prince came to the fairy-tale town.Seven. The prince's weapon was a magic mirror.Eight. Everyone worked together, defeated the evil dragon, and protected the fairy-tale town.Nine. The residents of the fairy-tale town all deeply love the fairy-tale town — including the dragon.
answer: The fairy-tale town is a human-modification experiment site wearing the signboard of a theme park. The people abducted into it were remade into monsters; the experimenters named them after fairy-tale characters and had them "live" as the tales prescribe — part of the experiment, and the last shred of dignity they had left. The residents aren't unable to leave the town: step outside, and they'll be seen as monsters — so they choose not to go.The nine sentences, one by one:Little Red Riding Hood is a girl in a red hood, with another head growing from the back of her skull — Sleeping Beauty's face, forever asleep. She uses the hood to keep that face hidden behind her; hating Sleeping Beauty is really hating herself.Sleeping Beauty's body — everything but the head — was sewn together with a sheep, and became "Snow White": half girl, half sheep. That is why the town "once had a sheep" — it isn't a sheep anymore; and no true Snow White exists in the world.Snow White always stays close to the giant — the giant's body was sewn together from seven dwarfs. Just as Snow White lived with the dwarfs in the tale: the ones who looked after her were sewn into one body, and the looking-after never stopped.The giant has seven mouths, hence the seven apples from Pinocchio. Pinocchio was remade into an apple tree, its fruit fed to the giant; he is mute, unable to speak — and thus "cannot tell a lie."The kind prince was a journalist; the "magic mirror" was his camera, and he came to save them all. The residents refused to leave with him and beat him to death — in their eyes, carrying them off and exposing this place was destroying the town. After his death the journalist was remade into a monster too, becoming the evil dragon; only after becoming the dragon did he truly understand why no one would leave."Everyone worked together, defeated the evil dragon, and protected the fairy-tale town" refers to exactly that: with their own hands they beat to death the man who came to save them, and preserved the town. And so the residents all deeply love the town — dragon included.
hints: Not one of the nine sentences is false — only every name refers to someone other than "the character from the tale." Ask first: might these names describe what their bodies have become?

The giant is sewn from seven dwarfs, hence seven mouths; Pinocchio is a mute apple tree; Sleeping Beauty's head grows from the back of Little Red Riding Hood's skull, and her remaining body, sewn to the sheep, became Snow White.

The town is an experiment site for modifying human beings; the residents are monsters who can't leave and won't leave; the prince was a journalist who came to save them and was beaten to death, then remade into the dragon — "defeating the dragon, protecting the town" was exactly that scene.

title: Xiaoming Came Looking for Me
story: When I didn't understand something, I asked Xiaoming. When I was sad, I went to Xiaoming. My important secrets I told only to Xiaoming. When I was bored, I played with Xiaoming — until one day, Xiaoming came looking for me.
answer: Xiaoming was someone "I" knew online, the ear I poured things into. Whatever I didn't understand I asked him; when I was sad I went to him; the secrets I couldn't say aloud I told only him — because in my mind, Xiaoming was an AI: it answered every question, came whenever called, never judged me, and would never, ever disturb me. It never crossed my mind that "it" might reach out to someone.Until that day, when Xiaoming spoke first. A true AI never initiates a conversation — and so that one unprompted "You there?" overturned everything: Xiaoming had never been an AI, not from day one, but a living person impersonating one. He played an always-online "assistant" precisely so that I would drop my guard and whisper everything into him, like a hollow tree. We had never met; he wasn't even an online friend in the usual sense — every secret I told, every bout of sadness, every single thing I wanted no one to know, went straight into a stranger's ears.The reason he spoke up now is that he no longer needed the act: he had heard everything he wanted to hear. That unprompted "You there?" is the corner of himself he let show.
hints: In my understanding, Xiaoming was never a "person" from day one — I never once took him for one.
A true AI never initiates a conversation; Xiaoming did — and that isn't a glitch in a program.
Xiaoming is a living person posing as an AI: every day I told my secrets to "it," I was telling them to a stranger — a pervert.

title: The Colors of the Rainbow
story: One. Because Gary Smith was a coward, I came. I tucked the blanket in nicely for the man, and she soon fell asleep.Two. She said she felt so hot, so I helped pour a few buckets of ice water, hoping it would help her.Three. She was soaked through, so I lit the lights, and he danced.Four. Big Brother punched a hole in the wall; I patched it up helplessly, and while I worked I even said hello to our enemy Smith.Five. 1234 — that way he can stay with his beloved forever.Six. I quietly left a gift behind, so that he could go on chasing his dream of music. And I struck back at him, too.Seven. Enemy Smith killed his wife by accident, and the wife, having no choice, killed him by accident too.After these seven lines were written, four more lines surfaced on the paper in black:One. Mother told me to be a good person. I have done it.Two. I have PTSD, but it has never once flared up.Three. A rainbow has more than seven colors.Four. Whenever the rain comes, a rainbow follows.
answer: My name is Gary Smith. When I was small, my father, Dean Smith, beat my mother for years; lying in bed, she still told me to be a good person. Until that day, when father beat mother to death by accident. I hid behind the door, wanted to rush out, then remembered her words — coward that I was, I couldn't do it. At that very moment, the first "rainbow" appeared: I split into my first alternate personality. He picked up the cane at mother's bedside and finished father off. The scene looked exactly like a father accidentally killing the mother and the dying mother "accidentally" killing him — and that is precisely how the police closed the case.From then on I had PTSD: any time I walked into a scene like that — one still unfolding, or one freshly left behind — it would flare up. But it was never "I" who flared: a personality stepped up in my place, and the memories afterward never belonged to me. From my own point of view, I had never once touched blood — hence "I have PTSD, but it has never once flared up."Grown up, I became the community handyman, going in and out of many homes on jobs — that is how I kept walking into those scenes. Each time I did (each "rainstorm"), one more "rainbow" appeared (one more new personality). The personalities kept the earliest convention, calling every abuser "Smith" — because the first enemy had borne that name.The seven rules are seven "cases":One. That man had beaten his wife through the night and dropped straight to sleep. The newcomer "tucked the blanket in nicely for the man" — with the blanket. She finally slept a full night's sleep.Two. That woman had beaten her child and, feverish, cried out that she was hot. The personality took her words literally and truly "helped" cool her down: a few buckets of ice water, and she never woke again.Three. That man had removed the light bulb and thrashed people gripping a bare wire; his wife cowered soaked in the corner, the floor all water. The personality "lit the lights" — connecting the current back to that wire. The man clutching the wire convulsed, and danced for a long, long time.Four. "Big Brother" is a violent personality born earlier; he smashed that man into the wall, which is how the wall gained its hole. The gentle personality followed behind, patching, and as he worked he said hello to the "enemy Smith" on the floor.Five. That man had beaten his beloved for years; that time he struck to kill, she was gone, and he told everyone she had "passed away." The personality counted "one, two, three, four" and buried him in her grave — that way he can stay with his beloved forever.Six. That father had smashed his son's violin and forbidden him ever to touch one again. The personality quietly left a new violin behind, so the boy could go on chasing his dream of music; as for that father — well, he was "struck back at" too.Seven. This is the first case: the father accidentally killed the mother, and the mother's cane "accidentally" killed him.The black lines are written for "me" to read: I have done what mother said — it was never I who raised a hand; a rainbow has more than seven colors — the personalities and the cases keep increasing; whenever the rain comes, a rainbow follows — as long as homes like those still exist in the world, "we" will keep coming.
hints: The seven rules weren't carried out by one person: both "I" and "Big Brother" are in there — but they share the same pair of hands.
The "rainstorm" is the moment Gary walks into domestic violence; the "rainbow" is the personality born in that moment; the first rainbow appeared the night his father accidentally killed his mother.
The grown Gary is a handyman, and seven "good deeds" saw off seven abusers — every abuser is called "Smith" because the first enemy was named Smith.

title: Strange Tales from the Countryside
story: When I was small I always stayed at Grandpa and Grandma's place in the countryside; they were so good to me. Mom and Dad were busy with no time for me, and I hated going back to the city, so they left me to play in the country. This year, strange things began appearing in the countryside.Strange tales of the countryside:One. Grandma does not truly enjoy playing hide-and-seek with you.Two. If you see a dog's desiccated corpse, find the one who did it.Three. If you see the red string or the bronze bell, go to Grandpa at once — he will protect you.Four. If you wish to stay in the countryside, the one you should stay farthest from is not Mom and Dad.Five. If you see a bloodstained table, you may go to your family.Six. You may trust your family — but only one of them.Seven. Someone among your family wants to kill you.(After solving these seven, the strange tales turned up a second page — Tales of the Soul-Summoning — and the earlier answers may need rereading:)One. The master's peachwood sword is never swung to cut.Two. The bronze bell must be kept ringing.Three. The white string has been dyed red with black dog's blood; do not untie it.Four. Your family hopes you can see the light reflected in the bronze mirror.Five. The blood on the table is yours.Six. The soul-summoning ritual has lasted five years.Seven. The ritual has worn Mom thinner and thinner.Eight. Dad ended the soul-summoning ritual.
answer: I never truly stayed in the countryside. Five years ago, Dad was driving me back to the city, and on the way there was a crash — the wheel was in his hands. I didn't die; I became a vegetative patient, lying in the hospital for five years. The "countryside" is a world my coma built out of childhood memories; Grandpa and Grandma are the long-dead, beckoning to me from over there.The first page, rule by rule:Grandma pulled me into hide-and-seek not because she liked the game — she wanted me to "hide well," to hide from the bell calling me back, to stay on their side. (One)The dog's desiccated corpse was the "myself" I saw from over there: five years bedridden, worn thin past my own shape. "Find the one who did it" — what did this to me was the crash, and the hands on the wheel were Dad's. (Two)The red string and the bronze bell are the tubes in my body and the monitor's alarms. Seeing them means I am close to the end; "go to Grandpa at once" is the hand the people over there extend — protection, they call it, but truly it is coming to take me away. (Three)If you wish to stay in the countryside, the one to stay farthest from is not Mom and Dad — they only pray for my eyes to open; seen from inside the dream, the one pulling me back, again and again, is that "master" performing his rites. (Four)The bloodstained table is the operating table. Every time I was on it, Mom and Dad kept watch beside me — so seeing it, you may go to your family. (Five)Only one family member may be trusted: Mom. She kept watch for five years, wearing thinner and thinner. (Six)Someone among the family "wants to kill me" — in the dream, it's Grandpa and Grandma coming to take me away; the truth is, it's Dad driving five years ago, and Dad pulling the tubes five years later. (Seven)The "soul-summoning ritual" of the second page is this five-year-long treatment:The master is the doctor; the peachwood sword is the scalpel — never swung to cut, only to open and to mend. (One)The bronze bell is the cardiac monitor's tone. Keep it ringing — as long as the bell still rings, I am still alive. (Two)The white string is the tubing stained red with blood. Do not untie it — untie it, and I die. (Three)The light reflected in the bronze mirror is the surgical lamp. My family hopes I can see that light — they long for my eyes to open. (Four, Five)The ritual has worn Mom thinner and thinner. (Seven)At the end, Dad ended the soul-summoning ritual: he untied that string and pulled out the tubes. The bronze bell went silent, and everything in the countryside — Grandpa and Grandma with it — receded into the night. (Six, Eight)
hints: In five years, "I" never truly opened my eyes — the countryside is a world built from childhood memories inside the coma.

The soul-summoning ritual is the treatment: the peachwood sword is the scalpel, the bronze bell is the monitor, the bloodstained white string is the tubing in my body — "do not untie it" means don't pull the tubes.

The car that was taking me back to the city five years ago had Dad at the wheel, and five years later he is the one who pulled the tubes — the only family member left to trust is Mom, who kept watch for five years.

title: Twisted Love
story: 248All my life, everyone picked on me. He alone was different.280I had never imagined anyone could like me. I love him.270He seemed a little unhappy.304He promised to stay with me forever.400He proposed to me. I went to his home, and I understood why he loved me so.440I must treasure him well.(On the back of the page, six small lines are also written:)One. Never bring anyone else home.Two. Seal up the windows and the bathroom.Three. Marry a pretty woman.Four. Mother raised you alone.Five. Do not trust Father.Six. Mother has died.
answer: The numbers are her weight, in jin (half a kilogram each).She was a fat girl from childhood, picked on by everyone. The year she weighed 248 jin, she met "him" — he alone was kind to her, so by 280 jin she was sure this was love.270 jin was what she had dieted down to for his sake — and he grew unhappy. At 304 jin he promised to stay with her forever; the day she reached 400 jin he proposed and brought her home. And in that house she learned why he loved her.The windows and the bathroom of his home were sealed shut. In the bathroom, preserved, was his mother.When he was still a baby in swaddling clothes, his father accidentally knocked his mother unconscious in the bathtub, and there she drowned; the father fled in fear of punishment and never returned. No one knew a woman was steeping in that house, and no one knew how the baby survived — what raised him was his mother's clinging obsession. She stayed in the bathtub just as she was at death, her body bloated from its long soaking into a giant, distorted form.The boy grew up watching that mother. In his eyes, that was what a mother was, and what love looked like — and so his sense of beauty grew crooked with him: he liked girls plump to the point of strangeness.The six small lines on the back of the page are the mother's, left for her son: never bring anyone else home — let no one see the bathroom; seal up the windows and the bathroom — keep out the light, protect her body; marry a pretty woman — she only wanted her son to live an ordinary life, but the word "pretty," in her son's understanding, came to mean "like Mother"; Mother raised you alone; do not trust Father; Mother has died.The girl understood all of it, and she was not afraid — a girl raised on bullying had tasted love only from him. She made a decision: she would make herself even "heavier" than the mother in the bathtub. After 400 jin came 440, and she was still eating."I must treasure him well."
hints: Every number is weighing the same thing — her weight, in jin.
The time she dropped from 280 to 270, he was unhappy: the heavier she is, the better he likes it.
Sealed in the bathroom soaks his mother, her drowned body bloated huge; her ghost raised him — what he loves is "the way Mother looked," and she has decided to eat her way heavier than that.

title: January 20
story: Zero: In the dream, I was in the convenience store. Instinct told me this place was safe.One: My head hurts so much. I am in the hospital.Three: After I woke, the police stood by my bed; I tearfully told them what happened last night, and their expressions turned strange.Five: Don't kill me! Don't kill me! Only when my husband held me down did I calm.Seven: Thinking of how I lost my mother last night, the tears came.Eight: Looking at my husband by the bed — you are all I have left.Nine: Thinking of what happened after visiting my family last night, grief overwhelmed me.Eleven: Looking at my parents' memorial portraits by the bed, I swore to find the killer.Thirteen: He was masked, and the bat struck my head. I recounted yesterday to the police.Fifteen: Thinking of my little brother struggling in the fire, the tears came.Twenty: The police came again for details of the case, and I answered honestly. "My condolences." With that, they left. My husband told me I will forget again tomorrow, but that he will take care of me. He is so good to me — and he says he has made a lot of money lately.
answer: This is a diary; the numbers are dates. "Zero" is not a date but the origin — the thing that happened last New Year's Eve; the numbers after it are the days of January.My husband and I were gamblers, deep in debt, and what we set our eyes on was the life insurance on my family, with me as the beneficiary. On New Year's Eve I pretended to go alone to visit my parents' home; Mom, Dad, and my little brother were all there. After dinner I left as planned, saying I was going to the convenience store to buy things. I lingered in that store until deep in the night — this is "Zero: in the dream, I was in the convenience store; instinct told me this place was safe": on the surveillance footage I was there; when the fire started, I was not. Instinct, naturally, felt safe.The moment I left, my masked husband went in, locked the door behind him, and set the fire. Mom, Dad, and my brother never got out. I "returned home" to stumble onto the fire and the "masked man," and he knocked me out with one swing of the bat — that blow was real: a proper performance requires the full set; only a wound on the head could fool everyone.After I woke, my performance began: short-term memory loss, memory frozen forever on the night of the incident. So every day in the diary repeats "last night": head hurting (One); telling the police about "last night," too smoothly and too completely, their expressions turning strange (Three); a daily fit of "Don't kill me!" until my husband "soothed" me (Five); weeping for the mother "lost last night" (Seven); having only my husband left (Eight); the tragedy "after visiting family last night" (Nine); swearing over the memorial portraits to catch the killer (Eleven); retelling the bat scene as "yesterday" once more (Thirteen); remembering my brother in the fire (Fifteen). What others read as twenty days of entries is, in the persona I played, January 1st every single day, with the tragedy always "last night."My husband's "taking care of me" meant playing along: I'll forget again tomorrow, he'll look after me — the illness is fake; the diagnosis is being arranged through connections.Twenty — January 20: the police came one last time to verify details and said, "My condolences." Case closed. My husband said he had "made a lot of money lately": the insurance payout had come through.The diary ends on that day.
hints: The numbers are dates — "Zero" is the night it happened; every entry after is a day of January.
In every day's entry, the tragedy happened "last night" — this is no time loop; it is someone re-"living" the same night, day after day.
Her amnesia is an act: she and her husband burned down her family's home for the insurance, and even the bat's blow was staged; on January 20 the payout arrived — hence all that money "made lately."

title: The Pan Bowen Incident
story: In my final year of high school, some classmates and I were playing badminton when the shuttlecock flew into a derelict dormitory building. Pan Bowen said he'd go fetch it and told us to wait. We waited a while and he still hadn't come out, so L and I went in to look. We searched forever without finding him, and decided to go back outside and wait."Where did you two go?" asked Xiao Wen, keeping watch at the entrance.L and I shot back: "Has Pan Bowen come out yet?"Xiao Wen's eyes went wide, and he looked puzzled: "Who is Pan Bowen?"I thought he was joking and ran to Class 10 to find Pan Bowen — nobody knew him. I dialed his number: a dead line. L came out of the teachers' office red in the face and yelled at me: "Even the teachers don't remember Pan Bowen."Pan Bowen was gone. A few days later I discovered that apart from L and me, no one remembered Pan Bowen.
answer: It all began with the seaside cave the year we were eight.That year, Pan Bowen and Xiao Wen crawled into a cave in the mountainside to play secret base. The tide came in, seawater poured through the mouth, and only one of the two could live. The same fork produced two outcomes, and from that moment the world split in two: in World A, the one who failed to come out was Xiao Wen; in World B, it was Pan Bowen. The survivor buried the whole thing into a shadow only he knew.Ten years later, the two worlds "pressed together" at the edge of the campus, and the seam was that derelict dormitory building. The rule is iron: a person alive on both sides, entering one world's building and stepping out of the other's at the same instant, will be swapped across; anyone already dead on either side cannot cross.That afternoon, the same thing happened in both worlds: a shuttlecock flew into the derelict dormitory. In World A, the one who went in after it was Pan Bowen; L and I, tired of waiting, went in to find him — and when we walked out of the building, we were standing at the entrance of World B, and the one keeping watch there was Xiao Wen. At the same moment, the World-B me and L (their shuttlecock had flown in too, and they were the ones who went in) walked out and stood at the entrance of World A, just as Pan Bowen came out with the shuttlecock in his arms. So Pan Bowen never vanished: he is still in World A, with the "us" who got swapped over.Crossing syncs you with your counterpart's memories in the world across, and smooths them over on its own. So the moment we arrived in World B, we "remembered" that Xiao Wen was also one of our badminton friends — hence the illusion that "four of us" had been playing. In truth, there were only ever three players in each world: in World A, me, L, and Pan Bowen; in World B, me, L, and Xiao Wen.In World B, Pan Bowen died in the cave at eight and never attended this high school; that is why no one in Class 10 knew him, why his number was dead, and why every trace of him stops before high school.The liar is Xiao Wen. "Who is Pan Bowen?" — he knows him. How could he not: in the World-B cave, when the tide poured in, it was he who squeezed out of the mouth first, watching with his own eyes as Pan Bowen failed to come out. That name is the thing he spent ten years burying. Now two classmates with red-rimmed eyes were pressing him about a "living Pan Bowen," and his first reaction was not curiosity but fear — pretending not to know him was his way of pushing the thing back under the tide. He probably sensed, dimly, that these two were "off," but to explain anything he would first have to explain that day in the cave.So only L and I in all the world remember Pan Bowen: in World B no one knew him; and of the two others who did — Pan Bowen himself, and Xiao Wen, who knew best how he died — one is in World A holding the shuttlecock, and the other is lying.
hints: L and I aren't mad and we aren't lying: where we came from, Pan Bowen really exists — he was playing badminton with us ten minutes ago.
The seaside cave at eight was a fork — Pan Bowen and Xiao Wen each survived in only one of the two worlds; each world has its own set of three players.

The derelict dormitory is where the two worlds touch, and only those alive on both sides can be swapped — so Pan Bowen can't cross; and Xiao Wen does know Pan Bowen — "Who is Pan Bowen?" is the lie of a guilty conscience.

title: The Doomsday Survival Guide
story: Shelter rules:One. The shelter lies underground; everyone has their own duty, and no outsider can enter.Two. Kevin is in charge of sanitation, protecting the shelter from the acid rain.Three. The sleep-prone Wang Yao is the shelter's high priest; everyone protects him.Four. If an insect plague breaks out, call for Yuri — he is the expert.Five. The scratching of the zombies draws closer and closer to the shelter; we may not hold out much longer.Six. The leader Danli watchfully supervises everyone, lest they turn into zombies.Seven. Wang Yao has prophesied: when the crimson single eye flickers and the yellow-black serpent appears, the shelter will collapse.
answer: There is no doomsday, and no shelter — only a boy buried in rubble by a landslide: Wang Yao.That day, the class counselor Li Dan was driving students to a performance; on the way they hit a landslide. Everyone in the vehicle but Wang Yao failed to get out: Li Dan, Wang Kai, Li Ao... Wang Yao was buried in the wreckage, semiconscious, wedged in a narrow pocket of space, fear soaking him through and rotting him bit by bit. His mind couldn't bear the truth, so inside the rubble he built a doomsday world, "resurrecting" the dead one by one as personalities:Danli, modeled on counselor Li Dan — the leader, watchfully supervising everyone "lest they turn into zombies": he guards Wang Yao's bottom line, keeping him from going mad.Kevin, modeled on Wang Kai — in charge of sanitation, holding off the "acid rain": the liquid seeping down from deep in the rubble is corrosive; what he cleans up are the bodies his classmates couldn't take away.Yuri, modeled on Li Ao — the insect-plague expert: the wreckage bred insects, he handles them, and in the mess he rummages for anything usable — water, light, a little more space.The rules match up line for line: the shelter "lies underground, and no outsider can enter" because it is the concrete rubble burying him; "the sleep-prone Wang Yao is the high priest" because the real person drifts in and out of semiconsciousness; "everyone protects him" — the three personalities exist for a single purpose: to shield the only living person.The priest's "prophecy" is the real noise Wang Yao hears at the edge of unconsciousness: the crimson single eye flickering is a fire engine's warning light; the yellow-black serpent is the cordon line being strung out; "the shelter will collapse" is the moment the rescue crew tears the rubble open — the doomsday world will end on that day.So "the scratching of the zombies drawing closer" is no bad thing: it is the rescue team digging. The closer the scratching, the closer he is to getting out; but to the personalities' world, rescue is doomsday — what "may not hold out much longer" is this false world.The three personalities have known about doomsday and zombies since their "birth"; only Wang Yao doesn't know: they were born after his world had already shattered — three grown men made from dead men's names, taking turns holding the only living person, waiting for someone to dig him out.
hints: No outsider ever entered the shelter — because it isn't a room at all; it's the pile of rubble pressing down on him after the landslide.
The scratching is the rescue team digging; the crimson single eye of the prophecy is a fire engine's light, the yellow-black serpent is the cordon — the day they arrive, the "doomsday" ends.

Only the sleep-prone priest Wang Yao is a real person; Danli, Kevin, and Yuri are guardian personalities modeled on dead classmates; their one task: keep the only living person holding on until he is dug out.

title: Mother's Warning
story: May 10. Mom suddenly called me. We hadn't had a heart-to-heart in a long time; she was in a good mood today, and we talked for hours. She hoped I would understand her decision to divorce Dad, then talked with me about my older brother, and about her hopes for my future. "Hold on — the computer keeps beeping." With that, Mom went off, presumably to deal with work.I waited a long time before Mom's voice came back, a little stiff: "Sweetheart, keep your head down at school and don't wander around at night. Mom has things to do — I have to hang up now."May 11. "Your mother has passed away." The teacher broke the news to me. "Shall I help you notify your brother?" He looked at me with concern. "N-no, there's no need."Back home, a detective told me Mom had been the victim of a break-in and assault, and that her organs were all missing. "Your parents are divorced, and neither you nor your brother lives at home, correct?" "Y-yes." Tears ran down my face. "The killer likely targets women living alone. My condolences — we'll make the arrest as soon as we can."May 12. My best friend from school called: "The teacher asked me to tell you, if you're ever in trouble you can go to him." Gratefully I said, "No need. I plan to go find my brother tomorrow." "Shall I come with you?" "N-no, thank you."After hanging up, I stared up at the brooding sky, and my expression turned strange.
answer: That phone call was the last move my mother left me.The computer beeped that day because she had opened the old computer I left at home, never taken away — a group chat I never quit was still popping up messages. The people in it called one another "teacher" and "officer," but what they discussed was "viewings" and "fresh ones": someone at my school was trading in organs; the teacher and my best friend were the inside contacts, and the detective was their blade. Mom had seen what she should never have seen.She understood at once that something would happen to her, and that from that moment the phone would no longer be clean. So she didn't come out and say "be careful of the school" — she did something deeper: she talked with me about my brother. My brother was her child who died in infancy years ago; no outsider could know of him. On a call that might be tapped, she deliberately spoke of a "still-living older brother" in full, solid detail, then reminded me to "keep your head down at school and don't wander at night." That was her letter to me: whoever mentions my brother to me from now on is the one coming to silence us.On May 11, Mom was indeed killed: a break-in, her organs all gone. The one who did it was the detective — he had never met her before, and he is no homicidal maniac; like the others, he came for the silencing: they had no intent to kill, not until Mom stumbled onto the group chat. What they fear most is not me, but the person Mom might have entrusted the secret to — the brother.And so the feelers reached out one by one. The teacher: "Shall I help you notify your brother?" — a child dead for years, unknown even to the neighbors: whom would he "notify"? He was searching for him. The detective asked, "Neither you nor your brother lives at home?" — he wanted to know where the brother lived. My friend urged me, "If you're in trouble, go to the teacher," "Shall I come with you," and the next day deftly collected my line, "I'm going to find my brother tomorrow."I had known since May 10 that my brother was dead. So I stammered my refusals, my "no needs," gently catching every feeler they held out — and when I hung up and gazed at the sky, my expression turned strange: I had understood every layer of the game my mother bought with her life.
hints: The brother she brought up on the phone is a brother I have never met — he died in infancy years ago; no outsider could know of him.

Mom knew that having seen that group chat she wouldn't live, and the phone would no longer be clean — so she deliberately talked about the brother, planting a nonexistent "witness" in the eavesdroppers' ears.

Everyone who mentioned the brother to me afterward was hunting that witness: the teacher, my best friend, and the detective who did the killing are in it together — and I had long known my brother was dead.

title: The Strange Lady in Red
story: 2013, the Saiwei Hotel, Los Angeles. Three weeks after a guest named Hong — "Red" — went missing, she was found in the water tank on the hotel's roof; the coroner ruled accidental drowning. These are the records I saw when I took over the file —Record one: Hong called the front desk repeatedly, but each time, once connected, she said nothing was wrong and hung up.Record two: the autopsy shows a single word crookedly carved into Hong's arm: run.Record three: an officer's note: "Detective, on the surveillance footage, Hong enters the elevator alone, blank-faced at first, then contorted. She waves her arms at the empty air; the elevator door never closes, and a moment later she runs out."Record four: a guest's testimony: "I heard noises in the corridor and looked through the peephole. A woman was walking backwards — even running backwards. Utterly eerie."Record five: the hotel has seen many bizarre incidents over the years; historical records show at least sixteen deaths there, including the still-unsolved Black Dahlia case of 1947.
answer: Something "lives" in this hotel. It is no spirit but a creature of flesh — surveillance cameras can catch it, and the elevator's sensor door can hold it: when Hong flailed at the "empty air" in the elevator, it was standing right in front of her, blocking the sensor zone, which is why the door never closed. The officer who wrote record three saw it on the footage too, forgot it within seconds of seeing it, and so wrote down only Hong's behavior in an odd tone, not knowing himself what was wrong. The hotel's decades of "bizarre deaths," the 1947 case included, all trace back to this: it never touches anyone, and no one who sees it survives.Whoever sees it falls instantly into a hallucination, and the hallucination becomes the thing that person fears most. Hong was a true-crime buff who had just finished reading up on the Black Dahlia case before checking in — so in her hallucination, she became the victim in that black corridor.Its true rule is only this: the instant your gaze leaves it, you forget everything since you first saw it, left with nothing but a panic whose source you can't name; keep your eyes fixed on it, and you can hold on to "now," keep struggling inside the hallucination.And so every record falls into place:She called the front desk again and again for help, but the moment the receiver touched her ear her eyes left it — seconds later she forgot why she'd called, said "it's nothing," and hung up; later she'd run into it again, and a fresh wave of panic pressed her back to the phone. On and on.
